Title: Digital and AI-enabled support for HACCP-based dairy food safety management: Functions, evidence, and implementation boundaries
Abstract: Dairy food-safety management spans primary production, purchasing, processing, packaging, storage, transport, and distribution. Biological, chemical, physical, and allergenic hazards vary with the product and process. Digital and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tools can extend how data are collected, interpreted, and connected to Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) and food safety management system (FSMS) activities. Their value depends on the function supported and the evidence for the intended use. This narrative, function-oriented review examines sensors, Internet of Things systems, traceability platforms, machine learning, predictive microbiology, rapid detection, knowledge graphs, retrieval-augmented generation, and large language models. The comparison covers five functions: hazard analysis and risk prioritization; monitoring and deviation detection; verification and the screening–confirmatory interface; documentation, traceability, and plan review; and decision support at the corrective-action interface. The analytical framework records dairy relevance, deployment stage, and validation scope. It also distinguishes analytical outputs and alerts from verified deviations, confirmatory evidence, and site-specific actions. The reviewed tools are best established for data capture, monitoring, and verification inputs. Evidence is thinner for hazard prioritization, digital plan review, and AI-assisted decision support. Food-safety use requires dairy product and process context, fit-for-purpose evidence, approved procedures, auditable records, and review by responsible personnel. Important constraints include interoperability, real-world dairy validation, model and sensor lifecycle control, organizational capacity, and food-safety culture. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Konjac glucomannan-modified ferrous fumarate emulsions with interpenetrating polymer networks: Physicochemical stability, microstructure, and bioaccessibility
Abstract: Ferrous fumarate (FF), a iron-rich organic fortificant, exhibits high oxidation stability; however, its poor solubility and severe sedimentation in neutral media limit bioaccessibility. This study developed an FF-loaded emulsion based on an interpenetrating polymer network (IPN) formed by whey protein concentrate (WPC), xanthan gum (XG), and konjac glucomannan (KGM). It investigated the physicochemical stability, microstructure, intermolecular interactions and iron bioaccessibility of the emulsions at different KGM concentrations. Increasing the KGM concentration reduced the emulsion particle size from 946.07 to 346.70 nm and raised the absolute zeta potential from 50.34 ± 1.17 mV to 53.34 ± 0.89 mV, thereby improving physical stability. The emulsions showed enhanced apparent viscosity with shear-thinning behavior and dominant elastic responses within the linear viscoelastic region. Microstructural analysis revealed that KGM incorporation converted a layered structure into a robust IPN architecture, confining FF near the oil–water interface and suppressing droplet aggregation. Spectroscopic results indicated strengthened intermolecular hydrogen bonding and increased β-sheet content. The incorporation of KGM effectively maintained the Fe2+ retention rate (∼95%) during thermal processing. The IPN emulsion achieved an iron bioaccessibility of 73.18%, representing an 11.86-fold increase over free FF. This study demonstrates the efficacy of IPN-structured emulsions in delivering poorly soluble active ingredients, providing a promising strategy for developing iron-fortified foods. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Analysis on dynamics and tipping points for a stochastic SIM model involving media influence

Abstract: In this paper, a stochastic SIM epidemic model involving media influences is proposed and the dynamical behavior of its solutions and the problem of tipping points are investigated. Title: Data-Driven Risk Allocation and Incentive-Compatible Payment Schemes in Construction Contracts: Integrating Comparative Standard Forms, Public Works Disputes, and Principal-Agent Modeling
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Construction projects worldwide suffer from misaligned risk allocation, poorly chosen payment schemes, and opaque claims and dispute processes, leading to chronic cost overruns and litigation. Building on comparative analyses of widely used international and national standard forms of contract, empirical public works dispute case studies, and principal-agent theory of payment methods, this research develops a data-driven framework for designing incentive-compatible construction contracts. First, we code and compare more than 60 distinct risk events and 40 claims and dispute procedures across several representative standard contract regimes for large infrastructure projects. Second, we construct a dataset of approximately 80 real dispute or major change-order cases (including highway, bridge, and building projects) and classify them by triggering risk, procurement mode, and payment scheme. Third, we calibrate a structural principal-agent model of contractor effort, cost uncertainty, and risk aversion to this dataset, comparing fixed-price, unit-price, cost-plus, and target-price contracts. The calibrated model is then used to simulate how alternative combinations of risk allocation clauses and payment mechanisms affect expected owner cost, contractor risk exposure, and the probability of disputes. Simulation results are used to quantify potential performance gains from better-aligned contract design; illustrative scenarios target a 15%-25% reduction in expected total project cost, a 30%-40% reduction in formal disputes, and a 40% reduction in claims processing time when more balanced risk-sharing clauses and incentive-compatible payment schemes are adopted. The research is useful as a guideline for international contractors and public agencies involved in mega infrastructure projects. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Bridging the privacy gap: Developers’ practices and the missing role of privacy engineers
Abstract: Context: Privacy has become a first order concern in software engineering, yet organizations still struggle to translate legal mandates into actionable engineering practices. Goal: This study investigates how Brazilian software practitioners perceive and operationalize privacy standards/practices. Methods: We conduct a conceptual replication of prior work via survey (N = 31). The instrument maps privacy-related perceptions/practices, use of standards/frameworks/techniques, organizational responsibility allocation, perceived challenges, and improvement opportunities. Results: Practitioners report distinguishing privacy from security, but formalization is limited. Although 60.7% report considering privacy across the software development, half do not use privacy-focused methods, and a substantial portion (46.4%) report being unaware of such approaches. Practices skew toward classic security controls (e.g., access control, 85.7%) rather than dedicated privacy engineering artifacts. The Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD) is the dominant compliance driver (82.1%), with low uptake of ISO 27701/NIST. Key barriers include unclear legal guidance (53.6%), insufficient training (42.9%), and late integration of privacy (39.3%). Automation remains incipient (14.3% fully automated; 42.9% manual). Organizational support is uneven (39.3% sufficient; 39.3% partial; 21.4% insufficient). Applying the Spearman correlation test revealed strong relationships (ρ up to 0.63) between experience, training, and integration practices, indicating that professional maturity and capacity building are strongly associated with privacy-by-design adoption. Conclusion: Results indicate a persistent gap between awareness and effective governance. We recommend (i) targeted training and curricular inclusion, (ii) clearer role/accountability assignments, and (iii) investment in tooling/automation to operationalize privacy-by-design. These actions can help shift privacy from reactive compliance to a sustained dimension in Brazilian organizations. Title: Dynamic Diffusion of Legal Compliance and Ethical Conduct among Construction Project Owners: An Epidemiological Modeling Approach
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Construction industries worldwide face persistent challenges of ethical misconduct, contractual violations, and regulatory noncompliance, imposing substantial legal liabilities and undermining sustainable development. Although legal frameworks exist to govern owner behavior, their dynamic enforcement effects and interactions with market-driven compliance mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study pioneers the application of epidemiological modeling to legal compliance and ethical behavior diffusion among construction project owners. An extended susceptible-exposed-infected-removed (SEIR) model was developed to analyze how statutory enforcement and voluntary market adoption jointly drive compliance diffusion, simulated via MATLAB. Three findings emerged: (1) the diffusion of ethical behavior exhibits S-shaped evolution with global asymptotic stability, providing a predictable basis for legal intervention design; (2) resistance parameters demonstrate positional asymmetry, revealing where legal safeguards are most needed; and (3) government-mandated enforcement and voluntary adoption generate superlinear synergistic effects, suggesting compliance frameworks achieve maximum efficacy when paired with market incentives. Title: How to deal with AI technology anxiety and its negative consequences? The role of strengths-based leadership
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into hospitality operations, employees’ AI technology anxiety has emerged as a salient managerial concern. Drawing on social information processing theory, this study examines the effect of strengths-based leadership on AI technology anxiety and the subsequent influence of this anxiety on employees’ social loafing behavior. Across a time-lagged field study and an experiment, the findings reveal the following key results. First, strengths-based leadership effectively alleviated hospitality employees’ AI technology anxiety, thereby reducing their social loafing behavior. Title: Plugging in feedback in the software development pipeline: Insights from DevOps practitioners
Abstract: In the rapidly evolving domain of software development, the integration and management of feedback within the development pipeline play a pivotal role in ensuring product quality and process efficiency. This paper explores the nuances of feedback mechanisms in contemporary software development practices, with a particular focus on DevOps and Continuous Integration (CI)/Continuous Deployment (CD) practices. Drawing insights from qualitative interviews with 19 experienced DevOps practitioners in various countries, the study delves into how teams incorporate feedback at different stages of the development pipeline. The findings highlight the use of modern tools and frameworks that facilitate automated feedback. The paper also introduces a comprehensive checklist designed to assess the health and effectiveness of feedback mechanisms. Through its findings, the study underscores the importance of balancing manual and automated feedback processes and proposes strategies to enhance the automation of feedback for improved responsiveness and decision-making in software development cycles. Title: Explainable spatiotemporal modeling in crime analytics: Robbery prediction via graph neural networks
Abstract: Urban crime prediction is a critical task for ensuring public safety, yet it faces challenges related to model accuracy and transparency. While crime is an inherently temporal phenomenon, its embedding within the city’s structure suggests that integrating spatiotemporal dependencies via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can improve model robustness, particularly in data-sparse environments. Traditional grid-based methods often fail to capture the complex network topology of cities, while the “black-box” nature of advanced models raises ethical concerns for predictive policing. This study proposes an explainable spatiotemporal framework to predict robbery risk by uniquely integrating three elements: (1) fine-grained, citizen-sensed data from a public safety application in Santiago, Chile; (2) a tailored graph neural network to learn how to represent the urban environment as a graph; and (3) an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) component using Integrated Gradients to ensure transparency. We evaluate the model’s performance against traditional classifiers across various prediction horizons (1, 3, and 7 days) and spatial granularities. The results show that the tailored architecture dramatically improves predictive accuracy (average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve -AUC-  ≈  0.85) compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, the XAI analysis provides novel empirical evidence that citizen reports of “suspicious activity” are highly significant predictors of future burglaries, often more so than prior robbery incidents themselves. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Quantifying Regulatory Bottlenecks in South Korea’s Clinical Trial Approval Process Through an Analytic Hierarchy Process Framework
Abstract: Purpose: Drug lag is a critical issue limiting South Korea’s pharmaceutical competitiveness and patient access, and it has been linked to delays in the Investigational New Drug (IND) review process. This study aimed to identify key barriers affecting IND review efficiency in South Korea by analyzing real-world industry experience and to propose concrete strategic actions to mitigate drug lag. Methods: We employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. First, we used grounded theory to identify problematic factors within the IND process through semi-structured interviews. We then applied the Analytic Hierarchy Process to evaluate these factors, followed by a quadrant analysis of importance and urgency to identify top-priority tasks. Results: Three core categories (rationality and patient-centricity, professional review, and operational efficiency), were identified as key domains for enhancing IND efficiency. Rationality and patient-centricity emerged as the most important and urgent criterion, followed closely by professional review. Within rationality and patient-centricity, four sub-criteria placed in the first quadrant (highly important and highly urgent): integration of patient needs into evaluation, global regulatory harmonization, acceptance of scientific evidence for new modalities, and adoption of overseas regulatory standards. Two sub-criteria within professional review (expert team review and standardized review guidelines) were also pinpointed in the first quadrant. Although operational efficiency ranked lowest, simplified Korean translation requirements stood out as the most critical factor within this category. Conclusion: Transitioning from focusing on procedural speed toward embracing regulatory flexibility to enhance scientific rationality and patient access is a viable pathway for mitigating drug lag in South Korea. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Closing the carbon loop: Recycled CO2 utilization in enhanced lacustrine shale oil recovery
Abstract: The application of CO2-enhanced oil recovery (EOR) in the highly heterogeneous lacustrine shales is challenged by severe gas channeling, poor sweep efficiency, and low carbon utilization performance by the conventional operation mode. To address the issues, this study proposes a Closed-Loop CO2 Recycling (CLCR) technology, in which the produced gas (including CO2 and light hydrocarbons) is captured, compressed, and reinjected to offset the total CO2 consumption amount. A compositional cross-scale numerical simulation model is developed that implicitly couples flow in the shale matrix, bedding fractures, and hydraulic fractures, including pressure-driven and diffusion-controlled mass transfer among the continua. The model is validated against field well history data from the Gulong shale, the most typical lacustrine shale in China, with a matching accuracy over 85 %. Based on a 20-year simulation, four metrics are evaluated including oil replacement ratio (ORR), CO2 sequestration efficiency (CSE), oil production multiplier (OPM), and net present value (NPV) for CLCR. The results show that an injection rate of 50 t/d in a 1650 m horizontal well gives the highest OPM of 2.39, and early CO2 injection without prior depletion is confirmed essential to formation pressure preservation and gas breakthrough delay. The reinjection start timing of the 5 % CO2 mole fraction in produced gas achieves the highest ORR of 0.152 t oil/t CO2 and a competitive OPM of 2.612. Early recycling preserves light hydrocarbons in the reinjected gas, which improves oil‑gas compatibility, strengthens the displacement efficiency, and enhances oil mobilization. By recycling, the CSE can be increased from 58 % to nearly 100 % which means most of the injected CO2 can be sequestrated in the shale formation. Single-well NPV by CLCR is 60.8 % higher than the conventional mode. CLCR enables substantially enhanced CO2 sequestration while increasing oil production performance, offering a viable pathway toward carbon–neutral shale oil development. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Collaborating with GenAI: A blessing or a curse for creativity?
Abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) are increasingly shifting creative work from individual creation toward human–AI collaboration. Drawing on evidence from various creative domains, such as writing, design, and product ideation, this review highlights the gains and constraints of collaborating with GenAI, distinguishing between outcome-related and process-related effects. While GenAI can increase the number of ideas, enhance idea quality, accelerate idea generation, and reduce cognitive load, it may also lead to idea homogenization, diminished perceptions of authenticity and ownership, reduced independent creative engagement, and weakened team collaboration. To clarify when GenAI supports rather than hinders creativity, this review identifies four key moderating factors: 1) when GenAI is used (i.e., timing of GenAI involvement), 2) how it is used (i.e., interaction design), 3) what it is used for (i.e., task characteristics), and 4) by whom it is used (i.e., user expertise). The findings highlight the need for future research on how to better structure human–AI collaboration to support both creative performance and the development of human creative capabilities. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Job shop scheduling problem with competing agents

Abstract: In this paper, we study the two-machine job shop scheduling problem with two competing agents. The goal is to minimize a given objective function for one agent, subject to a given upper bound of another objective function associated with the second agent. We prove the NP-hardness of this problem with respect to various criteria and settings. Title: Negotiation impasses as meaningful outcomes: How AI is changing the cost structure of walking away
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often expected to improve negotiation by strengthening information processing and analytical consistency. We argue that its effects on impasses are more selective. Extending the impasse cause, type, and resolution (ICTR) model, we distinguish two pathways. The first pathway is analytical augmentation: AI can reduce unwanted impasses caused by misunderstanding, poor option generation, and coordination failure. The second pathway runs through behavioral flexibility: Humans sometimes reach mutually acceptable agreements through aspiration adjustment, face-saving, and relational repair. Systems configured to apply stable decision thresholds and optimize focal-party outcomes without relational objectives reduce this flexibility and can thereby increase forced impasses. Which pathway dominates depends on AI's role as advisor or counterpart; its objective, training, and prompt; and whether agreement primarily requires analytical problem solving or interpersonal flexibility. These predictions concern system behavior, not whether AI experiences fatigue or social pressure: systems can be designed to respond to relational cues without experiencing them. Wanted impasses depend on both parties' underlying preferences, which AI does not change; AI instead helps negotiators recognize incompatibility sooner and justify walking away more openly. AI therefore changes the composition and meaning of impasses rather than uniformly increasing or decreasing agreement. Remaining impasses may reveal genuine incompatibility, but they may also reflect misspecified objectives or failures to encode principals' relational and economic costs. © 2026 The Authors

Title: When AI wears a face: How AI appearance shapes intentionality attributions in service success and failure
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Customer-facing AI agents are becoming frontline service interfaces, yet firms still face a consequential design question: should these agents look human-like or robot-like? This research examines how AI agent appearance shapes consumers' intentionality attributions in AI-mediated service encounters and how these inferences translate into satisfaction and future AI use intention. Drawing on attribution theory and anthropomorphism research, we propose that human-like and robot-like appearances do not have uniformly positive or negative effects; rather, their effects depend on consumers’ evaluations of service outcomes and their familiarity with AI. A 2 (AI agent appearance: human-like vs. robot-like) × 2 (service outcome: success vs. failure) between-subjects experiment was conducted with 350 U.S. participants in an airline customer-service chatbot context. Results reveal a reversal across outcome evaluations. When consumers experienced service success, robot-like AI elicited higher perceived intentionality than human-like AI, particularly among those with lower AI familiarity. When consumers experienced service failure, human-like AI elicited higher perceived intentionality than robot-like AI, although this effect weakened and reversed among consumers with higher AI familiarity. Perceived intentionality, in turn, increased satisfaction and future AI use intention, supporting a moderated mediation process. These findings reframe AI appearance as an attributional cue rather than a simple humanization strategy and demonstrate that consumers interpret the same AI appearance differently depending on how they evaluate the service encounter. Managerially, the results suggest that firms should not assume that increasing human likeness will universally improve customer responses. Instead, marketers should consider how different customer segments, particularly those varying in AI familiarity, are likely to interpret and respond to AI appearance cues across diverse service experiences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Prediction-correction dynamical systems for time-varying minimax problems with applications
Source title: Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
Abstract: This paper proposes three classes of prediction-correction dynamical systems (PCDSs) for solving a time-varying minimax problem (TV-MMP) under mild conditions. We propose an asymptotically convergent PCDS for TV-MMP and prove, via Lyapunov analysis, that its solutions converge asymptotically to the saddle point trajectory of TV-MMP with a vanishing tracking error. We also design a fixed time convergent PCDS for TV-MMP by replacing the linear correction term with the nonlinear one, and show its solutions converge to the saddle point trajectory of TV-MMP within fixed time. Moreover, we develop a predefined time convergent PCDS for TV-MMP by adding a scaling factor, and prove its solutions converge to the saddle point trajectory of TV-MMP within predefined time. In addition, we apply the above results to time-varying linear equality constrained optimization problems. Finally, we give several numerical examples to evaluate the efficacy of the proposed methods. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Towards a datafication framework for higher education institutions student success: A systematic review
Abstract: Customer success is key to customer retention. Seemingly, this is equally true in the higher education space, as students are customers of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) and, therefore, the primary reason for HEIs' existence. In view of this, it is important to understand and improve student success, which is dependent on different data indicators. Being guided by student success data indicators in HEI administration is necessary as it’s beneficial to both HEIs and their students, as through it, students can complete their qualification on time, and HEIs generate revenue. In the South African context, with its high unemployment rate and high dropout rates, understanding HEI student success is vital. However, HEIs are accustomed to collecting data rather than utilizing it for transformational activities, there has been an increase in research/publications on student success datafication frameworks in higher education in South Africa. However, these studies in isolation do not give the complete picture. This paper aims to systematically review the South African-based HEI student success data-related frameworks, including their underlying principles, trends, challenges, gaps, and future opportunities for improvement. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses method was used. Based on a clearly outlined search strategy, 508 publication abstracts were considered for review. Of these abstracts, 40 were selected for further review based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and thereafter, 16 publications were included in the final review. The systematic review findings indicated that mostly data point indicators exist as compared to datafication frameworks. Furthermore, limited studies have been conducted on private higher education institutions in South Africa. Additionally, public sector studies have focused on first-year students; therefore, no segmentation. The implication of this study is that it sets the tone for future work within datafication, student success, and higher education, potentially enabling HEIs to approach transformational data. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: When and why are negotiators overly pessimistic? The psychology of under-trust innegotiation
Abstract: Research on negotiation has devoted considerable attention to the risks of misplaced trust, particularly the possibility that negotiators may be exploited by deceptive counterparts. Less attention has been given to the opposite form of trust miscalibration: under-trust, and particularly, unwarranted pessimism regarding counterparts' honesty. This review focuses on such undue distrust and proposes a misperceived motivations account to explain its emergence. According to this account, negotiators' excessive distrust stems from an asymmetry between the motives that negotiators attribute to their counterparts and the motives that actually guide those counterparts’ behavior. When deciding whether to behave honestly, negotiators are driven not only by self-interest but also by concerns about moral self-image and anticipated moral emotions, which constrain dishonesty. However, when deciding whether counterparts are honest, negotiators assume that their counterparts are primarily motivated by self-interest and fail to foresee the constraining moral-identity concerns. We integrate evidence from the literature on negotiation, trust, and moral psychology to explain why pessimism is especially likely to emerge and persist in competitive bargaining contexts, highlight circumstances that may attenuate or amplify it, and identify implications for theory and research, alongside practical inferences for fostering truthful disclosure and credible honesty in negotiation. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Creative or uncreative partner: Comparing humans and AI in collaborative creative tasks
Abstract: Creativity is fundamentally a collaborative process. As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated into creative work, understanding how it reshapes collaboration becomes critical. This pre-registered study directly compares human-human and human-AI collaboration dynamics across two creative tasks: the Alternate Uses Task (AUT) and creative short story writing. Participants were randomly assigned to pairs in either human-human (N = 68 pairs) or human-AI (GPT-4o; N = 72 pairs) conditions, with partners alternating turns as first responders to examine how initiation order shapes the creative process. Our findings reveal that the apparent “AI advantage” in creative collaboration is illusory, driven primarily by increased AI verbosity rather than enhanced creativity. Critically, collaboration with AI partners negatively impacted humans' own creative responses compared to human-human partnerships, with human-AI collaboration failing to enhance idea originality or diversity relative to human-human collaboration. Human partners demonstrated higher collaborative creativity that strengthened over time, indicating that current generative AI systems, while producing more verbose outputs, do not replicate the collective creativity characteristic of human-human collaboration. These results challenge assumptions about AI's creative potential, with direct implications for AI system design and collaborative creative practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Do users trade performance for eco-visibility? Digital pollution awareness and stated preferences for social media platform configurations
Abstract: Digital platforms face growing pressure to demonstrate environmental responsibility, yet users’ preferences for eco-visible features remain underexplored relative to functional attributes. Using a full-factorial rating-based within-subject conjoint survey with a UK sample (N = 345) recruited to match national census distributions of age, sex, and ethnicity, combined with hierarchical linear modelling, this study decomposes willingness to use social media platforms across four attributes: media quality, loading speed, eco-visibility, and advertising frequency. Results show that technical attributes — media quality (relative importance = 34.9%) and loading speed (34.5%) — jointly dominate eco-visibility (8.1%), revealing a persistent performance-over-sustainability hierarchy in elicited trade-off preferences. A full 4 × 4 cross-level moderation analysis incorporating all 16 attribute-by-moderator interactions with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction identifies advertising receptivity — rather than green self-identity or environmental awareness — as the strongest individual-difference moderator, showing a dual pattern: it simultaneously attenuates the reduced-ads utility and amplifies the loading-speed premium. Green self-identity attenuates the media-quality premium but does not amplify eco-visibility utility; none of the eco-visibility moderations — by green self-identity, social comparison orientation, or digital environmental attitude — is confirmed. Exploratory benefit segmentation identifies three preference profiles — Technical Optimizers, Eco-Aware Pragmatists, and Ad-Averse Minimalists — revealing a sign reversal in eco-visibility utility across profiles. Theoretical and practical implications for sustainable platform design, multiple-comparison practices in conjoint moderation research, and green digital marketing are discussed. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Optimal Pricing Strategies and Channel Modes Selection for A Fresh Agricultural Product Supply Chain with Blockchain Traceability
Abstract: The traceability system supported by blockchain technology (BCT) provides consumers with authentic information, triggering the premium effect in the fresh agricultural product supply chain (FASC). This paper introduces BCT to the FASC, which consists of a powerful manufacturer and a retailer. We consider two channel modes: The dual-channel (DC) mode, in which the retailer sells products through an offline channel and the manufacturer sells through an online channel, and the buy-online-pickup-in-store (BOPS) mode, in which the manufacturer adds BOPS options to consumers. We analyse the optimal pricing strategies in scenarios with and without BCT and discuss the channel mode selection between DC and BOPS modes for the manufacturer and retailer with BCT. The results show that when the label cost is below the threshold, the manufacturer may adopt BCT, and the retailer is incentivised to join BCT when the premium effect is high. Furthermore, the channel mode selection of the manufacturer and retailer depends mainly on the demand for the BOPS channel. When the demand for the BOPS channel is low (high), both the manufacturer and retailer prefer the DC (BOPS) mode; when the demand for the BOPS channel is moderate, the manufacturer prefers the DC mode, and the retailer prefers the BOPS mode. To resolve the conflict of channel mode preference, we design a set of fixed transfer payment contracts to ensure the uniformity of channel mode preference between the manufacturer and retailer. The adoption of BCT may improve the consumer surplus when the premium effect is high, and the consumer surplus in BOPS mode is higher than that in DC mode when the demand of the BOPS channel exceeds the threshold. © The author(s) 2027.

Title: Why they come (back): Motive clusters of seasonal employees and their multiple workplace commitments
Abstract: This study develops seasonal employee typologies for the Alpine tourism and hospitality sector by connecting motives for seasonal work with varying levels of different workplace commitments and return intention. Conceptualizing the destination as an analytical lens rather than merely context, this study examines how employees’ social, economic, and leisure motives affect their commitment to the organization, coworkers, job, and destination. Drawing on survey data from 381 hospitality employees in an Alpine destination in Austria, cluster analysis, analysis of variance, and post hoc tests were applied. The analysis identified four employee clusters (lifestyle seekers, dedicated professionals, practical earners, and social contributors) that significantly differ in their motivational profiles, commitment patterns, and demographic characteristics. The findings demonstrate that commitment among seasonal employees extends beyond the organization and differs across motive-based segments. These differences may shape guest interactions and service delivery, ultimately impacting service quality, visitor satisfaction, and overall destination performance. By integrating a motive-based segmentation with a multi-target commitment perspective, this study advances research on seasonal tourism employment and underscores how destination-specific contexts impact employee attitudes and behaviors. Title: A multi-scale approach to hydrothermal liquefaction of two-phase olive mill waste: From laboratory test to regional biorefinery in Andalusia
Abstract: The olive oil industry produces over 3 Mt of two-phase olive mill waste (TPOMW) annually in Andalusia. Its management presents a significant environmental challenge due to its high moisture content and phytotoxicity. Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) is a promising valorization route utilizing the water content in the waste as a reaction medium, saving energy (no drying is needed). In this study a multi-scale approach has been used, integrating physicochemical characterization, laboratory scale experiments, kinetic modelling and a GIS-based location assessment for the location of HTL treatment plants. TPOMW shows high moisture (72 wt%) and a significant lipid content (16.4 wt% db), with a high heating value of approx. 23 MJ/kg. Kinetic results indicate that the solid fraction is the primary product for the first 22 min, after which the aqueous phase dominates due to rapid organic matter hydrolysis, obtaining a bio-oil yield around 20%. According to the resulting reaction network a model with three first order equation that can predict the behaviour of the process has been proposed. Finally, a GIS-based location-allocation analysis has been performed, proposing a decentralized network of 15 HTL plants across Andalusia. Results show a framework for the implementation of HTL-based biorefineries, supporting the transition toward a circular bioeconomy in the Mediterranean area. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Documentor mindsets: Considerations when contributing learning resources for software development technologies
Abstract: Many volunteers contribute learning resources for software development technologies online. Authors: Zheng Y.
Title: Understanding grey sheep users in recommender systems: A systematic and critical review of detection, modeling, and evaluation
Abstract: Grey sheep users (GSUs), characterized by weak or unstable alignment with the broader user population, remain a challenge in collaborative filtering-based recommender systems. Despite extensive efforts devoted to their detection and treatment, a clear and consistent understanding of GSUs is still lacking. Existing studies typically adopt model-dependent definitions and often assume that GSUs necessarily reduce recommendation quality. This paper presents a systematic and critical review of GSUs, covering their definition, detection strategies, modeling paradigms, and evaluation practices. We revisit the classical similarity-based interpretation and show that the effect of GSUs depends on model design rather than being inherently harmful. Based on this observation, we introduce a refined conceptual perspective that describes GSUs as users with consistently misaligned preference patterns, and further propose a dynamic view that distinguishes between short-term irregular behavior and stable preference differences. We then provide a comprehensive taxonomy of existing approaches, including detection-dependent methods and detection-free strategies, and analyze their underlying assumptions and limitations. We further show that the form in which a detection result is expressed constrains which handling strategies are available, and that this correspondence is rarely exploited in practice. A key finding of this study is that current research is limited by weak evaluation practices. In particular, the absence of ground truth, inconsistent definitions, and dependence on aggregate performance metrics lead to circular reasoning and unreliable conclusions. Finally, we outline future research directions toward more robust modeling frameworks and user-centered evaluation protocols, with the aim of establishing a clearer conceptual foundation and guiding the development of more reliable and inclusive recommender systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Abstract: Generative AI has introduced new possibilities for cultural and creative packaging design. Title: When culture meets citizenship: The moderating role of instructional leadership
Abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of organizational culture and instructional leadership in shaping the organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) of high school teachers, as well as to explain the social mechanisms underlying this relationship. The qualitative stage was carried out through semi structured interviews to deepen and explain the quantitative findings. Title: What drives versus what is required: Sufficient and necessary conditions for consumer intention in an unfamiliar wellness service
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Despite the growing importance of wellness and health tourism, little is known about how individuals who have never experienced thermal spa treatments form intentions toward such services. This study addresses this gap by mobilizing an extended Theory of Planned Behavior framework enriched with subjective knowledge and expected health benefits. Based on a large-scale survey of French non-users, we combine Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling and Necessary Condition Analysis to examine both enabling and constraining mechanisms of intention formation. The results show that all predictors contribute positively to intention, with subjective norm emerging as the most influential factor. However, the necessity analysis reveals a markedly different causal structure: only subjective norm, expected health benefits, and perceived behavioral control establish threshold conditions that must be satisfied for higher levels of intention to occur. In contrast, subjective knowledge and attitude, although significant, do not operate as indispensable conditions. These findings reveal an asymmetry between the factors that raise intention and those that set the threshold for it. They suggest that, in this context, intention depends on socially mediated validation, not on individual evaluation alone. Title: Self-awareness and negotiations
Abstract: How does directing attention toward oneself, or self-awareness, affect one's performance in a negotiation? Title: Clouds and crowds: A meta-analysis of air pollution and tourism demand-experience dynamics
Abstract: Empirical evidence on how air quality shapes tourist responses remains inconsistent. Drawing on a meta-analytical framework and cognitive-relational theory, this study synthesizes the effects of air pollution on demand- and experience-related outcomes across the travel process. The analysis pools 974 estimates from 58 demand studies and 92 estimates from 8 experience studies on destination-side pollution, as well as 483 estimates from 17 demand studies on origin-side pollution. After correcting for publication bias, air pollution has a mild, partly remediable adverse effect on tourism demand, while evidence for tourist experience is less consistent. The demand effect remains robust across destination-only and origin-destination settings, whereas origin-side air pollution has a negligible, statistically insignificant positive effect. Meta-regression results indicate that between-study heterogeneity is mainly driven by international tourism contexts, online word-of-mouth measures, PM2.5 or air quality index measures, and long-run effects. Title: Home economics and sustainable futures: A systematic literature review
Abstract: This study aims to systematically examine the development, thematic structure, and research trends in Home Economics from 2015 to 2024, with an emphasis on its contribution to a sustainable future. Through the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach with Scopus indexed article data sources, a total of 22 articles were analyzed using a combination of thematic synthesis methods and bibliometric visualization through the VOSviewer tool to identify developing research patterns, relationships, and clusters. The results of the analysis show that Home Economics research has shifted its focus from traditional discussions of household skills to a multidisciplinary approach that emphasizes sustainable education, family economic literacy, health, and social responsibility. The keyword mapping process uncovered to have five major clusters—education, sustainability, health, students, and digital literacy—that intersect to have within the broader framework of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). Quantitatively, publication trends show a significant increase over the past three years (2021–2024), reflecting to have the increasing global interest in issues concerning welfare and sustainability in the field of education. The main findings also suggest that Home Economics is increasingly being positioned as a transformative discipline that integrates economic literacy, environmental awareness and social responsibility. Theoretically, the results of this study expand the framework of Home Economics as a humanistic and ecological science, while practically, the implications confirm the need for contextual, collaborative, and project-based curriculum and pedagogy innovations to address the challenges of the 21st century. These implications are important for curriculum developers, educators, and policymakers in integrating sustainability values into the education system. In conclusion, this study confirms that Home Economics has a strategic role in shaping a sustainable future through education. © 2027, Malque Publishing. All rights reserved.

Title: CO₂ emission modeling and synthetic fuel energy recovery for hydrogen-integrated sustainable fuel systems
Abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions pose a major challenge to sustainable fuel and energy transitions; however, when accurately predicted and reutilized, CO₂ can become a viable feedstock for synthetic and hydrogen-compatible fuels. This study presents an AI-driven framework for predictive CO₂ emission modeling, explainable decision support, and synthetic fuel energy recovery tailored to sustainable fuel infrastructures. A Random Forest Regressor, configured as reported in Section 3 and trained on an agri-food environmental dataset, achieved R2 = 0.9808, RMSE = 33,023.39, and MAPE = 0.1883 on the held-out test partition. LIME and SHAP provide local and global explanations of the model predictions. Beyond forecasting, the framework comprises three coordinated modules: (i) a CO₂ Utilization Energy Management Hub that translates predicted emissions into theoretical synthetic-fuel energy potentials (MWh); (ii) a DiCE-based counterfactual module that identifies model-consistent emission-reduction scenarios; and (iii) a rule-based decision module that maps sensor readings and predicted emissions to IoT-enabled mitigation actions. The case studies illustrate forecasting, counterfactual analysis, and standardized fuel-energy recovery estimates. The resulting architecture links CO₂ analytics with synthetic-fuel and hydrogen-system planning while clearly distinguishing model outputs from plant-level validation. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Zhou C.; Yu Z.
Title: AI for guilt, human for encouragement? The interaction effects of creator type and emotional appeal on green purchase intention
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Green advertising inherently embeds emotional appeal to drive consumer responses. The proliferation of generative AI has shifted the creator from solely human-dominated to a hybrid landscape where AI-generated and human-generated coexist. Drawing on schema theory and attribution theory, this study investigates the interaction effects between creator type (AI-generated vs. human-generated) and emotional appeal (guilt vs. encouragement) in green advertising on consumers' green purchase intention. Three experiments, including two scenario-based lab experiments (one with a Chinese sample and one with an international English-speaking online sample) and a field experiment with actual purchase data from a live-streaming retailer, provide consistent support for our hypotheses. The results reveal that AI-generated guilt appeal elicits higher consumers’ green purchase intention than the human-generated one, mediated by reduced green moral pressure (a burden-alleviating pathway); conversely, human-generated encouragement appeal elicits higher purchase intention than the AI-generated one, mediated by green self-efficacy (a capacity-enhancing pathway). Furthermore, attribution focus moderates these interaction effects: behavioral attribution strengthens the advantage of AI-generated guilt appeal, whereas personal attribution strengthens the advantage of human-generated encouragement appeal. These findings move beyond the adversarial AI versus human comparison by demonstrating an interaction between disclosed creator type and emotional appeal in green advertising. The framework contributes to green advertising literature by integrating creator type and emotional appeal through an interaction logic, advancing schema theory and attribution theory in the green marketing context. The findings also provide actionable guidance for retailers on strategically collaborating AI and human in green advertising creation to maximize persuasive effectiveness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A longitudinal study of supervisor support as a moderator in maintaining work engagement during working from home: A moderated moderated-mediation model
Abstract: Maintaining employee work engagement during extended periods of work from home (WFH) is essential for sustaining productivity. Although prior research highlights the detrimental effects of job stress and imbalanced work demands on burnout and engagement, few studies explore how supervisor support mitigates these effects over time. This study examines such relationships as WFH progresses. Panel data from 145 participants, collected at multiple time points over a 10-month period, reveal that as the WFH period extends, supervisor support becomes increasingly effective in alleviating the negative impact of job demands and perceived stress on burnout. This reduction in burnout subsequently contributes to the sustained work engagement of employees. Title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
Abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Engaging consumers with varying budgets for battery electric vehicles in the post-subsidy era
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: China's BEV market must now engage the early majority to sustain broader penetration in the post-subsidy era. However, existing research inadequately explores how manufacturer-led strategies and psychological factors differentially shape the adoption decisions of this emerging consumer segment, particularly across varying budget levels. To address this gap, this study develops an integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) model to jointly examine the effects of psychological determinants and multiple manufacturer-led strategies on BEV adoption. The analysis draws on 1200 stated-preference responses from prospective BEV buyers in Beijing and Shenzhen. Findings indicate that budget level significantly drives consumer heterogeneity in psychological drivers, while the relative effectiveness of manufacturer-led strategies remains consistent across groups: bundled insurance packages yield the largest marginal effects, followed by advanced intelligent driving services and lottery-based discounts, with price discounts being the least effective. Title: What you see is (not) what you got: The human factor in PDF signature verification
Abstract: Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents. We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection. We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Research on the mechanism of linking time pressure to career growth among hotel employees
Abstract: Research overlooks how and why identical cognitive appraisals of time pressure translate into divergent coping behaviors. Drawing upon the cognitive appraisal theory of stress, this study investigates the mechanisms linking time pressure to the career growth of frontline hotel employees. Utilizing a three-wave time-lagged design, we collected survey data from 323 frontline hotel employees in China and analyzed it using PLS-SEM via SmartPLS 4.0. The results reveal that challenge appraisal and hindrance appraisal play differentiated mediating roles between time pressure and career growth, with job crafting serving as a crucial behavioral bridge in the transformation from stress appraisal to career growth. Furthermore, achievement motivation significantly moderates this transformation from stress appraisal to job crafting behavior. This study provides empirical evidence for the hospitality industry to implement differentiated stress management and employee development interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: MLOps for enterprise AI: A systematic literature review of frameworks, interpretability practices, and organisational readiness
Abstract: The rapid industrialisation of artificial intelligence has elevated Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) into a foundational discipline for organisations seeking to deploy, monitor, and sustain machine learning models in production. Despite a growing body of literature on technical pipeline orchestration and continuous delivery for ML, significant gaps persist in how enterprises-particularly within the financial services and FinTech sectors-integrate interpretability requirements, address organisational readiness, and govern data-driven decision-making at scale. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) following the PRISMA protocol, synthesising findings from 170 peer-reviewed publications spanning 2015 to 2025. We examine three interconnected themes: (i) MLOps frameworks, maturity models, and pipeline orchestration practices; (ii) explainability and interpretability integration within MLOps lifecycles; and (iii) organisational, team-level, and governance factors that determine successful enterprise MLOps adoption. Drawing on the SPACE and DORA frameworks for developer productivity analogy, we further contextualise these findings within large-scale FinTech settings, highlighting the particular pressures of regulatory compliance (SR 11–7, GDPR, EU AI Act), model risk management, and real-time fraud detection pipelines. We propose a four-tier integrative MLOps Maturity and Interpretability Framework (MMIF) and identify eight priority research gaps requiring empirical investigation. Title: Pet-friendliness in hospitality and tourism: Definition, scope, and governance
Abstract: Pet-friendliness is a widely used hospitality label, yet it remains poorly defined and inconsistently specified. This paper clarifies what pet-friendly tourism means and how its scope is delimited within hospitality and tourism. Drawing on a systematic literature review and evidence from a global mixed-method survey, it shows that pet-friendliness extends beyond unrestricted pet access or isolated amenities and operates as a governance-mediated form of conditional inclusion supported by clear rules, appropriate infrastructure, staff practices, welfare, hygiene, safety, and coexistence management. Title: Post-negotiation behavior and attitudes: We have a deal, now what?
Abstract: Negotiators often equate “winning” with securing favorable agreement terms, yet the agreement is only one outcome of the negotiation process—and may not be the most important, particularly when interactions continue after the deal. This review broadens the lens to encompass post-negotiation outcomes, including emotions, satisfaction, relational perceptions, contract implementation, and subsequent behaviors. Integrating post-negotiation behavior also reveals when and why economic and relational motives collide. Title: Ag-doped ZnTi-LDH-derived ZnO/TiO2 heterojunctions promote charge separation to achieve highly efficient photocatalytic H2O2 production
Source title: Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology A: Chemistry
Abstract: To achieve high-efficiency photocatalytic H2O2 production, it is essential to modulate the charge-carrier lifetime of the photocatalyst. Herein, a series of xAg-ZnO/TiO2 (x = 0, 20, 30, 40 mg AgNO3) materials are synthesized by pyrolysing Ag-doped ZnTi-LDH. Among these, compared with pristine ZnTi-LDH, the 30Ag-ZnO/TiO2 sample shows a 113.7-fold higher photocatalytic H2O2 generation rate, reaching 4.6 mmol g−1 h−1. Meanwhile, Ag-ZnO/TiO2 retains the two-dimensional morphology of ZnTi-LDH, and a 9.8-fold increase in specific surface area is observed for 30Ag-ZnO/TiO2 relative to pristine ZnTi-LDH. The presence of Ag optimises charge distribution and introduces impurity levels near the Fermi level, narrowing the bandgap. Concurrently, the ZnO/TiO2 heterojunction further accelerates carrier separation and migration, enabling highly efficient photocatalytic H2O2 production. Furthermore, the photocatalytic mechanism of two-step single-electron ORR (O2 → •O2− → H2O2) is confirmed via XPS, EPR and DFT. Title: Whose story do we live? Experiential authorship threat in AI-mediated hospitality journeys and its consequences for meaning, memory, and engagement
Abstract: AI now functions as hospitality's concierge, curating itineraries, wellness plans, and trip narratives at scale. While such systems boost efficiency and personalisation, they raise a symbolic concern central to hospitality: when algorithms pre-write the journey, do guests still feel like the authors of their own experiences? This research introduces and validates Experiential Authorship Threat (EAT), defined as the perceived loss of agency, ownership, and self-authored meaning when AI curation displaces the guest's narrative role. Across six studies (scenario-based, embedded-field, and interface experiments; total n = 2073), AI (vs. human) curation elevates EAT, especially under rigid itineraries (Study 1), and EAT, rather than adjacent constructs, drives symbolic and behavioural disengagement through diminished psychological ownership, particularly among guests high in narrative identity (Study 2). Framing AI as a co-creator rather than a curator, and offering editable rather than pre-filled itineraries, restores autonomy and authorship and improves engagement and satisfaction (Studies 3 and 4). The cost of EAT is greatest for symbolic, identity-relevant trips and high-identity-salience guests (Study 5) and persists in impoverished post-trip memory (Study 6). Theoretically, the research integrates self-determination, narrative identity, and meaning-maintenance perspectives to position EAT as a distinct psychological mechanism in hospitality. For managers, preserving guest authorship through framing, interface design, and symbolic sensitivity emerges as a design priority alongside accuracy and speed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The complex role of perspective taking in negotiations
Abstract: To reach an agreement, successful negotiators typically need to understand two things: what they themselves are willing to accept, and what the other side is willing to accept. Understanding the other party's threshold requires perspective taking. In negotiations over goods or services, these judgments shape perceptions of the bargaining zone: the range of outcomes both parties would prefer to walking away without an agreement. The present paper examines how negotiators form perceptions of the bargaining zone. These perceptions have important downstream consequences, influencing everything from the offers negotiators make to the agreements they reach. We review work on how negotiators form perceptions of what their counterpart is willing to accept. Perspective taking can help negotiators estimate the lowest price a seller would accept or the highest price a buyer would pay. However, it can also lead negotiators to erroneously internalize the other party's perspective as if it is relevant to their own valuation. As an example, we demonstrate that buyers are willing to pay more for the same good when the seller gives up an entire endowment rather than only part of it, although the seller's end state should not affect buyer's willingness to pay for the good. These findings show how taking the other party's perspective can shape valuations, fairness judgments and negotiations outcomes. We conclude by discussing implications for multi-issue bargaining and strategic framing, highlighting how psychological heuristics and social context interact to shape outcomes in complex real-world situations, such as salary negotiations and real estate transactions. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Selecting a project-delivery structure for Indonesia's first nuclear power plant: an expert AHP-weighted anchored-rating analysis of the bankability–strategic-control trade-off
Abstract: Indonesia's energy policy and supply plan include nuclear generation, shifting attention from adoption to delivery. This study evaluates five case-anchored delivery configurations against 14 criteria covering ownership, contractual risk allocation, strategic national value, and financing feasibility, using a hybrid AHP-weighted anchored-rating model: 19 purposively selected Indonesian experts derived criterion weights by pairwise comparison and rated each configuration on an anchored nine-point scale; each respondent's weights and ratings were combined before aggregation. Priority heterogeneity alone reversed the group choice for no respondent; assessment heterogeneity reversed it for five. A1 led in over 98% of resampling and weight-variation draws, but the lead reversed when its seven contracting and financing ratings were lowered together by more than about 1.2 points. Abstract: Tourism significantly contributes to the livelihoods of host communities, influencing their social, environmental, and economic development. Title: Too much of a good thing? The curvilinear effects of job clarity on career satisfaction and creativity among hospitality employees
Abstract: This study challenges the assumption that greater job clarity always benefits service employees. Drawing on self-determination theory and the Too-Much-of-a-Good-Thing framework, we test a moderated curvilinear mediation model linking job clarity, career satisfaction, and creativity, with career calling as a boundary condition. Title: Attention-boosted DistilBERT and Bi-GRU for cyber-attacks detection in electric vehicle charging networks
Abstract: The global transition to the Electric Vehicles (EVs) represents a major change of the transportation and energy industry, which is driven by a breakthrough in battery technology, positive government policies, and increased consumer demand. As the use of electric cars is becoming more accepted, it is necessary to implement Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) in the power grid to support the ecosystem. The interconnectivity, in its turn, makes the grid and EVSE infrastructure vulnerable to a variety of cybersecurity threats. The availability, dependability, and security of electric vehicle charging networks may be compromised by the vulnerabilities such as Denial of Service (DoS), Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, data manipulation, and malware threats. These attacks can disrupt power charging processes, cause financial damages, cause bodily injuries, or even destabilise the power systems. This paper introduces a hybrid architecture comprising of deep contextual proficiency of DistilBERT, the sequential modelling efficacy of Bi-directional Gated Recurrent Units (Bi-GRU) and an attention mechanism to detect cyber-attacks on Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) systems. The model is tested on CICEVSE2024 dataset, a high-rate collection of power consumption and network traffic data, which is based upon benign and harmful contexts. The study highlights the potential of AI-assisted methods of real-time cybersecurity monitoring in the framework of electric vehicle grid integration, which is steadily advancing, and explains the need to implement resilient and scaleable solutions to mitigate the increasing cyber threats. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Hierarchical DEMATEL-based key risk identification for urban public safety within grid management
Abstract: With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Large language models in software project management: A two-phase systematic literature review
Abstract: Background: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Software Engineering (SE) processes and practices. However, their application within Software Project Management (SPM) remains fragmented and insufficiently synthesized. This absence of systematic evidence prevents both researchers and practitioners from understanding where LLMs can meaningfully contribute to project management processes in relation to established standards such as the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK). Objectives: This study aims to systematically synthesize existing evidence on the application and integration of LLMs in SPM by means of a two-phase method where Phase I systematically searches for existing secondary studies in the topic of interest, and Phase II (whenever applicable) carries out an SLR in the topic of interest. Method: We conducted a two-phase method: Phase I is a tertiary study that used 14 research questions to assess the existence, coverage, and quality of prior secondary studies in LLMs applied to SPM. As no suitable SLR was identified from Phase I, we also conducted Phase II, which employed the SEGRESS guidelines to analyze primary studies that empirically evaluated the use of LLMs in SPM via five research questions. Phase II also assessed coverage across PMBOK processes and synthesized reported mechanisms, outcomes, research designs and evaluation approaches. Results: The SLR (Phase II) shows that studies employ encoder-only and decoder-only LLM architectures in equal proportion (17 studies each). Their applications focus on a narrow set of SPM tasks, including effort estimation, project planning, and requirements-related activities. Coverage across PMBOK processes is uneven, with limited attention to areas such as procurement, stakeholder, quality, and cost management. Most studies rely on proof-of-concept evaluations, with scarce industrial validation and heterogeneous evaluation metrics. Conclusion: The results indicate that current research on LLMs in SPM provides limited guidance for systematic adoption. One of the main drawbacks for such lack of guidance is the weak empirical validation in many of the included primary studies, limited PMBOK coverage, and lack of context-aware integration of LLMs in SPM.1 © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Ethics, economics, and environmental stewardship: Religious moral frameworks as constraints for rational policy choice
Abstract: Environmental policy often embeds ethical judgments implicitly in discount rates, welfare weights, prices, or informal constraints. This paper develops a constraint-based framework that makes major ethical commitments explicit before economic optimization begins. Drawing on convergent principles in Jewish, Islamic, Christian, Indigenous, Buddhist, and secular traditions, it identifies stewardship, restraint of waste, intergenerational responsibility, ecological limits, and institutional responsibility as candidate non-compensatory constraints. Economic analysis then compares costs, trade-offs, and institutional feasibility only among policies that satisfy the adopted constraints. Applied water-policy illustrations show how this approach can clarify minimum access, pricing, desalination, and wastewater-reuse choices without claiming that these policies were historically caused by the ethical framework. The contribution to ecological economics is methodological: moral commitments define the admissible policy space, while economics identifies efficient pathways within it. This division of labor improves transparency under moral pluralism and environmental scarcity. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Revisiting code readability improvement with LLMs: A critical assessment of fine-tuned models
Abstract: Code comprehension is vital for software development. Still, unreadable code remains a significant issue, costing substantial time and money losses. While tools to identify code exhibiting a low readability exist, take actions to improve such a quality aspect is far from trivial. To support developers in such a task, Vitale et al. introduced at ASE’23 an approach using a transformer model (T5) fine-tuned on code commits in which developers explicitly stated their goal to improve code readability. The authors reported that their model is able to generate readability-improving changes being identical to those implemented by developers (exact matches) in 21% of cases and that, even when they differ, they still improve readability in the vast majority of cases (80%). Given the major advances in AI made in the last few years, we questioned whether a fine-tuning for such a task was still needed in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), thus revisiting the work by Vitale et al. with state-of-the-art models. In doing so, we found out one major issue with the original study design: The training-test splitting was performed randomly (i.e., readability-improving commits mined from open source projects were randomly split between training and test) rather than by project, significantly inflating the reported performance due to repeating readability-improving commits done within the same project. Indeed, as we will show, even newer and more powerful LLMs fine-tuned for this task can only achieve a 1% of exact matches. Once fixed this issue, we shifted our attention on assessing whether fine-tuning on available developer readability improvements is actually needed given the recent advances in general-purpose LLMs. We compare the performance of fine-tuned state-of-the-art LLMs with what they achieve in zero-shot setting, also including in our study commercial LLMs (GPT-4.1). As we will show, quantitative metrics (e.g., exact matches, CrystalBLEU) tell very little about the readability-improving capabilities of LLMs and, thus, our study is mainly qualitative in nature, with a total of 9,500 inspected LLMs’ change recommendations. While all models do improve code readability, our results clearly show that fine-tuning using mined readability-improving commits does not help and, instead, results in sensibly poorer readability recommendations as compared to LLMs used in a zero-shot setting, with GPT-4.1 being the one achieving the best results. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Zheng Z.; Wang Y.; Tan H.; Lyu B.; Zhang J.; Xiang J.
Title: Thermo-mechanical analysis of energy piles with different pipe configurations using numerical simulations and machine learning models
Abstract: Energy piles, which combine structural support and ground heat exchange, are a promising technology for shallow geothermal utilization. However, systematic frameworks for rapidly evaluating the coupled thermo-mechanical responses of energy piles with different pipe configurations remain limited. In this study, five pile configurations, namely U-type, W-type, 2U-type, 3U-type, and double-helix-type, were investigated using a validated three-dimensional thermo-mechanical numerical model. A dataset of 8000 cases was generated through Latin hypercube sampling and a Python-COMSOL automated workflow. Based on this dataset, four machine learning models, including linear regression, random forest, back-propagation neural network, and XGBoost, were developed to rapidly predict outlet water temperature, pile head displacement, and axial forces under different design and operating conditions. Among them, the XGBoost achieved the best predictive performance, with an R2 value of 0.9938 for the training set and 0.9697 for the test set. Then, a systematic comparative framework was established to evaluate the thermo-mechanical performance and parameter sensitivities of different pipe configurations. The results showed that the 2U-type pile achieved the highest heat exchange efficiency owing to its more uniform pipe arrangement. In addition, the sensitivity analysis indicated that the outlet water temperature was mainly governed by inlet water temperature, pile length, mass flow rate, and soil thermal conductivity, whereas pile head load, inlet water temperature, and pile length had significant effects on pile displacement and axial forces. The proposed framework provides an effective tool for rapid prediction, systematic comparison, and preliminary design evaluation of energy piles with different pipe configurations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Artificial intelligence systems distort upstream selection in human social learning
Abstract: Humans are social learners who depend on observing others to acquire knowledge, norms, and behaviors, a capacity that underlies cumulative cultural evolution. Social learning unfolds in two stages: upstream selection determines what information becomes visible, and downstream selection determines what learners copy from that visible sample. Downstream selection occurs through biases such as conformity bias (copying what appears common) and prestige bias (copying those who appear highly respected). These downstream biases can be adaptive when upstream selection yields a sample that reflects the population's true distribution, so that what appears common is actually common and those who appear respected are actually competent. We argue that digital technologies disrupt this condition, creating an upstream selection problem. Engagement-based algorithms amplify the tails of the distribution, surfacing rare and extreme content, whereas generative AI collapses it toward the mode (of the population or the user), erasing the surrounding diversity. Crucially, in each system the optimization signal shapes both visibility and prestige. For engagement-based algorithms, the signal is engagement: creators who post extreme content become more visible and, through the likes, shares, and followers, appear more prestigious. For generative AI, the signal is statistical typicality: it makes a modal answer dominant and, with no alternatives shown, makes the model that produced it appear more prestigious. These distortions can give rise to emergent group-level phenomena, including pluralistic ignorance and illusory consensus. Synthesizing evidence across psychology, cultural evolution, and computational social science, we provide a framework for how digital technologies disrupt social learning and outline interventions for restoring functional cultural transmission. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The increasing sensory richness of digitally-mediated experience
