Title: RARSGAN: An End-to-End Intelligent Generative Framework for Regime-Faithful and Risk-Aware Electricity-Market Scenario Generation
Abstract: Electricity-market scenario generation is most difficult when synthetic paths must preserve not only marginal price behavior but also regime shifts, state-dependent risk, tail pressure, and heterogeneous hub conditions. This paper develops RARSGAN, an integrated end-to-end regime-faithful and risk-aware framework for forward hub-level electricity-market scenario generation. The framework transforms trading records into structured market states, dynamically validates latent regimes through a Student-t Markov layer, constructs a multi-component risk state, recursively simulates future regime-risk conditioning sequences using only information available at the simulation origin, and generates synthetic market-state paths through a conditional TimeGAN-based architecture. The method provides finite-sample structural-error bounds linking fitted risk, regime-occupancy, and transition discrepancies to the structures it is designed to preserve. Evaluation follows a locked chronological train-validation-test protocol with repeated runs and compares the generated paths with held-out observations through mechanism-aligned structural metrics, independent path-level diagnostics, synchronized cross-hub dependence tests, and downstream procurement-risk measures. The results show that joint regime-risk conditioning provides the most balanced mean preservation across the model’s primary structural objectives, while the supplementary tests identify important remaining limitations in real-synthetic distinguishability, simultaneous multi-hub stress, and tail-loss calibration. RARSGAN therefore offers a transparent framework for generating, stress-testing, and evaluating forward electricity-market scenarios without conflating improved structural balance with universal statistical or economic dominance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: More alike than unalike: Contextually aligned authority arguments amplify sustainable choices across cultures
Abstract: Most research is conducted in Western societies, with few studies from Latin America. This oversight has led to a narrow understanding of the effectiveness that various sustainability-oriented interventions have in countries with different cultural values. As consumers play a vital role in mitigating climate change issues, this behavioral field experiment investigates whether reliance on the authority and commitment-consistency principles from social influence increases individuals' inclination to choose sustainably, and whether the effectiveness of these principles is culturally contingent. Participants from Ecuador and Norway (N = 346) were randomized to one of three conditions (control vs. authority vs. commitment-consistency), with the latter two conditions containing a message tailored to its associated social influence principle. After replying to some survey items, participants made a choice between a more (vs. less) sustainable option. A chi-square test revealed that both social influence conditions jointly boosted choice likelihood of the more sustainable option relative to the control condition, supporting our initial preregistered hypothesis. However, contrary to our second preregistered hypothesis, a regression-based simple moderation analysis using the PROCESS macro (Model 1) showed no country moderation in the effectiveness of these social influence principles; instead, the results were largely attributable to the authority condition alone, which was considerably more effective than both other conditions across countries, regardless of participants' trust in authorities and their need for consistency. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of contextually aligned authority arguments as a viable way to foster pro-environmental behaviors. © 2026 The Authors

Title: When regulatory-focus language matches the product category: A within-person computational analysis of reviews from an online retail platform
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Online review platforms use helpfulness votes and related signals to rank and solicit reviews. This study tests whether regulatory-focus-related language is associated with helpfulness in a category-sensitive manner. We analyze 391,047 Amazon reviews from eight product categories classified a priori as promotion-oriented or prevention-oriented. Promotion language concerns gains, aspirations, and enjoyment. Prevention language concerns safety, reliability, and problem avoidance. Category assignments and language measures were benchmarked against human ratings of 800 products and 1136 reviews, respectively. The primary analyses compare within-reviewer deviations in 153,655 reviews from 20,787 reviewers represented in both category types, thereby accounting for additive time-invariant reviewer differences under the specified model. The same reviewers used a higher density of promotion language in promotion-oriented categories and a higher density of prevention language in prevention-oriented categories, with paired Cohen's d values of. 20 and. 14, respectively. Within reviewers, matched-language count was positively associated with log(1 + helpful votes), and its coefficient exceeded the mismatched-language coefficient, p <. 001. Category-specific count estimates were positive in all eight categories, although their magnitudes varied. The median count-based double/debiased machine-learning point estimate across five seeds was also positive. The association was small. A one-standard-deviation within-reviewer difference in matched-language count corresponded to a 2.39% difference in the model-implied geometric mean of 1 + helpful votes. Adding promotion and prevention density terms and their category interactions increased internal five-fold cross-validated R2 by ΔR2 =. 0002. The hypothesized response-surface pattern did not characterize the central data region. The findings are associational and do not distinguish regulatory fit from informational attribute relevance. Title: Exploring Technology Probe applications in software engineering practice
Abstract: Background: The development of software systems relies on user feedback, which can be captured with Validation Sessions (VS); however, VS are often conducted in an ad hoc manner. Technology Probe (TP) offers a participatory design method for capturing user perception; however, its application in software engineering lacks structure. Aim: This study consolidates evidence on TP applications in software engineering and identifies practices that support the systematic use of TP. Methods: A Literature Study, inspired by Rapid Reviews, was conducted in Scopus using backward and forward snowballing, screening 530 studies and selecting 53 primary works across the trials that support the results. Thematic analysis was employed to extract motivations, outcomes, and challenges associated with the use of TP in software engineering. Results: Through thematic analysis and open coding, 11 evidence-based characteristics were identified describing the use of TP in software engineering. These characteristics formed the foundation of an evidence-based checklist developed to assess and guide the development of TP techniques. Conclusion: It was found that TP has been applied across a variety of domains, with diverse techniques being crafted. Title: When AI meets DEI: Employee AI-beliefs and their implications for workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workplace, its impact on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has been examined primarily through the lens of what AI actually does (i.e., system design, outputs). This review shifts the focus to humans' subjective beliefs about AI, identifying mechanisms through which three dimensions of AI-beliefs (competence, warmth, and morality) may affect DEI goals: improving representation of underrepresented groups, closing career gaps across groups, and fostering inclusion. Our synthesis shows that, independently of what AI does, AI-beliefs can disadvantage underrepresented groups in some contexts, while creating opportunities for bridging human subgroups in others. Title: Emotional Factors in Quality Negligence: A Study of Residential Real Estate Construction Professionals
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Quality negligence in the construction industry, a significant originator of legal crises, is predominantly attributed to technical and procedural failures. However, the pivotal role of construction professionals' emotions as a precipitating factor remains a critically unexamined research area. This study addresses this gap by investigating the influence of specific emotions on quality negligence and its subsequent escalation into legal crises for construction firms. The research employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. Initially, a comprehensive literature review and unstructured interviews with industry experts identified seven prominent emotions (anxiety, guilt, pride, shame, elevation, injustice, and gratitude). Subsequently, a quantitative phase involved distributing a self-administered questionnaire to 162 Indian construction professionals within the Indian residential construction sector to assess their emotional states and quality negligence levels. Data analysis using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) indicated a statistically significant positive relationship between quality negligence and five emotions. The effects, in descending order of magnitude, were elevation (β=0.406, p<0.001), shame (β=0.405, p<0.001), gratitude (β=0.321, p<0.001), pride (β=0.261, p=0.009), and anxiety (β=0.179, p=0.047). In the final phase, consultations and brainstorming sessions with industry experts were used to identify the resulting legal crises and to establish a novel emotion-quality negligence-crises framework. This framework models the pathway from emotional antecedent to quality negligence and its culmination in a legal crisis. The study provides a critical diagnostic tool for practitioners in the real estate sector to mitigate risk and offers a new theoretical model for academics analyzing this psycho-legal connection.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Trust begins at home: The role of psychological distance in trust transfer for emerging technology
Abstract: The widespread adoption of emerging technologies holds substantial potential to benefit societal development. However, fostering public trust and acceptance of emerging technologies, which involve complex underlying principles and are in pre-commercialization stages, remains a critical multifaceted challenge. To address this issue, this study draws on trust transfer theory to identify an effective mechanism for enhancing people's trust in emerging technologies. Specifically, we propose and test that trust in emerging technologies can be transferred from that in familiar institutions of the public by reducing psychological distance to such technologies. Analyzing quota-sampling data, we find that greater consumption of news about local brain–computer interface (BCI) achievements was associated with greater trust in local technology institutions. Institutional process and purpose trust were, in turn, associated with lower psychological distance to BCI, which was associated with greater general trust in BCI and, subsequently, stronger BCI use intention. The corresponding pathway was not supported for performance trust. These findings extend trust transfer theory by introducing psychological distance as a vital mechanism. Practically, this study demonstrates a route through which practitioners can promote public acceptance of unfamiliar and emerging technologies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: MetaTwin: A reconfigurable digital twin framework
Abstract: Digitalization initiatives have led to the widespread adoption of digital twins (DTs), particularly in manufacturing. The explosive growth of DTs makes us think about what the most abstract parts in building the DT systems are and how to promote the reconfigurability of DTs so that they can be agile to adopt the flexibility needs from Industry 4.0 manufacturing systems. However, the heterogeneous granularity and dynamic evolution of manufacturing systems present significant challenges to the reconfigurability of their corresponding DTs. To address these challenges, this paper presents MetaTwin, a reconfigurable DT framework as an integrated solution to abstract DTs into general domains. To be more specific, a novel Domain-Meta structure is first proposed, which addresses the granularity misalignment problem by decoupling the system into stable Domains and reconfigurable Meta units. Then, a dual-dimensional reconfiguration mechanism decomposes complex reconfigurations into macro and micro dimensions, achieved by composing Meta units and reconfiguring their internal pattern-driven Meta Models. A prototype-based case study involving the progressive reconfiguration from an assembly-only DT to a printing-and-assembly DT illustrates how MetaTwin supports reconfiguration scope identification, macro-level structural changes, micro-level behavioral adaptations, and runtime coordination. Title: Risk propagation and vulnerability in the global industrial robot trade network: A cascading failure model with adaptive resilience
Abstract: Industrial robots underpin intelligent manufacturing and high-end equipment systems, and the stability of their global trade network is directly related to the continuity of international manufacturing specialization. Because trade data cannot separate domestic production, processing trade, and re-exports, the propagation results describe network vulnerability and scenario-based trade vulnerability. The results show that network expansion and densification have generated more complex risk transmission paths; simulated risk diffusion is not determined solely by trade scale but by structural position, accumulated import gaps, and substitution absorption capacity; and adaptive supply reallocation can reduce simulated infection scale in some scenarios but cannot fully eliminate cascading risks caused by core-hub failures. Authors: Zhou L.; Wang S.; Zhou Y.; Wan S.
Title: Flying low for greener farms: Configurational pathways linking the low-altitude economy to agricultural green total factor productivity in China
Abstract: The low-altitude economy is increasingly viewed as a new technological frontier for agricultural transformation, yet its relationship with agricultural green total factor productivity remains poorly understood. This study examines how low-altitude economy-related conditions are associated with high agricultural green total factor productivity in China. We develop an institutional-technological-scenario framework and apply a sequential mixed-method design that combines qualitative coding, necessary condition analysis and dynamic fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The empirical analysis uses a balanced panel of 30 Chinese provinces from 2014 to 2022, covering 270 province-year observations. The period is treated as a formative and pre-consolidation stage of the low-altitude economy rather than as a fully mature integrated system. The results show that no single condition constitutes a statistically supported necessary condition for high agricultural green total factor productivity. Exploratory bottleneck analysis nevertheless reveals descriptive threshold patterns at higher outcome levels. The dynamic configurational analysis identifies three pathways associated with high agricultural green total factor productivity, namely technology-application coupling, institution-innovation coupling and scale-application diffusion. The non-high productivity configuration further shows that enterprise development, policy support and market support may fail to translate into green productivity improvement when industrial application is absent. Regional and temporal analyses reveal substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity. The findings suggest that the low-altitude economy is better understood as an emerging socio-technical enabling system rather than as a single UAV-based technology, and that agricultural green transformation depends on the configuration of institutional support, technological capacity and application scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Evolution and lifecycle mapping of research methods based on the Boston Matrix in library and information science from 1995 to 2025
Abstract: Developing an evolution framework for research methods is essential for advancing Library and Information Science (LIS), but existing research method schemas remain fragmented and limited. This study proposes an automated framework combining AI-driven methods to mine, classify, and a temporal analysis based on the Boston Matrix to map the lifecycles of research methods. Using a comprehensive dataset of 31,913 articles from 21 LIS journals (1995–2025) as a validation corpus, the framework integrates semantic clustering for bottom-up entity extraction with generative top-down ontology mapping. This approach dynamically maps methods into a four-stage lifecycle schema: mainstream, emerging, marginalized, and mature, revealing distinct evolutionary trajectories and the broader computational turn within LIS. Validated through quantitative threshold testing and qualitative evaluation, the proposed framework significantly reduces manual coding subjectivity and enhances replicability. By empirically comparing the subfields of librarianship and information science, this study accounts for inherent thematic variations and uncovers their distinct paces of methodological adoption. Ultimately, this study offers a robust automated framework for longitudinal methodological tracking, theoretically demonstrating how diverse AI-driven and traditional methods synergistically coevolve and assume distinct scholarly roles within the emerging AI4Science paradigm. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Author full names: Wu, Zhenyu (57218914565); Rong, Chengze (60602149600); Chen, Zhaoxiang (57194714572); Zhang, Wenjuan (57217057547)
Title: A physics-cognitive proactive opportunistic maintenance and routing collaborative framework for offshore wind farms under extreme met-ocean conditions
Abstract: Reliable offshore wind operation requires maintenance decisions that account for multi-source uncertainty including stochastic degradation, environmental shocks, and incomplete condition information. Extreme met-ocean conditions also restrict maintenance access, coupling uncertainty in asset health with fragmented vessel operating windows and high operation and maintenance costs. To address these uncertain issues, this study proposes a proactive opportunistic maintenance and routing strategy. A physics-based competing failure model is developed to capture both cumulative degradation and shock-induced damage. To reduce the physics-cognitive divergence, defined as the inevitable divergence of state estimations from physical wear, an air–sea collaborative fleet using unmanned aerial vehicles enables active monitoring and dynamic replanning. A marginal-benefit-driven opportunistic maintenance strategy is introduced to exploit short and variable weather windows. A continuous weather filtering module proactively schedules critical tasks before adverse conditions, integrated with a bi-level mixed-integer non-linear programming model, which is solved by a bi-stage collaborative solution algorithm to co-optimize multi-vessel routing and maintenance bundling. Simulations on a 78-turbine offshore wind farm over a 90-day period show that the proposed strategy reduces total O&M costs by 96.4%, 46.4%, 19.4% and 46.2% compared to corrective, condition-based, non-opportunistic baselines and sequential scheduling and routing strategy, respectively. The framework offers a scalable and computationally efficient solution for multi-vessel routing and opportunistic maintenance, contributing to the development of cost-effective offshore asset management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Who gets to negotiate? Tracing gender gaps in structural empowerment with people analytics
Abstract: Gender differences in compensation and career advancement are often examined through the lens of negotiation behavior, initiation, outcomes, and stereotyping. We shift attention to the organizational structures that precede and shape formal negotiations. Drawing on organizational gender research, we use structural empowerment as an organizing framework to review and synthesize the literature on organizational structures that may shape who gains access to negotiations and the negotiation power employees bring to them. Existing research documents gender differences in access to opportunities, information, support, and resources, yet their implications for negotiation access and power remain underexamined. We explain how people analytics can help scholars and practitioners trace these dispersed and longitudinal processes and outline directions for future research. We conclude with methodological, ethical, and theoretical considerations associated with using people analytics to examine these questions. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Song J.; Yuan G.; Li J.
Title: PSG-Net: Physical saliency guided adaptive fusion network for infrared and visible image fusion
Abstract: The core challenge in infrared and visible image fusion lies in achieving a seamless integration where thermal saliency does not overshadow critical texture details. Existing deep learning frameworks, however, often struggle with a fundamental disconnect, the inability to explicitly translate the inherent physical priors of thermal targets into learnable spatial guidance. This frequently leads to saliency-texture trade-offs, where fine visible textures are suppressed within high-thermal regions, compromising image fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Physical Saliency Guided Adaptive Fusion Network. Our approach begins by systematically analyzing the physical characteristics of high temperature IR targets and translating these properties into network design principles. By effectively coupling the physical saliency prior with learnable feature representations, PSG-Net achieves the synergistic enhancement of salient objects and background details, significantly improving the visual quality, detail fidelity, and application robustness of the fused images, demonstrating excellent performance on the MSRS, M3FD and LLVIP datasets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Yuan L.; Zhu J.
Title: The security unlock: How rural social pension makes people more entrepreneurial?
Abstract: Previous literature on the determinants of entrepreneurship has not explored the role of social pension. Leveraging variation in the roll-out timing of a universal rural pension program across Chinese counties, our analysis, at both the individual and aggregate levels, reveals that pension provision led to an increase in entrepreneurship among the younger generation. We show that this effect operates through two primary channels: an intergenerational transfer channel and a local demand channel. Specifically, the pension program mitigates upward transfers from adult children to elderly parents, while boosting local consumer demand, which exerts a demand-side “pull” effect on enterprise establishment. Our findings may shed new light on the interplay between pension, intergenerational resource allocation, and entrepreneurial activity. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Liu J.; Xie X.-H.
Author full names: Liu, JiaCheng (60998726200); Xie, Xian-Hua (60979616500)
Title: Emotion-aware retailing: Using biometrics to decode consumer experience in physical–digital environments
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The physical retail space, when blended with digital touchpoints, has created a multi-sensory consumer experience that cannot be fully measured in real time using legacy survey-based approaches. The work examines the opportunities offered by biometric technologies, such as electrodermal activity (EDA), facial action coding, eye-tracking, and heart-rate variability (HRV), to decode shoppers' affective experiences in a phygital retail space. The study is based on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework and affective computing theory, and has a mixed-methods experimental design that involved 312 study participants, who were offered four types of retail formats: department store, grocery hypermarket, experiential flagship store, and click-and-collect hub. All participants were given biometric sensors to wear and were monitored across three consecutive stages: browsing, assessment, and purchase decision. Behavioral and transactional data were used in real time and fused with multimodal biometric responses to create emotion maps for spatial retail areas. The findings show statistically significant positive relationships among high EDA arousal, positive facial affect, and conversion rates at digital interface points. Quantitatively, an optimal engagement window was identified at moderate stimulation levels (EDA = 2.10 μS), yielding a peak conversion rate of 41.2%. In contrast, HRV suppression was associated with decision paralysis at higher stimulation levels. Demographic cohorts and segmentation analysis showed that younger consumers reacted with much more emotion to augmented reality features and individualized digital signs. Eye-tracking and facial action coding confirmed that younger shoppers (<35) sustained an 8.42-s fixation duration with high positive affect (0.74) in flagship zones, whereas older cohorts (≥35) exhibited severe sensory avoidance. The article contributes to the theoretical understanding of emotion-behavior relationships in the store setting and offers practical guidance for store designers, digital experience architects, and consumer psychologists. Embargoes on biometric retail analytics that protect privacy are also discussed. Keywords: biometric sensing, emotion-aware retailing, phygital retail, electrodermal activity, consumer experience, affective computing, eye-tracking, heart-rate variability. The updated structural framework successfully bridges the gap between environmental retail inputs and transactional behavioral choices through intermediate biometric telemetry. Phygital spaces with heavy digital footprints create pronounced shifts in physiological processing, where elevated electrodermal activity predicts transaction completion up to an threshold point, beyond which severe heart-rate variability suppression signals choice paralysis. © 2026

Title: Governance and renewable energy adoption: Assessing the state's role in solar energy uptake in Iran
Abstract: This study investigates how government managers in Golestan Province, Iran, interpret and respond to national directives aimed at promoting solar energy adoption. Despite Iran's substantial solar potential and supportive national policies, the uptake of solar technologies within public institutions remains limited. Drawing on 28 semi-structured in-depth interviews with senior and mid-level government officials and employing thematic analysis, the study identifies two overarching themes: Managers' Actions and Managers' Orientations. The findings demonstrate that socio-political acceptance within the state is severely constrained by institutional decoupling. Provincial managers face conflicting mandates—such as national renewable targets that conflict with provincial security directives requiring diesel generators—leading to symbolic compliance (e.g., installation of decorative solar panels) while continuing reliance on fossil fuels. By integrating socio-political acceptance with institutional decoupling, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Diffusion of Innovations, this study extends renewable-energy acceptance research from public and market actors to acceptance and resistance within the state apparatus. The findings suggest that aligning national and provincial directives, strengthening inter-agency coordination, and improving managerial capacity are essential for renewable-energy implementation in centralized governance systems and other Global South contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Algorithmic fairness as a human–technology interaction problem
Abstract: Algorithms shape high-stakes decisions across society. While promising efficiency, algorithms also raise fairness concerns. This article proposes that algorithmic fairness is best understood as a human–technology interaction problem rather than a purely technical challenge. Algorithms can reproduce human biases, amplify them through feedback loops, or create new forms of unfairness through objectives, proxies, and seemingly neutral variables. Yet they can make decision processes more explicit, disparities more visible, and actively mitigate discrimination. Fairness depends not only on statistical properties but also on how algorithms are designed, used and experienced by those affected by their decisions. This article therefore offers an interdisciplinary perspective that integrates insights from social justice, psychology, computer science, judgment and decision-making, and management. © 2026 The Author

Title: When do hedonic appeals backfire? Credibility, scepticism and the disconnect between emotional engagement and pro-environmental intention
Abstract: This study examines why emotional engagement with hedonic sustainability communication does not always translate into pro-environmental behavioural intention. Drawing on the Persuasion Knowledge Model and Truth-Default Theory, it investigates consumer responses to pleasure- and comfort-based hotel food-waste messages. A sequential mixed-method design combined a laboratory experiment, projective interviews, and a follow-up online experiment testing green scepticism. Findings show no robust statistically significant physiological differentiation across message types, but substantial differences in perceived credibility, sincerity and emotional meaning. Pleasure-based appeals were interpreted as enjoyable but superficial and less trustworthy; comfort-based appeals were warmer and more relational, yet both hedonic appeals produced lower behavioural intention than the control message. Green scepticism strengthened this negative effect, particularly for comfort-based appeals. The findings suggest that hedonic sustainability communication operates less through heightened physiological arousal than through interpretive credibility evaluation, particularly among sceptical consumers. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Qin F.; Yu C.; Qin Y.; Qiu N.; Meng F.
Title: Incremental railway infrastructure detection via prototype-guided proposal refinement and frequency-based prompts from noisy-annotated UAV imagery
Abstract: Railway infrastructure incremental object detection (IOD) aims to generalize to new classes while retaining previously learned knowledge, requiring the model to balance stability and plasticity. Despite their effectiveness, the existing methods are limited in the following ways. On the one hand, they overlook the class ambiguity induced by fine-grained infrastructure structures. On the other hand, they underestimate the spatial ambiguity caused by noisy annotations. Furthermore, they ignore the knowledge corruption caused by spatial imitation in IOD tasks, which limits the discriminative knowledge transferred across tasks. To address the above issues, a robust IOD framework is proposed to enhance semantic discrimination and knowledge retention by integrating prototype-guided proposal refinement and frequency-based prompts. The prototype-guided proposal refinement consists of distribution-aware prototype and adaptive proposal refinement, which respectively model distinguishable infrastructure prototypes and perform iterative localization refinement. Specifically, the distribution-aware prototype constructs distinguishable infrastructure prototypes that serve as the stable class representations for proposal refinement. Moreover, frequency-based prompts are proposed to preserve discriminative representations between the current and previous IOD tasks, which are optimized only after each incremental task and kept frozen during task training so that they serve as stable knowledge carriers. Comprehensive experiments on real-world railway infrastructure datasets validate the superiority of the proposed framework over state-of-the-art baselines. Title: The role of psychological factors on the mathematics achievement among alternative learning students in the Philippine context
Abstract: This study examined the role of key psychological factors such as self-efficacy, self-regulation, and time management in explaining the mathematics achievement among students enrolled in an alternative learning system (ALS) at selected public high schools in the school districts of Cebu, Philippines. Grounded in educational psychology, a descriptive-correlational research design was employed to specifically investigate the factors relating to mathematics achievement in nonformal learning environments. Data were collected from 180 ALS students through validated survey questionnaires and a mathematics achievement test. The respondents were identified through a convenience sampling technique. The data gathered were treated via descriptive statistics to determine the levels of prychological factors and inferential statistics to examine their predictive influence on mathematics achievement by multiple regression analysis. The results revealed that the students demonstrated high self-efficacy, while self-regulation and time management were rated at moderate levels. Multiple regression analysis revealed that all three psychological factors significantly predicted mathematics achievement, with self-efficacy emerging as the strongest predictor, followed by self-regulation and time management. These findings indicate that students’ belief in their capabilities and their ability to regulate learning behaviors contribute meaningfully to mathematics achievement, even within flexible and nontraditional learning environments. The study contributes empirical evidence on the psychological factors of mathematics achievement among ALS students which remains underrepresented in the literature. Findings underscore the importance of strengthening learners’ psychological competencies to support academic achievement in alternative education settings. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating mastery-based tasks, strategy instruction, and time management support within ALS programs to strengthen students’ psychological competencies, enhance achievement in mathematics, and promote more effective learning outcomes. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: Psychological vulnerability in conversational AI: How incentive and urgency manipulations alter trust formation and privacy behaviour across healthcare, financial, commercial, and security contexts
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Users increasingly interact with conversational AI systems in sensitive domains, yet little is known about how psychological manipulation techniques systematically alter privacy decision-making and trust formation across different contexts. We examined how two manipulation mechanisms, incentive-based (Need & Greed) and urgency-based (Time), influence user behaviour in healthcare, financial, commercial, and home security interactions.In a within-subjects experimental study (N=30[jls-end-space/]) using an interactive, scenario-based methodology, we investigated how context shapes vulnerability to manipulation. Participants engaged with control, Need & Greed, and Time conditions across four domains whilst we measured trust, comfort levels, willingness to disclose information, and perception of privacy and security.Both manipulation techniques significantly reduced comfort (p<0.001[jls-end-space/]) and increased information disclosure (p<0.05[jls-end-space/]), but context moderated these effects substantially. Time pressure increased trust in healthcare contexts whilst decreasing it in financial domains, revealing domain-specific vulnerability patterns. Qualitative analysis identified psychological mechanisms underlying these effects: prior digital experiences, agent characteristics, urgency sensitivity, and context-dependent risk assessment.These findings demonstrate that psychological vulnerability to manipulation operates through context-specific pathways, challenging one-size-fits-all protection approaches. The research provides empirical evidence for developing domain-aware security frameworks that address psychological dimensions alongside technical protections, advancing both human-computer interaction theory and practical system design. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Chen Z.; Ma J.; Tan Z.; You D.
Title: Diffusion-augmented adversarial poisoning in QoS-aware cloud API recommender systems
Abstract: Data poisoning attacks pose a serious security threat to QoS-aware cloud API recommender systems by injecting carefully crafted fake user profiles into training data, thereby manipulating recommendation outcomes and compromising prediction reliability. Existing GAN-based poisoning methods often suffer from discriminator overfitting under limited interaction data, leading to pronounced distributional discrepancies between generated and real users, which significantly degrades both attack effectiveness and stealthiness. To address this limitation, we propose DA-GAN, a Diffusion-Augmented Generative Adversarial Network for poisoning attacks against QoS-aware cloud API recommendation systems. DA-GAN integrates diffusion probabilistic modeling into the adversarial training by constructing multi-step noise-augmented real users through a diffusion forward process, and generating fake users via noise-aligned posterior sampling in the reverse process. To further stabilize training, we design a multi-step noise-aligned discriminator that performs joint discrimination across multiple diffusion levels, providing reliable gradient supervision and effectively mitigating discriminator overfitting in small-sample settings. Extensive experiments on real-world cloud API QoS datasets demonstrate that DA-GAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art poisoning baselines in both attack effectiveness and stealthiness across multiple mainstream QoS-aware recommender systems. Our findings reveal previously underestimated vulnerabilities in existing cloud API recommender systems and underscore the urgent need for diffusion-aware and attack-resilient defense mechanisms. Title: From smart cities to smart villages: Evolution, domains, and policy implications for smart rural development
Abstract: Smart villages have evolved from early parallels with urban smart city models into a comprehensive, multidimensional framework that integrates digital infrastructure, agriculture, local enterprises, tourism, and sustainability. This expanded framework recognizes the unique characteristics and potentials of rural areas, moving beyond the urban-centric logic of technology adoption. This review aims to examine the conceptual evolution of smart village research, track emerging methodological trends, and analyze global implementation trajectories. In the early stages, many studies concentrated on definitional debates and approaches that were primarily centered on technology. However, more recent perspectives have begun to emphasize the importance of integrating technological innovation with social innovation, community empowerment, participatory governance, and environmental stewardship. Methodological approaches have also advanced significantly, shifting from conceptual reflections and single-case studies toward more diverse methods including comparative studies, bibliometric mapping, and participatory action research. These evolving methods enable a deeper and more nuanced understanding of smart village dynamics. Regional approaches demonstrate distinct emphases: European initiatives focus on service revitalization and smart specialization; Asian and African strategies prioritize connectivity, renewable energy access, and digital inclusion; while Latin American programs increasingly integrate climate-smart agricultural practices. Despite regional differences, common challenges remain, including the persistent rural digital divide, fragmented coordination among multiple stakeholders, issues of financial sustainability, and the emergence of new forms of inequality. Policy directions increasingly stress the importance of place-based strategies, building local capacities, establishing supportive governance structures, and fostering inclusive participation. The review concludes by identifying critical areas for future research, such as the creation of unified evaluation metrics, conducting longitudinal impact assessments, and embedding smart village initiatives within broader rural development and climate resilience agendas. Overall, smart villages represent dynamic and promising pathways for driving innovation-led, inclusive, and sustainable rural transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. All rights reserved.

Authors: Hu C.; Zheng J.; Lai N.; Wang Q.; He S.
Title: Can digital-real integration effectively curb urban sprawl? Evidence from China using double/debiased machine learning
Abstract: Urban sprawl (URS) has become a major challenge to China's sustainable development under the backdrop of rapid urbanization. Digital-real integration (DRI) provides a new pathway for urban spatial governance, yet its concrete impacts and mechanisms remain insufficiently tested. Based on panel data from 280 prefecture-level Chinese cities between 2013 and 2023, this study constructs a multidimensional DRI index and employs a partially linear double/debiased machine learning (DML) framework to estimate the effect of DRI on URS. Multiple robustness checks, including complementary instrumental-variable analyses, yield results consistent with the baseline finding. The findings show that a one-unit increase in DRI is associated with a 0.06-unit reduction in the URS index, and this conclusion holds under various robustness tests. The mechanism analysis provides evidence consistent with three potential transmission pathways: industrial structure upgrading, stronger aggregate city-level correspondence between employment opportunities and resident population, and reduced dependence on highway commuting. Further heterogeneity analysis reveals that the restraining effect of DRI is more pronounced in eastern regions, major national urban agglomerations, and cities at more advanced stages of urban development. This study not only provides empirical evidence on how digital technologies reshape urban spatial structures but also offers policy implications for implementing differentiated digital governance strategies and enhancing the effectiveness of spatial planning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Dehghani A.; Salaripour A.
Author full names: Dehghani, Alireza (57929731000); Salaripour, Aliakbar (57216638429)
Title: From design attributes to social life: Modelling conviviality in urban underground spaces
Abstract: From being infrastructure utilities, urban underground spaces (UUS) have developed into multipurpose public spaces that combine commercial, cultural, and transit functions. While their technical and spatial contributions to compact urbanism are evident, their capacity to foster conviviality, the experiential quality of inclusiveness, sociability, and shared belonging, is less understood. This study develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework that operationalizes conviviality in UUS by linking seven spatial-perceptual dimensions (safety and security, identity and meaning, accessibility, functionality, environmental comfort, aesthetics, and structure and form) to behavioral mediators of willingness to use and social interaction, culminating in perceived conviviality. Using the Theatre-Shahr underground complex in Tehran as a case study, data were collected through structured surveys and analyzed via Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that although environmental factors generally have a positive indirect effect on perceived conviviality, social interaction emerges as the primary mechanism shaping conviviality in urban underground spaces, while willingness to use plays only a complementary and limited mediating role in this process. Among the environmental factors, accessibility, environmental comfort, and safety and security show the strongest effects. In contrast, some variables, particularly identity and meaning and structure and form, do not demonstrate statistically significant effects in certain pathways. These findings suggest that planning and design strategies for urban underground spaces should prioritize environmental qualities that support social interaction, to enhance perceived conviviality. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
Abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. Title: Identification of subgroup causal effects in randomized trials under nonignorable missingness of covariates and outcome variables simultaneously
Abstract: Randomized experiments are widely regarded as the gold standard for causal inference. However, identifying subgroup causal effects becomes particularly challenging when pretreatment covariates and outcome are subject to simultaneous nonignorable missingness. The study investigates the identifiability of subgroup causal effects under five increasingly complex missing data mechanisms, ranging from an ignorable mechanism to nonignorable mechanisms in which missingness depends on different combinations of treatment, covariates, and outcome. Identification is established under several nonignorable mechanisms without imposing restrictive parametric assumptions. For the most challenging mechanism, identification is established under a parametric model with specific assumptions on the outcome distribution and the missingness mechanism. For estimation and inference, a fractional-imputation Expectation-Maximization algorithm is developed to maximize the observed-data likelihood. Simulation studies compare the proposed estimator with complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, and a full-data oracle estimator, demonstrating satisfactory finite-sample performance across the considered missingness mechanisms. The practical utility of the proposed method is further illustrated using data from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Workplace responses to perpetration of family and domestic violence: a global scoping review
Abstract: Introduction Family and domestic violence (FDV), which includes intimate partner and family violence, affects workplace safety through spillover impacts on workers, organisations, and occupational health systems. To date, workplace interventions addressing the issue of FDV have predominantly concentrated on providing support to victim-survivors, while there is limited research regarding employer responses to employees who perpetrate such violence. Method A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which examined existing evidence from workplace policies, practices, and organisational mechanisms addressing FDV perpetration by workers. Peer-reviewed studies and high-quality grey literature on workplace responses to perpetration of FDV were systematically searched across multiple databases and online sources, and 28 documents on workplace responses to FDV perpetration were analysed. Results Findings from the scoping review reveal four dominant insights across the literature: 1. Perpetration of FDV is a major workplace problem, yet responses are under-researched; 2. Workplaces employ wide-ranging and varied responses, from zero tolerance dismissal of perpetrators to responsibility avoidance; 3. Responses lack a solid evidence-base and regulatory frameworks to address the problem remain weak; 4. Practical strategies are provided to better manage risk, strengthen safety, and reduce violence. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for clearer organisational guidance, evidence-based strategies, and robust regulatory frameworks to strengthen workplace responses to FDV perpetration and improve occupational safety outcomes. Title: The relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and fear of missing out: Evidence from network analysis and a daily diary study
Abstract: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and fear of missing out (FoMO) are common psychological vulnerabilities during emerging adulthood, yet their item-level organization and daily temporal associations remain underexplored. Study 1 ( N = 875) used item-level network analysis in an undergraduate sample to examine the conditional association structure of IU and FoMO. Study 2 ( N = 235) used a 14-day diary design and dynamic structural equation modeling to examine their within-person temporal associations at the construct level. In Study 1, IU and FoMO formed two communities with stronger within-community than cross-community connections. In Study 2, both constructs showed autoregressive continuity and positive bidirectional cross-lagged associations. Higher daily IU was associated with higher next-day FoMO, while higher daily FoMO was associated with higher next-day IU. Together, the findings describe complementary aspects of the IU-FoMO relationship: Study 1 identifies candidate item-level interface domains, whereas Study 2 independently shows temporal coupling between daily IU and daily FoMO at the construct level. These findings may inform future research and the development of interventions for uncertainty-related distress and socially specific missing-out concerns among college students. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Audit fees under accounting and auditing standards: A communicative action perspective
Abstract: This study investigates audit fee determination under accounting and auditing standards by moving beyond dominant economic and agency-based explanations toward a critical, normative perspective. The study conceptualizes audit fees as a social construct shaped by the interaction between professional judgment, regulatory systems, and market forces by using Theory of Communicative Action developed by Jürgen Habermas. Using a semisystematic literature review (SsLR), this research synthesizes empirical audit fee studies published between 2010 and 2024 and analyzes them through a Habermasian lens to explore the tension between the auditors’ professional lifeworld and the systemic logic embedded in accounting and auditing standards. A comprehensive search of the Scopus database resulted in a final sample of 33 empirical studies. These studies were then used as the basis for an analysis examining how accounting and auditing regulations contribute to the colonisation of audit fee-setting practices. The findings indicate that standards such as IFRS, auditing standards, and regulatory oversight regimes function as steering mechanisms. These standards orient audit fee determination toward instrumental rationality, compliance, and risk mitigation. While these standards enhance transparency and comparability, they also increase audit complexity, documentation requirements, and litigation risk. The limitation of this study is that it depends on empirical literature with quantitative data. Nevertheless, this study contributes by expanding audit fee research into a normative-communicative framework, highlighting audit fees as a guiding medium in modern audit systems. This study offers a novel critical perspective by positioning audit fees as outcomes of communicative and power relations rather than purely economic transactions. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Authors: Zhang H.; Luo S.; Xie N.; Pan L.
Title: Precise integration of attack path and syntax logic analysis for vulnerability severity assessment
Abstract: Accurate assessment of vulnerability severity at the source code level is essential for anticipating potential risks and prioritizing remediation efforts. However, current approaches face two key challenges: (i) analyzing exploitability at the basic block level fragments syntactic and semantic logic, causing critical exploitation conditions to be overlooked and leading to severity misjudgments; and (ii) inferring attack paths from inter-block relationships often fails to distinguish benign control flows from exploit chains, polluting attack graphs with false paths and resulting in inaccurate exploitability assessment, especially for access-complexity-related evidence. To address these issues, we propose ASVA (Attack path and Syntax logic analysis for Vulnerability severity Assessment), a novel patch-aware source-code framework that integrates multi-scale syntactic logic extraction with attack path modeling. ASVA employs convolutional kernels with varying receptive fields to capture multi-scale syntactic patterns and leverages an attention mechanism to highlight exploitation logic, reducing misclassification. Furthermore, it utilizes CodeBERT to encode code lines and compute inter-line semantic relationships, enabling the construction of robust attack path representations that effectively distinguish genuine attack flows from normal control transitions. Experiments on two public datasets demonstrate that ASVA outperforms selected state-of-the-art baselines, improving accuracy and robustness over existing methods. This work underscores the importance of fine-grained logic modeling and attack path correlation in advancing automated vulnerability severity assessment. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Early-life adversity and long-term outcomes: evidence from the cocoa swollen shoot virus outbreak in the Gold Coast
Abstract: How do early-life economic shocks that do not directly affect human biology shape long-term development outcomes? While a large body of work documents persistent effects of early-life exposure to health crises, famines, and natural disasters, much less is known about shocks that operate through economic disruption. This study addresses this gap by examining the long-term effects of the Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus Disease (CSSVD), an agricultural epidemic that devastated cocoa production in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) during the 1940s. Combining historical data on climatically suitable cocoa-growing areas with georeferenced household survey data, I exploit variation in exposure across birth timing and space to estimate the epidemic's long-term effects. The results show that exposure during early childhood and school-going years led to substantial and persistent human capital deficits. Individuals exposed during early childhood lost about one year of schooling and were 8.5 percentage points (pp) less likely to obtain formal education, while those exposed during school-going years lost about 0.8 years of schooling and were 7.0 pp less likely to obtain formal education. Exposure is also associated with worse health outcomes, increasing morbidity by 6.2–8.5 pp and disability by 5–7.5 pp. In contrast, there is no systematic evidence of long-term effects on employment type or labor supply. Evidence on potential mechanisms points to both educational and occupational channels. Conditional on ever attending school, exposed individuals completed fewer years of schooling and were more likely to have incomplete primary education, indicating disruptions to both school progression and initial access to schooling. In addition, exposed individuals are more likely to work in the agricultural sector in adulthood, consistent with reduced educational attainment having narrowed their occupational options. These findings demonstrate that industry-specific economic shocks can generate long-term human capital deficits, even in the absence of direct biological exposure. © 2026 The Author

Authors: Yang Y.; Li J.; Li Y.; Zhang S.; Guo K.
Title: Facilitator or hallucination trap? A social-cognitive account of AI-generated misinformation handling in GenAI-assisted L2 writing
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has demonstrated remarkable potential in second language (L2) learning, yet it is prone to hallucinations. Empirical research on how GenAI-generated misinformation is handled in educational contexts remains scarce. Accordingly, little is known about how these practices shape learning processes and outcomes. Guided by social cognitive theory, the current study frames students' GenAI-assisted L2 writing (using a tailored GenAI writing agent) in a hallucination-prone context in which misinformation was implanted. We examine AI literacy, higher-order thinking resources (i.e., critical thinking and creativity), L2 writing resources (i.e., L2 writing grit and self-regulatory writing strategies), English writing self-efficacy (EWSE), AI-generated misinformation detection (AI-MD), and L2 writing performance within this framework. Using a multi-method approach, combining a qualitative interview study (N = 35), two lab experiments (N = 140), and a large-scale questionnaire survey (N = 406), we find that critical thinking positively predicts GenAI-assisted L2 writing performance via AI-MD, and that negative priming on AI hallucinations significantly improves students’ AI-MD and their GenAI-assisted L2 writing performance, relative to neutral or positive priming. Furthermore, the cross-sectional survey focuses on personal factors and shows that AI literacy significantly predicts EWSE both directly and indirectly through a cognitive–generative pathway involving higher-order thinking resources and a motivational–regulatory pathway involving L2 writing resources. These findings extend social-cognitive accounts of GenAI-assisted L2 writing and inform instruction that helps learners evaluate AI outputs, manage misinformation risks, and sustain their own writing processes. © 2026

Title: Journey to the bargaining table: Signaling, seeking, and screening
Abstract: Negotiation scholarship has focused extensively on what happens at the bargaining table—how parties make offers, manage conflict, and reach agreements. Far less attention has been paid to how parties get to the table in the first place. In this article, we argue that the journey to the table deserves greater scrutiny. We organize pre-table dynamics around three behaviors: signaling (communicating whether and how negotiation might proceed), seeking (approaching a counterpart to propose bargaining), and screening (deciding whether to engage with or withdraw from a seeker). We review recent and foundational work bearing on each, identifying where the field has made progress and where significant gaps remain. These pre-table processes have important implications for negotiated outcomes, for negotiations that never occur, and for understanding how opportunity and bias operate before parties ever sit down together. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Guan Y.; Guo H.; Wang X.; Zhou X.; Fu W.; Ding X.; Xia D.; Zhao S.
Title: Enhancing anaerobic digestion of lignite with nano-Fe2O3 modified biochar: roles of liquid phase reconfiguration and microbial metabolic promotion
Abstract: Anaerobic digestion of lignite represents a promising approach for low-rank coal resource utilization and energy structure optimization, offering broad application prospects. To this end, nano-Fe2O3 modified biochar (NIBC) was synthesized and evaluated against biochar. Synthesis and characterization confirmed the successful loading of nano-Fe2O3 onto biochar, which led to significantly improved material properties (e.g., surface area, porosity, and surface functional groups). Consequently, NIBC substantially enhanced methane production (81.88 ± 6.78%, 4.89 ± 0.41 mL/g), system stability, and substrate degradation. Mechanistic analyses revealed a synergistic reconfiguration of dissolved organic matter, characterized by a shift toward more bioavailable intermediates (tryptophan-like and protein-like components), alongside a marked enrichment of key microbial taxa (e.g., Pseudomonadota, Methanobacteriota, Methanosarcina) and their associated metabolic pathways (e.g., glycolysis, reductive acetyl-CoA pathway). This work elucidates the integrated physicochemical-biological mechanisms by which NIBC enhances lignite anaerobic digestion, revealing previously overlooked cross-scale linkages between material properties, liquid-phase chemistry, and microbial ecology. The findings suggest potential opportunities for the development of biowaste-derived additives and the utilization of low-rank coal resources. Future research could focus on process scale-up, continuous operation, and techno-economic assessment to evaluate the feasibility of such strategies under practical conditions. Overall, this study provides a mechanistic foundation for advancing the clean conversion of lignite and supports the development of more sustainable bioenergy technologies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Management: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
Abstract: This study presents an examination of artificial intelligence (AI) in the disaster management (DM) cycle to support human decision-making systems. There is an urgent need for holistic application strategies that support disaster risk reduction given the increasing frequency and severity of disaster events. This stems from the growing adoption of AI technologies, including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and natural language processing in transforming disaster management. This is to enable the development of high-performance tools for assessing disaster impacts and addressing un-met human needs. This study reviewed journals and conference proceedings articles from three different academic databases: Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Article selection and query refinement were conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to support methodological approach. The review explored scholarly perspectives on AI application in DM phases to support human-centered decision-making processes in reducing disaster impacts on human lives. Findings from the review indicate that most existing studies focus primarily on the AI application in the response phase. Despite its potential, integrating AI into disaster management remains challenging, particularly due to widespread misconceptions about adoption of AI, as well as ongoing ethical, trust, and security concerns. This study emphasizes the comprehensive application of AI to enhance planning, encourage proactive measures, and improve response and recovery efforts during disaster events. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Pu Y.; Chen H.; Guo Y.
Title: Autonomy-supportive mediation and scam susceptibility: The role of literacy among middle-aged and older adults
Abstract: Although online scams increasingly threaten middle-aged and older adults, existing research has largely focused on individual literacy and short-term interventions, leaving the development and application of scam literacy in everyday contexts less understood. Drawing on parental mediation theory and self-determination theory, this study conceptualizes autonomy-supportive mediation (ASM) as a family-based socialization context for developing aging parents' scam-related literacy. It also considers face concern, a personal orientation reflecting individuals’ motivation to protect their social image from potential social judgment. This study tested two complementary models that distinguish between the foundation of scam literacy (scam knowledge) and its activation (cyber-risk beliefs). Data were collected through a cross-sectional vignette-based survey of 404 middle-aged and older adults in China between February 13 and February 27, 2025, using a volunteer-assisted convenience sampling strategy. The results indicated that higher levels of ASM were linked to lower scam loss, with this association mediated by scam knowledge and moderated by face concern. Moreover, ASM was positively related to cyber-risk beliefs, which were subsequently linked to greater systematic information processing and suspicion toward potential scams. These findings suggest that effective scam prevention depends not only on what individuals know, but also on whether they recognize and respond to risks in real-world situations. This study highlights the importance of autonomy-supportive family communication in combating online scams. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: “The Right to Repair”: A systematic literature review and research agenda for an emerging interdisciplinary field
Abstract: The Right to Repair (R2R) is an important arena in which restrictive repair practices, including limits on access to spare parts, manuals, software, and specialised tools, as well as product designs that inhibit repair, are being contested. Although scholarly interest in R2R is growing rapidly, research remains fragmented across disciplinary and empirical domains, limiting the development of a coherent understanding of its implications for technology-society relations. In response, this paper presents a systematic literature review that maps and synthesises existing research on R2R. Specifically, it (1) consolidates empirical evidence on the implications of R2R; (2) examines how the concept has been theorised across disciplines; and (3) identifies key conceptual and methodological gaps that constrain theoretical and empirical advancement in the field. By organising this literature into coherent thematic domains and tracing the relationships between them, the review argues that the effective realisation of R2R depends on a socio-technical capacity: the practically exercisable ability to repair produced through the interaction between legal entitlements, technological architectures, economic arrangements, and social capabilities. It also reveals disciplinary and geographical imbalances and identifies four tensions structuring future research: formal ownership versus effective control, legal entitlement versus practical repair capacity, universal frameworks versus situated repair practices, and systemic transformation versus continuity. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Dependent development at the energy transition: placing lithium imaginaries in Neoliberal and Contentious Peru
Abstract: We examine lithium and development imaginaries in mining-dependent Peru, asking: What are these imaginaries? What narratives underpin them? Who articulates and shares them, and from where? What forms of state (in)action are envisioned in relation to them? The case study elucidates how alternative “imagined futures” coexist within a natural resource–dependent economy. The ruling national elites in Lima have a neoliberal imagination, treating lithium like any other mineral resource in the country. In contrast, professional elites in the mineral-rich but peripheral region of Puno adopt a resource nationalist view, advocating for direct state involvement in lithium industrialization and the transformation of the domestic energy system, shaped by beliefs on Bolivia's developmental pathway. Among rural community leaders as well as political and social leaders in the districts near lithium and uranium deposits, however, the prevailing idea is that of a social license. In this view, each community has the capacity to negotiate development terms with mining companies independently. In the broader imagination at the resource periphery of a peripheral national economy, the state is perceived primarily as a minimalist governmental actor, necessary only to oversee and ensure the enforcement of mine-community agreements and to provide basic infrastructure. Thus, elites at the political center and communities near expected resource developments converge in their immediate pursuit of rents promised by resource commodification. Title: Fractional class-specific weighted random forest optimization

Title: Turning rivals into partners? emission reduction technology licensing strategies under market encroachment and Cap-and-Trade regulation
Abstract: This study examines the optimal licensing strategy for an emission reduction technology (ERT) innovator under Cap-and-Trade (C&T) regulation and the threat of market encroachment by a new entrant. Furthermore, under entrant cost heterogeneity, licensing to the incumbent establishes an effective entry barrier to lock out the entrant, whereas royalty-licensing to the entrant serves as a flexible co-optation tool when entry is inevitable. Abstract: Carbon markets have encountered challenges such as limited flexibility and substantial price volatility. Intertemporal trading mechanisms, as one of the important ways of green finance, have been proposed as a potential solution to improve market efficiency. However, existing studies frequently overlook whether the intricate internal mechanisms of carbon markets are suitable for introducing intertemporal trading. To comprehensively analyze the effect of intertemporal trading, this study employs a computable general equilibrium model incorporating an intertemporal dynamic mechanism and a carbon market module. This study designs scenarios focusing on total quotas, sectoral coverage, quota allocation, and intertemporal trading to simulate and compare their macroeconomic impacts. The results suggest that intertemporal trading is particularly beneficial in carbon markets that prioritize later-stage reduction, experience rapid sectoral coverage, or have a high auction rate. Under these conditions, introducing intertemporal trading can help reduce long-term carbon prices while promoting the development of cumulative GDP and household welfare. Title: A socio-technical maturity framework for design firms to enable the transition to design-out-waste in Indonesia's construction sector
Abstract: The construction sector remains a major driver of resource depletion and solid waste generation, with a substantial share traceable to early design-stage decisions. Design-out-Waste (DoW) strategies, including waste-efficient documentation, modern construction methods, and prefabrication, represent a proactive approach to enhancing lifecycle resource efficiency. However, their implementation remains fragmented, particularly in developing-country contexts, partly due to the lack of a structured framework for assessing organisational maturity. This study addresses this gap by developing an empirically grounded socio-technical maturity framework for DoW implementation in building design firms. The framework integrates five socio-technical dimensions into a single operational model encompassing processes & procedures, people & culture, industry structures, technology, and goals & incentives. Using data from 116 construction professionals, Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed to validate the measurement and structural relationships, while Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) provided empirical importance values for weighting the maturity dimensions and attributes. These weights were subsequently integrated with a five-level maturity scoring scheme to operationalise the assessment framework. The results reveal an interdependent socio-technical structure, with Industry Structure emerging as the most influential dimension and an important upstream driver of other organisational capabilities. The resulting framework provides an empirically weighted basis for assessing organisational readiness, identifying capability priorities, and guiding DoW implementation towards circular construction. It also provides a structured basis for informing environmental assessment, project appraisal, and policy interventions aimed at improving resource efficiency and waste prevention. © 2026

Title: GenAI-enabled human–AI collaboration: An integrative review of local augmentation, hidden work, and governable synergy
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming part of everyday knowledge work, where it can accelerate drafting, coding, summarization, ideation, customer communication, and other language-intensive tasks. Yet the organizational problem is conversion: local GenAI gains create organizational value only when they survive the full work system, including verification, coordination, learning, ownership, risk, and accountability. Drawing on 251 academic and practice-facing sources across information systems (IS), management, human–computer interaction, human factors, organizational theory, and responsible AI, this article synthesizes why GenAI-enabled work often produces local augmentation but less often yields governable organizational synergy. The review develops three findings. First, GenAI shifts the relevant unit of collaboration from a one-step task interaction to a recurrent production-and-revision workflow in which human framing, prompting, verification, correction, and reuse become part of the value-producing system. Second, the augmentation-to-synergy boundary is net work-system value: visible task gains and reallocation benefits must exceed work displaced across roles and time into verification, rework, coordination, learning, ownership, risk, and accountability. Third, durable synergy requires behavioral embedding and multi-outcome governance: prompts, memory, feedback traces, review routines, and escalation rules must improve local fit while keeping reliance, learning, ownership, risk, and accountability observable. The article contributes a work-system conversion account that distinguishes substitution, augmentation, and synergy as different organizational states; a trace-centered behavioral-embedding view of how recurring GenAI use becomes a persistent, history-dependent workflow state within established sociotechnical IS theory; and a governance-instrumentation account that evaluates visible gains together with hidden labor, learning, ownership, risk, reviewability, and accountability. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Events under fire: Developing an urgent anthropology for events during armed conflicts
Abstract: This conceptual and methodological research note addresses event industry dynamics during armed conflicts, proposing an urgent anthropology approach to document transformations in real time. Using Ukraine as an example, we illustrate how event organizations have adapted to existential threats since the 2022 Russian invasion, demonstrating resilience through cultural initiatives, charitable events, and creative repurposing of resources. We argue that these practices have the potential to sustain cultural identity and to contribute to economic development, social cohesion and morale in conflict settings. To overcome the methodological and ethical challenges of traditional ethnography in war zones, we propose a novel citizen science framework within the urgent anthropology paradigm, leveraging digital technologies, social media, and participatory methods. Title: A multi-similarity matching framework for remaining useful life prediction based on spatiotemporal health indicators
Abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction is a critical task in prognostics and health management (PHM) of industrial equipment. Health indicator (HI) based RUL prediction methods have attracted increasing attention because they represent equipment degradation using low-dimensional and interpretable trajectories. However, most existing similarity-based methods assess degradation similarity primarily through health indicators, without adequately exploiting temporal degradation characteristics and spatial dependencies among sensor data. Moreover, most methods provide only point estimates, limiting the characterization of prediction uncertainty and prediction reliability. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel RUL prediction framework that performs multi-similarity matching based on spatiotemporal feature representations and HIs. The proposed framework consists of three modules: a degradation trajectory module, a health indicator construction module, and a multi-similarity prediction module. Specifically, the degradation trajectory module utilizes sensor data to construct degradation trajectories and extract temporal and spatial features. Based on the learned degradation trajectories, the health indicator construction module employs a change-point detection method to identify the onset of degradation and generate health indicators, while an offline HI library is established by constructing health indicators from multiple equipments. A multi-similarity matching strategy is developed to estimate the RUL of target equipment, and prediction intervals are constructed to quantify prediction uncertainty. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves improved prediction accuracy and robustness compared with existing approaches. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.
