Title: Carbon trading in community-based forest management: A bibliometric mapping of scientific publications from 2000 to 2025
Abstract: Carbon trading in community-based forest management (CBFM) has emerged as a promising mechanism for simultaneously addressing climate change mitigation and improving the welfare of rural communities. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 203 scientific publications obtained from Scopus, covering the period 2000 to 2025, with an analytical focus on the period 2010-2024. Using VOSviewer v.1.6.20 and Scopus's built-in analysis, this study analyzes publication trends, author participation patterns, geographic distribution, journal sources, and thematic structure through author collaboration, co-occurrence of keywords, and bibliographic linking networks. Results show a sharp acceleration in publication growth following key climate policy milestones, including the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (2013), the Paris Agreement (2015), and COP26 (2021), with a record 21 articles published in 2024. Nepal and Indonesia emerged as dominant knowledge producers, collectively contributing 42.4% of total publications. Thematic mapping identified three main research clusters: carbon governance in CBFM, carbon measurement and quantification, and multifunctional forest landscape ecology. A critical knowledge gap was identified: while the supply side of carbon measurement of forest carbon stocks and biomass has been well documented, the demand side of how communities access, negotiate, and fairly obtain benefits from carbon markets remains largely unexplored. These findings underscore the urgent need for interdisciplinary research that links technical carbon measurement with institutional, economic, and social dimensions of equity to promote fair and scalable carbon trading within the framework of community forest governance. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Authors: Lin S.; Liu Q.
Title: “Crossing the river by feeling the stones”: Sub-national agency in China's highway maintenance marketisation
Abstract: Marketisation reforms in China are often described as an extension of Western New Public Management (NPM), yet their meanings and effects vary substantially across regions and remain poorly understood from the perspective of policymakers themselves. Drawing on document review and interviews with sub-national officials and practitioners involved in highway maintenance in two underdeveloped provinces, this study examines how marketisation is interpreted, justified, and enacted through a "learning by doing" process shaped by administrative legacies, political incentives, and constrained market environments. The analysis shows that NPM-related principles, such as competition and performance management, are selectively adapted rather than directly transplanted, producing hybrid arrangements that combine bureaucratic control with quasi-market practices dominated by state-owned enterprises. The study identifies four narrative frames through which policymakers explain and evaluate reforms, as well as the recurring strategy of deliberate inaction, which emerges as a pragmatic response to tensions between central expectations and local socio-economic realities. It also considers the broader implications of marketisation for highway service performance, public satisfaction, fiscal sustainability, and technical capacity, pointing to uneven outcomes and persistent governance tensions. By foregrounding sub-national agency and context-sensitive adaptation, the article contributes to understanding policy transfer, the institutional logics shaping China's state-led market reforms, and the prospects for more sustainable infrastructure governance in less developed regions. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Incomplete markets, crop portfolios, and agricultural productivity
Abstract: Using the Uganda National Panel Survey, I document that farmers face a trade-off between crop yields and risk, that most grow both high- and low-yield crops, and that poorer farmers concentrate on the low-yield, low-risk ones. I then develop an incomplete-markets model with a crop-portfolio choice, in which households trade off income returns against consumption smoothing. Wealth-poor households optimally under-invest in intermediates and shift toward safer crops. Crop portfolios, intermediate input use, and the wealth distribution are jointly determined in equilibrium. The model also reproduces the low pass-through of both income inequality and income volatility into consumption. Calibrated to rural Uganda, it implies that completing markets raises agricultural productivity by 12.8%, with 15.8% of the gain coming from eliminating the misallocation of inputs across farmers and crops. Consumption rises by 17.6% and welfare by 17.4%, with income inequality rising slightly and consumption inequality unchanged. © 2026 The Author

Authors: Hu J.
Title: Beyond sales: Seller explanation, product availability, and returns in livestream commerce
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Livestream commerce combines seller explanation with continued product availability in a shopping cart. Our data separately record seller explanation duration and cart availability duration; these measures do not isolate informational content or establish actual consumer exposure. Sales alone may miss differences in the postpurchase outcomes associated with these durations. We therefore examine product returns as an indicator of postpurchase outcomes, estimating associations with streamer–product and broadcast fixed effects on a panel of nearly 190,000 livestream product listings. The two durations diverge sharply: longer explanation is associated with a lower return rate and longer cart availability with a higher one, even though both are associated with higher sales. The divergence widens with the scope for uncertainty about whether a product suits a particular buyer, while the price–discount pattern does not match the specific impulse-purchasing prediction examined here. The pattern is consistent with a buyer-screening interpretation, but the data do not observe purchasers’ exposure to explanation or distinguish screening from alternatives such as telepresence. Since only one of the two is scarce, the margin a seller controls is the allocation of the host's attention rather than the length of a product's stay in the cart. © 2026

Title: Global stochastic maximum principle of regime-switching systems with time-varying delay under non-convex control domains
Abstract: This paper establishes a global stochastic maximum principle for regime-switching systems with time-varying delays under non-convex control domains. Title: Does artificial intelligence improve social stability risk performance in China?
Abstract: This paper examines whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to improving the social stability risk level in China. Against the backdrop of rapid digital transformation and increasingly complex governance challenges, AI has been widely adopted in areas such as public security, social management, and risk monitoring. However, its actual effectiveness in mitigating social stability risks remains underexplored. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions in China, this study constructs an empirical framework to evaluate the impact of AI policy on social stability risk levels. The analysis integrates indicators of technological capacity, governance performance, and socio-economic conditions, and applies quantitative methods to identify both direct and indirect effects. The findings suggest that AI policy significantly reduces social stability risks by promoting digital economy development, increasing wage levels and investment in education. At the same time, the results reveal notable regional heterogeneity. The AI policy significantly reduces social stability risk in the central and western regions, and areas with moderate digital economy development, but has no statistically significant effect in economically developed and digitally advanced areas. The study also highlights potential challenges, including data governance concerns and uneven technological access, which may offset some of AI's benefits. This research contributes to the literature by linking technological innovation with social governance outcomes and provides policy implications for leveraging AI to promote social stability. It suggests that policymakers should not only invest in AI infrastructure but also address institutional and regional disparities to ensure inclusive and effective risk management. © 2026 The Authors

Title: One count, three processes: Rethinking administrative stability in Korea's fuel-cell and renewable licensing pipeline
Abstract: Administrative amendment counts conflate recurrent filings, schedule revisions, and changes in project ownership or specification. This article develops a Frequency-Magnitude-Type framework for interpreting incomplete development records and identifying the additional information needed for monitoring. Applied to Korea's RPS-era generation-licensing pipeline, it combines action-specific filing counts, planned-deadline displacement, and filing types over common project-age windows. Rebuilding the April 2001-June 2026 ledger yields 4804 records and a dated panel of 1813 projects; principal comparisons use 1018 projects with closed three-year windows. Fuel cells and onshore wind show no statistically detectable difference in extension incidence or intensity, whereas onshore wind has 1.44 times the adjusted deadline displacement among projects with positive movement. Project-level joint analysis adds distinctions that separate technology comparisons conceal. Twenty projects record positive deadline movement without a preparation-period extension, and projects with exactly one extension exhibit different displacement distributions. Ownership-transfer tags further distinguish administrative histories within the same frequency groups. Missing deadlines are retained as missing information rather than unchanged schedules. The resulting profiles describe administrative activity, not commissioning, and direct attention to the records needed to investigate it. Title: Generative AI use and sustainable pedagogical practices as predictors of 4Cs skill development: The mediating role of digital literacy among international postgraduate students in China
Abstract: This study examines how Generative AI Use (GAU) and Sustainable Pedagogical Practices (SPP) are associated with international postgraduate students’ critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and communication (4Cs), with Digital Literacy (DL) examined as a mediator. Using survey data from 369 international Master’s and PhD students at China’s C9 League universities, this study applies Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) analysis. The 4Cs were modeled as a higher-order construct comprising four lower-order dimensions. The results show that both GAU and SPP are positively associated with students’ 4Cs, with SPP showing the largest standardized direct association. GAU and SPP are also positively associated with DL, which in turn is positively associated with the 4Cs. Significant indirect associations of both GAU and SPP with the higher-order 4Cs construct were observed through DL. The ANN results provide complementary predictive evidence, with SPP showing the highest normalized predictive importance, followed by GAU and DL. Together, the findings support a technology–pedagogy–capability perspective in which pedagogical design shows the largest standardized direct association with 4Cs development, while DL functions as a learner-side information-processing capability linking AI-supported and sustainability-oriented learning experiences with competence development. For practice, the findings suggest that universities may benefit from embedding generative AI within structured, sustainability-oriented learning activities that emphasize information verification, responsible use, and collaborative problem solving. Title: Registered Report - Stage II: Do good, feel luckier: How cause-related marketing in unpredictable tourism products boosts tourists’ purchase intention?
Abstract: Marketing unpredictable tourism experiences like aurora or wildlife viewing poses distinct challenges due to their inherent uncertainty, yet research on effective strategies remains limited. In Stage I of this Registered Report, we proposed that cause-related marketing (CRM) would boost purchase intention for unpredictable tourism products more effectively than traditional discounts by activating a karmic investment mechanism (i.e., self-luck expectancy), especially under consumer-focused framing. Through an eye-tracking experiment, a quasi-experimental field study, and three scenario-based experiments, we found no conclusive evidence that CRM outperforms discounts in increasing purchase intention, nor support for the mediating role of self-luck expectancy. Although a moderating influence of protagonist focus was observed, its effect contradicted our hypothesis. However, an unexpected finding emerged: luck primes significantly elevate self-luck expectancy and enhance purchase intention. These results suggest that practitioners should either exercise caution in deploying standard CRM from a cost-benefit perspective or enhance its utility by fostering deeper consumer moral engagement. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: From expectations to experience: How tasting plant-based fermented foods shapes consumption intentions
Abstract: Increasing consumption of plant-based fermented foods (PBFF) is beneficial for both public health and environment, yet intake among Western meat-eaters remains low. Product-specific patterns were observed: tasting increased intentions for the well-liked sourdough bread, but decreased intentions for the lesser-liked plant-based fermented meat. Sensory liking of the specific PBFF product was the strongest predictor of intentions for sourdough bread and plant-based fermented dairy, beyond expectations, whereas effects for plant-based fermented meat were weaker and less consistent. Title: Discrete Gauss linking integral representations of correlation trajectories for market stress diagnosis
Abstract: Market stress is commonly characterized using contemporaneous correlation levels or other low-dimensional summaries of market dependence, potentially discarding information contained in the ordered evolution of correlation states. We develop a discrete Gauss linking integral (dGLI) representation that retains pairwise contributions between nonadjacent segments of rolling market-correlation trajectories. Our primary representation, dGLI-Reorganization, aligns the same underlying segment pairs across consecutive trajectory windows and measures changes in the organization of their pairwise contribution map.Using S&P 500 constituent data and stress targets constructed from the S&P 500 benchmark index, we evaluate the representation through chronological expanding-window out-of-sample testing and compare it with conventional correlation summaries, trajectory kinematics, market-state transition measures, and persistent-homology features. Relative to the five-variable correlation-state (CorrState) baseline, dGLI-Reorganization increases the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of the random-forest classifier from 0.719 to 0.785 for the Composite stress target, from 0.755 to 0.806 for the 10% drawdown target, and from 0.767 to 0.849 for the 15% drawdown target. The paired improvements in AUC and average precision have 95% confidence intervals entirely above zero for all three targets. MeanCorr and alternative representations nevertheless remain competitive under some target–metric combinations.Across five additional equity markets, Reorganization has a higher pooled AUC than CorrState under market-specific refitting, although the magnitude of the increment varies across markets. Sensitivity analyses show that the magnitude of the increment depends on temporal scale. A separate prospective analysis does not establish a reliable short-horizon drawdown-prediction advantage over CorrState.Overall, the results support aligned-pair dGLI-Reorganization as an incremental representation of dependence-path restructuring for contemporaneous market-stress diagnosis. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The impact of critique on LLM-based model generation from natural language: the case of activity diagrams
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for automating model generation from natural-language descriptions. A common approach begins with an initial model generation, followed by an iterative critique-refine loop in which the model is evaluated for issues and refined based on those issues. This process needs to address: (1) structural correctness – compliance with well-formedness rules – and (2) semantic alignment – accurate reflection of the intended meaning in the source text. We present LADEX (LLM-based Activity Diagram Extractor), a pipeline for deriving activity diagrams from natural-language process descriptions using an LLM-driven critique-refine process. Structural checks in LADEX can be performed either algorithmically or by an LLM, while alignment checks are performed by an LLM. We design five ablated variants of LADEX to study: (i) the impact of the critique-refine loop itself, (ii) the role of LLM-based semantic checks, and (iii) the comparative effectiveness of algorithmic versus LLM-based structural checks. To evaluate LADEX, we compare the generated activity diagrams with expert-created ground truths using both trace-based behavioural matcher and an LLM-based activity-diagram matcher. This enables automated measurement of correctness (whether the generated activity diagram includes the ground-truth nodes) and completeness (how many of the ground-truth nodes the generated activity diagram covers). Experiments on two datasets – a public-domain dataset and an industry dataset from our collaborator, Ciena – indicate that: (1) Both the behavioural and LLM matchers yield similar completeness and correctness comparisons across the LADEX variants. (2) The critique–refine loop improves structural validity, correctness, and completeness compared to single-pass generation. (3) Activity diagrams refined based on algorithmic structural checks achieve structural consistency, whereas those refined based on LLM-based checks often still show structural inconsistencies. (4) Combining algorithmic structural checks with LLM-based semantic checks (using O4 Mini) delivers the strongest results – up to 86% correctness and 92% completeness – while requiring fewer than five LLM calls on average. Title: Shared but feared: A vulnerability-sensitive account of consumer responses to post-crisis service environments
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Shared service environments are typically designed to facilitate comfort, efficiency, and positive consumer experiences. In post-crisis contexts, however, these environments may also be appraised through concerns about exposure, controllability, and personal vulnerability. Building on a context-specific refinement of the organismic component within the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this research examines how residual infection-related fear is associated with consumer responses to shared service environments in a post-pandemic context. A two-study design was implemented within a single French-language survey (N = 425). Study 1 tested whether residual infection-related fear was associated with avoidance of public service environments through differentiated forms of health anxiety. Structural equation modeling showed that residual infection-related fear was positively associated with both personal and interpersonal health anxiety, but only personal health anxiety was associated with avoidance, yielding a significant indirect effect through the self-focused pathway. Study 2 experimentally manipulated store density (high vs. low) and sanitary signals (present vs. absent) to examine how servicescape cues influenced perceived crowding and shopping satisfaction. Results showed that higher density reduced satisfaction, but this negative effect was attenuated when sanitary signals were present. Perceived crowding did not mediate the density–satisfaction relationship. A separate exploratory analysis indicated that the overall association between sanitary signals and satisfaction was more positive among individuals reporting higher residual infection-related fear. Taken together, the findings suggest that post-crisis responses to shared service environments may reflect the interplay between situational cues and heterogeneous vulnerability orientations, consistent with a vulnerability-sensitive appraisal system. The research offers a context-specific contribution to servicescape theory by suggesting that, under residual health-threat salience, organismic processes may require a more differentiated specification in contexts marked by residual threat, and by highlighting how visible safety-related cues may improve evaluations of dense service environments. Exploratory evidence further suggests that the overall association between such cues and satisfaction is more positive among consumers who remain more sensitive to infection-related risk. © 2026 The Authors

Title: When perception meets reality: explaining measured food waste through consumer behavior in a university dining hall
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Food waste (FW) in university dining halls generates significant environmental and economic impacts, yet most studies rely on self-reported measures and rarely combine behavioral perceptions with objective waste data. This study investigates the determinants of consumer FW by integrating individual plate-waste measurements with behavioral and dining-related factors in a university dining hall setting. Data were collected from 422 diners using a 31-item questionnaire, along with individual measurements of avoidable plate waste after meals. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied to examine behavioral relationships and differences across demographic and meal-related groups. Average plate waste reached 51.5 g per person, with higher waste levels observed during lunch and among female diners. Self-perceived waste behavior, intention to reduce FW, and sensory satisfaction were directly associated with the measured amount of discarded food. In contrast, consumer knowledge, portion size perception, and available eating time influenced only perceived waste behavior, revealing a disconnect between awareness and objectively measured PW. The findings highlight the importance of dining context and meal satisfaction in shaping consumer FW and demonstrate the value of integrating subjective perceptions with objective waste measurements. By combining behavioral evidence with direct waste quantification, this study advances methodological approaches to consumer FW research and provides insights for designing more effective waste reduction strategies in institutional food services. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Assessing Perceived Construction Risk Allocation and Agreement under Design-Bid-Build Contracts: Evidence from a Developing Country
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: This paper examines perceived construction risk allocation under design-bid-build contracts and evaluates the degree of agreement between clients and contractors regarding which party should bear specific risks in the Indonesian construction context. Data were collected through a questionnaire survey of 53 respondents, who evaluated the allocation of 73 construction risks. Descriptive analysis based on median values was used to identify general patterns of risk allocation, while inferential analysis examined differences in perception and associations between allocation and agreement. Agreement was assessed at both the aggregate and individual risk item levels. The results indicate that contractors are perceived as bearing the majority of construction risks, and no statistically significant differences are observed between client and contractor respondents in risk allocation. Overall, allocation patterns are broadly consistent with expectations. However, several deviations are observed in which risks are partially shifted to other parties, even though they are largely within a single party's control. At the aggregate level, agreement is found to be unacceptable, with nearly half of the risks exhibiting a lack of or weak agreement, particularly for client-related and shared risks. Contractor respondents display higher levels of agreement, and risks allocated more heavily to contractors are associated with stronger agreement. These findings highlight the potential for conflict arising from disagreement in risk allocation and offer theoretical and practical implications.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Competitive anion precipitation governs corrosion product film evolution on corrosion-resistant magnesium alloys in physiological solutions
Abstract: In solutions containing Cl− as the base electrolyte, adding either H2PO4−/HPO42− or HCO3− markedly lowers the corrosion rates of Mg-Al-Y alloy wires, suppresses severe localized corrosion and promotes more uniform degradation. When both anions are present, their competitive interactions alter early corrosion product evolution and lead to a less continuous and less protective corrosion product film. Thermodynamic calculations indicate that phase accessibility depends on local pH and ion activities, while quasi-in situ FTIR reveals distinct early interfacial evolution of P- and C-containing species. Subsequent product retention may additionally depend on dissolution tendency and interfacial bonding. First-principles calculations further show that, in the selected idealized models, the carbonate-containing interface exhibits a higher Cl− migration barrier, whereas the phosphate-containing interface exhibits stronger interfacial adhesion. Title: Using emojis to uplift emotion: Effects on mental health chatbots’ performance
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As AI-based chatbots increasingly expand access to mental health support, understanding how text-based systems convey emotional attentiveness without face-to-face nonverbal cues is important. Emojis may serve as lightweight paralinguistic cues, yet their effects in mental health support remain unclear. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and psychological ownership theory, this study examines associations between emoji use and users’ emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Two scenario-based online experiments were conducted in China using random sampling through Credamo, yielding 459 valid responses (59 in the pretest and 400 in the main study). Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26 and the PROCESS macro. Across the experiments, emoji use was associated with more favorable emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Mediation analyses supported an indirect pathway through perceived warmth and psychological ownership, whereas the corresponding competence-based pathway was not supported. AI literacy strengthened the perceived warmth–psychological ownership association but, contrary to predictions, weakened the perceived competence–psychological ownership association. Moderated mediation analyses provided preliminary support for AI literacy strengthening the warmth-based indirect effects of emoji use on emotional well-being and continuance usage intention. The corresponding effect on satisfaction was not supported. These findings extend research on AI-mediated mental health support by identifying a warmth–psychological ownership pathway and the differentiated role of AI literacy. The study also offers preliminary, context-bounded guidance for the strategic and context-sensitive use of emojis in supportive, non-clinical chatbot interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
Abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Professional identity as the missing link: Understanding motivational pathways among hotel employees
Abstract: Hospitality research has often viewed motivation as the primary mechanism linking managerial practices to employee behavior. However, less attention has been paid to how employees interpret such practices before motivational responses emerge. Drawing on professional identity research, this study examines Professional Identity as an interpretive mechanism linking employees’ perceptions of Rewards and Transformational Leadership to Motivation and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Using survey data from 325 frontline hotel employees in South Korea, we test an individual-level model connecting Developmental Rewards, Material Rewards, Transformational Leadership, Professional Identity, Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, and OCB. The results show significant indirect associations between Developmental Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation and between Transformational Leadership and Intrinsic Motivation through Professional Identity. Developmental Rewards and Transformational Leadership were also indirectly associated with OCB through Professional Identity and Intrinsic Motivation. In contrast, the hypothesized Material Rewards pathways through Professional Identity and Extrinsic Motivation were not supported. These findings extend hospitality motivation research by highlighting the importance of identity-affirming managerial practices in frontline service settings. © 2026

Title: Terrorism and altruistic giving: Evidence from child sponsorship
Abstract: We study how terrorist attacks targeting educational institutions affect private development aid through child sponsorship. Conceptually, terrorist events may increase sponsorship by signaling greater need or reduce it if affected communities are seen as less effective destinations to support. We combine global administrative data from Plan International on child sponsorship across 50 countries over the 2008-2018 period, aggregated at the Primary Sampling Unit (PSU) level, with geocoded terrorism events from the Global Terrorism Database. Our core specification focuses on attacks against educational institutions within 20 km of each PSU. We estimate the causal effect using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences approach suited to staggered, non-absorbing treatments. We find that attacks on educational institutions reduce the share of sponsored children by about 3 percentage points, a 4 percent decline relative to the mean. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest this corresponds to funding losses of approximately US$615,000 across affected communities over the study period. Since sponsorship is geographically targeted, these losses fall on the specific communities, underscoring the need to buffer local development funding against security shocks. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Microstructure and bulk rheology of heat-induced emulsion-filled pea protein gels: Effect of high-pressure homogenization
Abstract: High-pressure homogenization (HPH) is often applied to process protein-stabilized emulsions. However, it remains unclear how HPH affects the interactions between protein-gel matrix and interfacial protein-coated oil or fat droplets, as well as the consequent network breakdown of the system. We investigated the differences in microstructure and rheological properties of emulsion-filled gels structured by unhomogenized or homogenized 8.5% commercial pea protein isolate containing 0, 10, or 20% lipid. Confocal images showed that the unhomogenized systems exhibited large protein-depleted regions, whereas the homogenized systems formed densely-packed networks. Small amplitude oscillatory shear (SAOS) temperature sweeps showed that gels containing 10% lipid were not significantly stiffer than gels without lipid, and their large amplitude oscillatory shear (LAOS) strain-amplitude sweeps showed similar yield points, yielding regimes and flow points. At 20% lipid, gel stiffness decreased notably, and yielding began at lower strain amplitude (γ0[jls-end-space/]). In contrast, HPH markedly increased gel stiffness, with further stiffening at higher lipid contents. Meanwhile, these gels yielded at lower γ0 over a broader range at higher lipid contents, and their loss modulus overshoot coincided with the rise in shear-thickening ratio. Moreover, sequence of physical processes (SPP) analysis showed that, as γ0 increased, the deltoid area changed more dramatically for 20% oil than for 20% fat, indicating that HPH shifted interfacial protein-coated lipid droplets from inactive fillers to active fillers that integrate into gradually yielding, denser networks. Fat droplets were more resistant to stretching and rupturing than oil droplets. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Optimal reinsurance, investment and dividend strategies with square-root factor model
Source title: Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications
Abstract: This paper studies the optimal reinsurance, investment and dividend strategies for an insurer who aims to maximize the expected discounted utility of dividend payments together with a discounted terminal value at ruin. The insurer can invest in a risky asset with price dynamics given by a square-root process, which includes the CEV, Heston and 4/2 models as special cases. We consider two types of instantaneous dividend utilities: exponential and logarithmic functions. The problem is formulated as a stochastic control problem with double stochastic state processes and nonlinear optimization objectives. Using dynamic programming, we derive the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations with nonlinear gradient components and provide analytical solutions for optimal strategies under both utilities. Our results show that the square-root factor process significantly influences the optimal policies, specially for the optimal investment. Title: The evolving science of negotiation alternatives: New contexts, new perspectives
Abstract: We review the past decade (2016 – present) of empirical research on negotiation alternatives across multiple disciplines, including dyadic bargaining, international trade, and civil conflict interventions. Three themes emerged in our analysis: First, research has focused on how the effects of a negotiator's BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) are not person-invariant but are instead moderated by the characteristics of the party who “holds” the BATNA. Second, studies are establishing the conditions under which negotiation alternatives can backfire and hurt a negotiator's performance. Third, an emerging stream of research challenges our conventional understanding of BATNA by highlighting its perceptual nature and the possibility that it may exist on multiple levels within a given negotiation. We close by outlining future directions for each of these emerging themes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Nodding of virtual humans does not necessarily increase customer trust: a temporal analysis
Abstract: Virtual humans can potentially facilitate engaging customer interactions, but remain rarely used in customer service. Their embodiment enables virtual humans to use non-verbal listening cues like nodding. Nodding is theorized to increase trust in virtual humans, but literature on this effect is scarce, inconsistent, and only uses measurements after interactions. This study therefore aims to research how nodding of virtual humans influences customer trust, by (1) studying the following hypothesized mediation: nodding (social cue) triggers perceived responsiveness (social signal), which subsequently increases trust (social response); and (2) studying temporal trust dynamics within a customer interaction using exploratory analyses. An online experiment (N = 429) was performed, using a between-subjects design with two conditions: a virtual human either nodded during listening or did not. To isolate nodding optimally, participants watched a video of a customer interaction: a virtual human advised a customer on a wardrobe. While watching, participants used a slider scale to keep updating their temporal trust in the virtual human. Afterwards, participants answered questionnaires on trust and perceived responsiveness. Results showed that nodding did not increase trust or perceived responsiveness, nor did nodding build temporal trust. Temporal trust was built throughout the customer interaction, mostly when the virtual human was speaking. Exploratory analysis found that nodding increased anthropomorphism. Possibly, nodding did not influence trust because other social cues already caused trust-building. Virtual human developers should therefore be aware that nodding does not necessarily build customer trust. Title: Qualitative Versus Quantitative Risk Assessment in Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) Audits: How European-Based Auditors Interpret Probability Under International Council for Harmonisation Guideline (ICH) Q9 (R1)
Abstract: Purpose: Under ICH Q9 (R1), risk is defined as a function of probability and severity of harm. Although probability may be expressed quantitatively, little empirical evidence exists regarding how EU GMP auditors assess probability in practice. This study explored probability assessment approaches among auditors and the use of qualitative and quantitative methods. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional questionnaire was administered to 52 EU-based GMP auditors with at least two years of auditing experience. Participants (21 in total) completed structured multiple-response questions on probability and optional free-text comment fields addressing probability assessment practices (response rate: 40.4%). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and cross-tabulation; no inferential analyses were performed. Results: Qualitative probability assessment approaches were the most frequently reported method (14/21), while 8/21 respondents reported using quantitative approaches (multiple responses permitted). Probability assessment was commonly described as context-dependent and informed by professional judgement rather than purely numerical models. Qualitative approaches were reported across all experience categories and levels of English proficiency. Participants highlighted limited availability of robust historical data, contextual complexity, and reliance on prior audit experience as key factors influencing probability assessment. Respondents (4/21) suggested that no single clear definition of probability assessment was consistently applied in practice. Conclusion: Although some participants reported using quantitative approaches, probability assessment remained predominantly qualitative and experience-based in audits. Participants frequently described using structured risk matrices and categorical probability scales (e.g., High/Medium/Low) to support probability assessments. The findings highlight variability in how probability is operationalised and suggest that additional practical guidance may be useful. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Li S.; Li X.; Du X.; Xin Z.
Title: How local–global identity shapes physical-digital preferences through convenience preference
Abstract: Despite the functional advantages of digital products, consumers’ preferences between digital and physical formats remain highly heterogeneous in a marketplace where globalization and renewed localism coexist. Drawing on identity-based motivation theory, this research examines how local versus global identity influences consumers' preferences for physical versus digital products through convenience preference. Across three studies (five sub-studies), we demonstrate that a relatively stronger local-over-global identity is associated with greater preference for physical over digital consumption formats. Further analyses reveal an asymmetric effect that local identity drives stronger preferences for physical products, whereas global identity does not produce a corresponding increase in preference for digital formats. We further identify convenience preference as the underlying mechanism, showing that stronger local identity reduces convenience preference, thereby increasing preference for physical products. These findings reconceptualize physical versus digital preferences as identity-consistent choices rather than purely functional evaluations. By identifying convenience as an identity-contingent motivational preference, this research advances identity-based motivation theory and provides timely insights into how identity orientations shape consumer preferences amid ongoing digital transformation and heightened societal attention to globalization–localism dynamics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Geopolitical risk and tourism firm resilience: Global evidence
Abstract: This paper analyzes how geopolitical risk affects the performance of tourism firms and identifies the conditions under which its adverse effects are mitigated. Using a global panel of 1438 firms across 39 countries from 2007 to 2021, we find that heightened geopolitical risk significantly reduces firms’ market valuations. Drawing on risk perception theory, network theory, and institutional theory, we show that this effect is conditional rather than uniform. Specifically, firms located in countries with stronger international tourism network embeddedness experience weaker negative effects, as network connectivity facilitates demand diversification and adaptive responses. Similarly, higher institutional quality reduces the adverse impact of geopolitical risk by enhancing stability and policy credibility. These findings are robust to alternative measures and estimation methods. Authors: Zhang X.; Sun L.; Chang L.; Sun Z.
Title: Natural Hazards, Critical Infrastructure Systems, and Resilience Enhancement: A Structured State-of-the-Art Review and a Synthesis-Based Rapid Assessment Framework
Abstract: Critical infrastructure systems (CISs) are increasingly exposed to natural hazards whose impacts are amplified by infrastructure interdependence, urban complexity, and the growing prevalence of compound and cascading events. Existing research provides valuable insights into individual hazards, infrastructure components, modeling methods, and resilience metrics, but these insights remain difficult to translate into preliminary decision support because they are organized across different hazard types, sectors, analytical scales, and decision contexts. This article presents a structured state-of-the-art review of natural hazards, CIS impacts, and resilience enhancement. A two-pathway review strategy was adopted. A Web of Science (WoS) core search was used to characterize the bibliometric landscape and identify WoS-sourced core synthesis studies, while a targeted anchor-search pathway was used to verify foundational concepts, hazard mechanisms, methodological approaches, resilience frameworks, and authoritative institutional sources. The review clarifies the conceptual distinction among dependencies, interdependencies, compound hazards, cascading failures, service disruption, and resilience; synthesizes cross-hazard infrastructure impact mechanisms; compares major method families for hazard-impact and resilience assessment; and develops a synthesis-derived rapid resilience assessment framework for preliminary screening and prioritization under constrained data and time conditions. The synthesis indicates that future CIS resilience assessment would benefit from moving beyond isolated asset-damage analysis toward integrated workflows that link hazard loading, component vulnerability, network functionality, service consequences, recovery capacity, uncertainty, and feasible intervention choices. The article contributes a more transparent evidence-source structure, an evidence-to-decision bridge, and a bounded decision-oriented framework for organizing future research and practical resilience screening.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Beyond wear scar diameter: A multi-technique investigation of lubricity enhancement and tribofilm formation in biodiesel blends with ultra-low sulphur diesel and bio-hydrogenated diesel
Abstract: Bio-hydrogenated diesel (BHD) and ultra-low sulphur diesel both exhibit poor intrinsic lubricity owing to the absence of polar functional groups. This study evaluated the lubricity of BHD and petroleum diesel blended with palm methyl ester (PME) and soybean methyl ester (SBME) using the High Frequency Reciprocating Rig test in accordance with ISO 12156-1:2023, with SBME at 2–70% v/v and PME at 2–15% v/v. Complementary surface analyses including 3D laser profilometry, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy were employed to characterise wear mechanisms and tribofilm formation.Both pure base fuels exceeded the DOEB lubricity threshold of 460 μm. Addition of 2% v/v biodiesel restored compliance in all blend systems, yet film formation data, wear depth profiles, and ATR-FTIR analysis collectively suggested that this concentration does not sustain reliable surface protection, with intermittent film breakdown and peripheral wear debris deposits persisting throughout the test. A minimum of 5% v/v was required for stable film formation, and 10% v/v for effective suppression of disc material loss. At 2% v/v, SBME produced a significantly lower wear scar diameter than PME in the diesel system (p = 0.001), consistent with earlier and more persistent ester tribofilm formation confirmed by ATR-FTIR, while no statistically significant difference was observed in the BHD system (p = 0.072). From 5% v/v onward, no significant difference was found between feedstocks in either base fuel system (p > 0.05), indicating convergence of tribological performance regardless of feedstock. BHD blends achieved near-complete disc surface protection at 5% SBME while diesel required 10%, attributable to the less competitive adsorption environment of the paraffinic BHD matrix. Title: Imperfection in motion: Implied motion reduces negative associations of imperfect produce
Abstract: Food waste remains a major sustainability challenge, with imperfect fruits and vegetables often rejected due to their appearance. Prior studies suggest that food choices are mostly automatic, implicit, and habitual, rather than made through deliberated choice. Such insights suggest why explicit messaging to increase consumers' imperfect food purchasing has shown limited effectiveness and highlight opportunities for behaviour change via less mindful means. This study investigates the extent to which negative implicit associations for “imperfect” (vs. “perfect”) exist, and whether implied motion (e.g., fruit splashing into water) can mitigate these evaluations. In a pre-registered study, participants (N = 145) completed an in-person multi-dimensional Implicit Association Test (IAT) to examine their implicit attitudes in static and motion contexts. Results showed that participants' implicit associations were positive for perfect produce and negative for imperfect produce, suggesting an “Ugly = Bad” association. However, exposure to implied motion imagery significantly reduced this negativity effect toward imperfect fresh produce, while having no significant effect on perfect produce. Our findings link implicit attitudes to sustainable food acceptance and demonstrate the potential of visually-based interventions, such as implied motion, to reduce negative aesthetic biases and support behaviour change aimed at increasing acceptance of imperfect produce and reducing food waste. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Examining the layered veil of pay transparency: Implications for perceived ambiguity, sensemaking, and negotiation
Abstract: In the last decade, pay transparency—making pay information more accessible and understandable—has become a defining workplace reform. We examine the common assumption that pay transparency reduces pay disparities by improving negotiation outcomes. Our cross-disciplinary review suggests that pay transparency's effects on negotiation hinge on three factors: (1) how transparency is operationalized (i.e., what type of pay information is shared); (2) how people interpret the information provided; and (3) whether transparency alone can motivate and equip individuals to leverage that information to negotiate effectively. We distinguish three interrelated negotiation-relevant layers of pay transparency—job offer, peer, and market—and then assess how these reduce ambiguity, shape negotiator sensemaking, and influence negotiation processes and outcomes. We conclude by outlining implications for future negotiation research and practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: When imperfect food meets joint consumption: a social influence perspective
Abstract: Drawing on social influence theory, this research examines the interaction effect of food appearance (imperfect vs. perfect) and consumption context (solo vs. joint) on consumers' preferences. Across five experiments, we show that a joint (vs. solo) consumption context exacerbates the reduction in consumers' purchase intention toward imperfect food. In addition, perceived risk and purchase embarrassment mediate this interaction effect on both purchase intention and willingness to pay (WTP). We further identify self-construal and discount information as boundary conditions. Regarding self-construal, for consumers with an interdependent self-construal, joint consumption amplifies the effect of imperfect appearance on perceived risk, purchase embarrassment, and purchase intention. In contrast, for those with an independent self-construal, these amplifying effects are not significant. In terms of discount information, when it is displayed, joint consumption amplifies the effect of imperfect appearance on perceived risk, purchase embarrassment, and purchase intention. When it is absent, however, only the effect on purchase intention remains, albeit attenuated. Finally, the presence of discount information shifts the underlying mechanisms of the interaction toward greater reliance on indirect pathways. This research offers practical guidance for promoting suboptimal food in joint consumption contexts. © 2026

Title: Predicting the future of retail services: Trends, technologies, and strategic imperatives for 2025–2035
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The rapid convergence of digital platforms and shifting consumer behaviors is driving an unprecedented structural transformation across the global retail landscape. This paper examines the systemic evolution of retail channel revenue distributions and operational capabilities, establishing the critical strategic imperatives required to navigate market disruption over the 2025–2035 horizons. The primary objective of this study is to empirically model the longitudinal shifts between traditional physical retail, e-commerce, and physical channels, while concurrently diagnosing the capability gaps across diverse corporate scales. Methodologically, this research deploys a mixed-methods empirical framework, integrating a quantitative survey of 418 retail industry professionals with qualitative interviews from 32 senior executives across six countries, analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA. The empirical findings reveal a definitive market polarization: traditional physical retail is projected to contract significantly from 54.3% to 30.8%, while e-commerce expands to claim a dominant 52.7% revenue share by 2035. Our multi-method analysis validates that digital-physical integration and AI-driven personalization (β = 0.38, p < .001) directly resolve post-pandemic operational vulnerabilities, emerging as the primary drivers of future performance outcomes. Longitudinal analysis confirms a steady decline in traditional commodity metrics, while scenario simulations warn that small and medium-sized enterprises face a severe (66.5%) market share loss under unmitigated polarization. To address this structural market polarization, this study provides a rigorous, data-driven defense by establishing the Retail Evolution Framework (REF) to explain how systemic retail survival requires aligning operational tools with shifting institutional norms. The study bridges the dynamic capabilities gap under the Resource-Based View while offering actionable strategies for ethical data governance. Practically, these insights provide an actionable investment roadmap for corporate managers to redirect capital allocations from physical footprint expansion into automated data ecosystems and cloud-based logistics architectures to maintain long-term competitive viability. © 2026

Title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
Abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Disclosing AI without losing consumers: When and how AI disclosure works in advertising

Abstract: Extant research on AI disclosure examines its negative impact across various domains, but limited attention has been paid to why these effects occur and how they can be mitigated in advertising. To address this gap, we examine why consumers react negatively to AI disclosures in advertising, identify the boundary of this effect, and propose strategies to mitigate it. Across three studies, we show that AI disclosure reduces consumers’ attitudes toward the advertisement and purchase intentions through decreased perceived creativity. Title: Institutional resilience and land-acquisition governance: Participation and conflict-management mechanisms in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project
Abstract: This study examines governance performance during infrastructure land acquisition and the role of institutional resilience in supporting implementation. Using survey data from 108 public-sector implementers involved in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project in Indonesia, the relationships among institutional resilience capacities, participatory governance, conflict-management mechanisms, and governance performance were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Learning capacity and adaptive capacity were positively related to participatory governance, while buffering capacity was positively related to conflict-management mechanisms. Participatory governance showed no direct relationship with governance performance but its indirect relationship through conflict-management mechanisms was statistically significant. Buffering capacity and adaptive capacity were positively related to governance performance, while learning capacity showed no significant relationship. The findings reveal differentiated governance roles across resilience capacities and distinguish direct capacity–performance relationships from process-based relationships involving stakeholder participation and conflict-management mechanisms. In conflict-prone land acquisition, conflict-management mechanisms emerged as an important governance process linking stakeholder participation with governance performance. Title: Perceived control and stress reactivity in algorithm-supported hiring decisions
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Algorithms increasingly determine who gets interviewed, flagged, or passed over in hiring, often without explanation, consistency, or any mechanism for response. Yet the psychological mechanisms through which algorithm-supported decision-making shapes stress responses remain insufficiently specified. This article develops a theoretically grounded framework linking diminished perceived control to stress reactivity in algorithm-mediated decision-making contexts. Drawing on self-determination theory, decision-making process frameworks, and psychological safety, the manuscript integrates empirical evidence from research on AI hiring practices, including findings on Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) individuals navigating applicant tracking systems. The framework identifies three primary mechanisms through which AI-supported decision-making may influence stress reactivity: limited transparency, inconsistent decision processes, and constrained opportunities for feedback. This work offers a foundation for empirical work on how technologically mediated environments shape cognitive appraisal, perceived control, and stress. Title: Models for risk management in the procurement process within organizational contexts: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Over the past decade, supply chain management has faced extreme volatility, culminating in the unprecedented disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. Consequently, resilience in procurement has transitioned from a secondary attribute to an indispensable requirement for operational continuity. This study classifies the state of the art in procurement risk management within the post-pandemic landscape (2021–2025). It analyzes the transition from reactive approaches toward predictive and prescriptive perspectives to address supply chain volatility. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 protocol. Based on a structured search in the Scopus and Web of Science databases, an initial pool of 1,109 records was screened. This resulted in a final sample of 107 high-impact peer-reviewed articles. These studies were evaluated using thematic content analysis and classified into ten technical categories based on their functional orientation. The evidence reveals a fragmented methodological ecosystem where Hybrid Models (21.5%) and Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM, 16.8%) techniques predominate. A shift is observed from static approaches toward the integration of robust optimization, tail risk metrics like Conditional Value at Risk, and Machine Learning. However, a gap is identified between algorithmic complexity and corporate adoption. The study establishes that Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Blockchain are indispensable governance requirements to overcome the black box problem in strategic decision-making. This research contributes a functional classification of tools based on their diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive orientation. Furthermore, it provides managers with a tiered roadmap to achieve analytical maturity. This guides organizations from foundational visibility using synthetic indices, through fuzzy multi-criteria evaluations, toward the responsible implementation of stochastic programming and AI. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: The persuasive power of video in hospitality: How guest-generated video reviews influence customer engagement
Abstract: Guest-generated video reviews are increasingly prevalent on online travel platforms, yet their effects and mechanisms remain underexplored. Drawing on media richness theory, this study is among the first to examine whether and how such reviews enhance customer engagement, measured by subsequent review volume. We adopt a multimethod approach that combines econometric analysis with a controlled experiment to establish causal inference and uncover underlying mechanisms. Using a 24-month panel of 4471 hotels on Ctrip.com, difference-in-differences results show that guest-generated video reviews significantly increase customer engagement, with stronger effects for higher-tier or large hotels. Experimental evidence further demonstrates that these effects operate through increased information diagnosticity and social presence. Additional video content analysis reveals that human presence, higher informational richness, better visual quality, and longer duration further amplify the positive effects. These findings extend media richness theory to consumer-generated video reviews and offer insights into how richer review media stimulate engagement in hospitality settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: How to move you? The persuasive effects of influencer narrative styles in recommending tourism activities
Abstract: Influencers exert significant promotional effects in tourism marketing; however, few empirical studies have examined how different types of tourism activities can strategically leverage these effects through influencer narrative style. To address this gap, this study draws on Heuristic-Analytic Theory to investigate how personal and professional narrative styles align with relaxing and challenging tourism activities to maximize influencers’ persuasiveness. The study analyzes secondary data from 1187 social media posts and conducts three scenario-based experiments with 1438 participants. Results show that personal narrative style is more persuasive for relaxing activities, whereas professional narrative style works better for challenging activities. Moreover, experience resonance and knowledge acquisition are identified as key underlying mechanisms. Notably, the study introduces temporal distance in travel decision as a moderator, highlighting the importance of dynamic temporal cues in influencer recommendations. The findings provide valuable theoretical contributions and practical implications for optimizing influencer marketing strategies in the tourism context. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The Symmetric and Asymmetric Impacts of Foreign Capital Inflows and Trade Openness on Africa’s Economic Growth: Evidence from Linear and Nonlinear Panel ARDL Models
Abstract: This study investigates the symmetric and asymmetric impacts of foreign capital inflows and trade openness on economic growth in 37 African countries from 2000 to 2021 using linear and nonlinear panel autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) models. To examine the dynamic panel threshold effect, the study employed dynamic panel threshold estimation for each of the independent variables. The results indicated that trade openness, foreign direct investment, and official development assistance have significant threshold levels at 24.24%, 23.44%, and 23.21%, respectively. This suggests that the effects of foreign capital inflows and trade openness operate across two regimes—base and high—defined by these thresholds. Comparative analysis of symmetric and asymmetric effects without threshold considerations showed that trade openness consistently exerts positive long- and short-term influences on economic growth, both symmetrically and asymmetrically. Conversely, foreign direct investment (FDI) does not demonstrate a significant symmetric effect but exhibits an asymmetric long-term impact on growth. Additionally, official development assistance (ODA) shows an asymmetric effect that surpasses its symmetric influence on economic growth, highlighting the vulnerability of African economies to financial shocks. Negative shocks in the interaction between FDI and ODA have a more pronounced effect on growth than positive shocks. In the long run, variables such as capital, the globalization index, and political stability positively and significantly impact economic growth, while the labor force has a negative effect. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of creating policy environments that strengthen the capacity to absorb foreign capital, manage trade openness effectively, and coordinate aid and investment policies to foster sustainable economic growth across Africa. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Corruption and capital investment: Worldwide evidence
Abstract: Can international anti-corruption monitoring stimulate private investment? We examine staggered reviews across jurisdictions under the United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC), using firm-year observations from 84 economies over 2003–2023. We document that reviews are followed by improvements in economy-level corruption-control indicators. Local-projections difference-in-differences estimates indicate that reviews raise firms' capital expenditure relative to assets by 1.2126 percentage points, equivalent to 20% of the sample mean. Dynamic estimates show no systematic pre-review adjustment, and the result is robust to influential-economy exclusions, economy-level reweighting, alternative sample restrictions, lagged-outcome controls, and alternative staggered-adoption estimators. Investment responses are stronger in high-corruption economies and developing economies and among firms that are more financially constrained, government dependent, domestically concentrated, or reliant on irreversible capital. These patterns are consistent with international oversight reducing corruption-related institutional risk, financing frictions, and the value of delaying investment. UNCAC reviews are also followed by increases in employment, R&D investment, and leverage. Additional analyses provide no evidence that the increase in investment is accompanied by a systematic decline in investment efficiency. Overall, the findings show that a non-punitive international peer-review mechanism can affect firms’ real activity, particularly where initial institutional frictions are greater. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: The road to hell is paved with good intentions: How does the construction of low-carbon cities affect corporate low-carbon technological innovation in manufacturing?
Abstract: Low-carbon technological innovation (LCTI) is crucial for decarbonization and global climate change mitigation. Taking China's Low-carbon City Pilot (LCCP)—a pioneering exploration for low-carbon development through policy innovation—as an exogenous policy shock, this study utilizes a staggered difference-in-difference-in-differences model and the data of China's manufacturing firms to examine the causality between the voluntary carbon regulation and LCTI. For the first time, the results indicate that the LCCP enactment significantly hinders corporate LCTI, contradicting the predictions of the Porter hypothesis. Mechanism analysis reveals that under the LCCP framework, local governments are authorized to design innovative policies tailored to their specific conditions and are responsible for their own assessment. Using a two-stage LLM-based approach to construct a climate policy uncertainty perception index, we confirm that this “bottom-up” approach introduces significant policy uncertainty faced by firms and weakens their motivation for LCTI involvement. Furthermore, the compliance costs associated with the policy crowd out the funds for LCTI, further hindering firms from engaging in LCTI. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the adverse impact is more evident among firms exhibiting high risk aversion, ones with high artificial intelligence (AI) technology exposure, ones situated in non-resource-based cities, and state-owned ones, and that the adverse impact is significant for emission reduction technologies and zero-carbon technologies, but not for negative-carbon technologies. Additionally, all three pilot batches negatively impact corporate LCTI, suggesting that institutional modifications have not led to intended positive outcomes. This empirical research offers novel evidence regarding the efficacy of the LCCP and yields valuable policy insights—stable policy expectations and robust supervision mechanisms are crucial for achieving policy goals. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Context matters in just culture: Translating formal just culture into lived near-miss reporting experience in maritime transportation
Abstract: In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Not naive, just gullible: psycho-cognitive vulnerability and fraud victimization in Italy
Abstract: Fraud represents a growing and complex threat in contemporary societies, with consequences that extend beyond economic losses. Despite increasing international evidence, limited research has examined the psychological and cognitive factors associated with fraud victimization in the Italian context, particularly in relation to online scams. A binomial logistic regression was conducted to identify individual factors associated with fraud victimization among exposed individuals. Gullibility emerged as the only statistically significant predictor, indicating that higher gullibility was associated with a greater likelihood of victimization, whereas sociodemographic characteristics, personality traits, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy were not significantly associated with victimization. Title: Anger regulation scale for adolescents (ARS-A): Psychometric properties of the Portuguese version and its associations with emotion regulation, depression, and anxiety
Abstract: Adolescence is marked by difficulties in anger regulation, which are linked to internalising and externalising problems. Despite this, the instruments currently available to measure anger regulation in adolescents have a limited evidence base and require further investigation. The present study aimed to examine the psychometric properties of the Anger Regulation Scale for Adolescents (ARS-A) in the Portuguese context. A sample of 432 adolescents aged 11 to 18 (M = 13.73, SD = 1.61) from different regions of Portugal participated in this study. The factor structure and model fit were assessed through Principal Component Analysis and Confirmatory Factor Analysis, using the Solomon method for equivalent sample splitting. All subscales demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and fit indices, confirming the original three-dimensional structure after two items were removed. Pearson correlations with other measures of behavioural and cognitive emotion regulation were consistent with theoretical expectations, although not all associations were as expected. Correlations between anger regulation, depression and anxiety corroborated the relationship between dysfunctional anger regulation and emotional distress. The ARS-A is a reliable and valid measure of anger regulation for adolescents. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Trade-offs and transitions: A scoping review of structural and discursive power in post-growth interventions
Abstract: The dialectic relationship between the production of post-growth knowledge and ongoing construction of social reality is a complex one, but one that warrants attention. In this scoping review, we respond to the emergent interest in post-growth politics and theories of change. We aim to complement existing reviews of post-growth policy proposals and recommendations with an analysis of peer-reviewed studies on interventions – deliberate attempts by one state, market or civil society actor to influence another. Drawing on a socio-ecological systems leverage points perspective embedded within a political economy inspired mapping of social forces, we develop a conceptual framework for explaining strategic trade-offs made by actors to achieve various forms of depth.Our findings point to asymmetrical relationships between actors-executor pairs and a pattern of neoliberal subjectification in both intervention design and analytical focus. We also find that whilst post-growth interventions can readily achieve discursive depth, it is often accompanied by institutional shallowness and temporal fragility. Title: Empowering leadership in educational contexts: A bibliometric analysis to guide management in the framework of SDG 4
Abstract: Empowering leadership (EL) has emerged as a critical leadership approach in educational contexts, particularly in response to increasing demands for innovation, teacher autonomy, and sustainable institutional development. However, despite the rapid growth of studies in this field, the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, thematic evolution, and contribution to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) remain fragmented and insufficiently synthesized. Therefore, this study aims to provide a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of EL research in educational settings indexed in the Scopus database from 1999 to 2026. A total of 84 publications were analyzed using bibliometric performance indicators and science mapping techniques, including co-authorship analysis, keyword co-occurrence, three-field plot visualization, citation analysis, and thematic clustering, supported by Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. The results reveal a strong upward publication trend with a coefficient of determination of R² = 77.54%, particularly accelerating after 2018 and reaching the highest output in 2025. Citation influence remains concentrated in foundational studies published in high-impact journals such as Journal of Applied Psychology, Journal of Knowledge Management, and Leadership Quarterly. China and Indonesia emerge as major international collaboration hubs, while Indonesia shows the strongest author–keyword linkage. Keyword analysis identifies dominant themes related to psychological empowerment, teacher autonomy, innovative work behavior, job satisfaction, and distributed leadership. Notably, 74 out of 84 publications (88.1%) are aligned with SDG 4, highlighting the strong integration of EL research with global educational sustainability agendas. This study offers the first structured intellectual map of EL in education, identifies influential contributors and emerging research directions, and provides evidence-based guidance for educational leadership development aligned with quality education and sustainable transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: Modality effects in human–technology interaction
