Title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
Abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life. Authors: Wang Y.; Dan B.; Sui Y.; Ding Y.; Pu L.; Li H.
Title: Self-built or retailer-based? Online direct-to-consumer channel introduction strategies for the fresh producer under retailer competition and disruption risk
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The sharing of logistics resources among competing retailers provides a new avenue for fresh producers to introduce online direct-to-consumer (OD) channels. However, differences in operational cost and stability create a strategic trade-off between two approaches. Producers may either build the OD channels by themselves, accepting exposure to disruption risk, or rely on retailers, which ensures consistent operational stability. This study develops game-theoretic models of a fresh supply chain comprising one producer and two competing retailers across three scenarios: no OD channel, a self-built OD channel, and a retailer-based OD channel. The results show that, once an OD channel is introduced, higher operational costs lead the producer to reduce direct-sales quantities and lower wholesale prices to stimulate retailer orders. In the self-built OD channel model, the producer must adopt a “conservative,” “aggressive,” or “balanced” operational strategy, depending on the delivery cost, to mitigate profit losses from rising disruption risk. The retailer-based OD channel model becomes the producer's equilibrium strategy only when the logistics service fee falls below a threshold. This threshold increases when the delivery cost is low and exhibits a U-shaped pattern when it is high, as disruption risk rises. Additionally, the retailer-based OD channel model expands the range of equilibrium strategies as disruption risk increases and weakens the moderating effect of wholesale prices on retailers' order quantities. This leads to an asymmetric competitive landscape in which the producer is constrained, the logistics-sharing retailer benefits, and the non-sharing retailer is disadvantaged. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Hu J.
Title: Hero products and the value of position in live streaming commerce evidence from Douyin
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Every livestream sales session has one product that sells best, and the minutes in which it is shown are when the broadcast's audience peaks. This paper asks what that moment is worth to the products around it: can the items that follow the hero, or those shown just before it, turn the traffic it attracts into sales of their own? Using 260,252 product–session observations from 8123 Douyin sessions and an event-study design with session fixed effects, we find conversion highest in the slot immediately after the hero, exceeding products more than five positions away by 0.0177. The advantage is not borrowed traffic. It appears before the hero as much as after it, and only the adjacent slot breaks that symmetry; when the same product is compared with itself across sessions in which it sat at different distances, most of the advantage disappears except beside the hero. The running order therefore reveals mainly which products a streamer places near the featured item, and we report a positional association rather than an attention spillover. What survives is conditional. Scoring each product's own listing title with a large language model, we find that credibility signals attenuate the advantage while informativeness moves it in both directions, and the advantage exists only where the hero appears in the first third of the running order, vanishing when it is held until the end. For managers, the slots flanking an early-placed hero are worth allocating deliberately; positions further down the lineup are not. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: EXPSO: A PSO-based ensemble gene expression classifier for plant species using histone and chromatin accessiblity data
Abstract: Gene expression in plants is regulated by complex interactions among chromatin features, including histone modifications and chromatin accessibility. Accurate prediction of gene-expression states from epigenomic information can provide insights into transcriptional regulation and facilitate functional genomic studies. However, the nonlinear and high-dimensional nature of epigenomic data presents challenges for conventional statistical approaches. Here, we developed EXPSO, a PSO-assisted ensemble learning framework for classifying plant genes into high- and low-expression states using integrated histone modification and chromatin accessibility data. The framework uses Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to optimize Random Forest hyperparameters within an ensemble comprising Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost classifiers. The framework was developed and evaluated independently across five plant species, including Arabidopsis thaliana, Hordeum vulgare, Phaseolus vulgaris, Setaria viridis, and Sorghum bicolor. EXPSO achieved an AUROC of 0.904 for Arabidopsis thaliana and demonstrated competitive predictive performance across the independently evaluated species. Model benchmarking against DeepChrome, ShallowChrome, and PatternChrome was performed using stratified five-fold cross-validation, with performance reported as mean ± standard deviation and 95% confidence intervals. Paired two-sided t-tests were used to assess fold-wise differences between EXPSO and the benchmark models. Comparative benchmarking included DeepChrome, ShallowChrome, and PatternChrome under the evaluation framework used in this study. Feature-attribution analyses using SHAP, LIME, and PDP consistently identified H3K36me3 and H3K56ac as important predictive features, consistent with their reported associations with transcription-associated chromatin states. To facilitate practical application, we developed the freely accessible EXPSO web server, which enables users to submit gene IDs together with histone modification and chromatin accessibility data as individual entries or CSV files and obtain gene-expression predictions with associated prediction probabilities and downloadable results. EXPSO provides an accessible and interpretable computational framework for plant gene-expression prediction from epigenomic features and a practical web-based implementation for supported plant datasets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Miao Z.; Gu H.; Xia Y.; Xu J.; Zhu M.
Title: Multi-scale design and techno-economic optimization of copper-mesh reactors for methanol steam reforming
Abstract: Structured copper-mesh catalysts offer axial heat conduction for endothermic methanol steam reforming (MSR), yet deployment requires optimizing geometry, operating conditions and economics. We present a multi-scale Python framework integrating (i) Peppley-type Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics calibrated on 36 points (R2 = 0.955; the lumped Ea = 37.1 kJ mol−1 is an empirical coefficient; the model-free apparent value is 89–96 kJ mol−1). (ii) Finite-volume modeling of the plain-weave unit cell, giving 3-fold radial-to-axial conductivity anisotropy. (iii) A 1-D plug-flow reactor justified by a 270-point dimensionless analysis. (iv) A techno-economic model across 1575 configurations on the measured voidage. Because the dry reformate contains 75–8090 ppm CO, LCOH is route-dependent: 7.7–8.7 $ kg−1 with vacuum-swing adsorption, 2.9–3.5 $ kg−1 feeding a high-temperature PEM directly, and 3.3–3.9 $ kg−1 with two-stage preferential oxidation to 10 ppm for a stationary low-temperature PEM with anode air bleed, each dominated by methanol and electricity. Against two commercial Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 pellets within the same system boundary, the mesh meets the same hydrogen duty in one third of the volume at about 10 % lower cost and 18–28 % lower cost at equal reactor volume, with the gap arising from heat transfer and packing density, not activity. Electricity price is the principal cost driver (S1 = 0.77–0.81), a ranking that is range-dependent, heater efficiency leading under normalized ± 25 % ranges and the methanol price held fixed in the index set; geometry remains decisive for pressure drop, productivity and scale-up. Title: Digitalising the intensive care unit diary: mapping users' perceptions in healthcare settings – a scoping review
Abstract: Aim: To map literature on perceptions of patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals regarding the use of digital diaries in healthcare, to inform pre-implementation of an ICU diary by identifying factors relevant to feasibility, acceptability, and integration into ICU workflows. Methods: The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Studies including patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals with experience of digital diary use in healthcare settings were eligible. Included studies reported perceptions of digital diaries. Data were synthesised using inductive content analysis. Findings: From 679 identified records, 13 studies (2014–2025) were included, covering symptom diaries (n = 7) and ICU diaries (n = 6). The synthesis generated three overarching categories across user groups: relational connectedness and person-centred care; empowerment and meaning-making; and implementation and technological readiness. Across contexts, digital diaries were described as shaping communication, participation, and continuity of care, while also enabling reflection and meaning-making during illness and recovery. However, their perceived value was highly context-dependent and shaped by implementation conditions. Conclusions: Digital diaries were perceived by patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals as influencing communication, continuity, and engagement in care. Patients highlighted reflection, increased awareness, and participation, while relatives emphasised connection and involvement. Healthcare professionals focused on usability, workflow integration, and organisational conditions shaping use. They were perceived as valuable when they supported communication and made patients' experiences more visible, but as less useful when poorly integrated into clinical routines. Their perceived value depended on how they were embedded in practice and shaped by interactions between users, technology, and organisational context. Implications for Clinical Practice: Digital diaries have the potential to support communication, involvement, and continuity of care. However, realising this potential requires deliberate integration into clinical workflows, role definition, and user-centred design. Ongoing evaluation is essential, particularly in ICU contexts where experiential and person-centred outcomes remain underexplored. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Masculine honor, social visibility, and safety non-compliance: intentions and approval judgments in high-risk sectors in Turkey
Abstract: Unsafe work in high-risk sectors cannot be explained only by knowledge deficits or weak safety management; workers may also attach reputational meaning to visible compliance. Drawing on honor theory and occupational-safety research on risk perception and social context, this study examined whether masculine honor values (hereafter honor values)—the belief that a man’s worth depends partly on a publicly defensible reputation—were associated with unsafe work intentions, lower perceived risk, and greater approval of safety-rule non-compliance among male workers in Turkish construction and shipbuilding. A worker survey (N = 244) was combined with a within-person vignette experiment in which the focal hazard was held constant while visibility was manipulated and audience identity and prior social comment varied orthogonally. Honor values were positively associated with unsafe work intentions (H1a) and approval of others’ violations (H1b), and negatively associated with perceived risk (H2). Perceived risk partially accounted for the honor–intention association (H3). The association between honor values and approval of non-compliance was stronger when the violation was public rather than private (H4), consistent with a reputational, visibility-contingent account. These findings identify a micro-level sociocultural pathway that complements knowledge- and risk-based accounts of safety decisions. They also suggest that safety communication and supervisory practice should address the social meaning of compliance, while the cross-sectional mediation and judgment-based vignette outcome limit causal and behavioral inference. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: UK bioenergy policies and implications for global land use change
Abstract: Bioenergy is central to UK decarbonisation policy, yet its reliance on imported biomass and crop-based biofuels raises concerns about land use change (LUC) and indirect land use change (ILUC) in supplier countries. This study provides a data-driven, ex-post assessment of land use implications associated with two UK bioenergy policy pathways: forestry-derived biomass supported by the Contract for Difference (CfD), and 1st generation biofuels supplied under the Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation (RTFO). Import data for 2015–2022 were linked to forestry biomass productivity and country-specific crop yields to estimate direct land use footprints in major supplier countries. Wider ILUC-consistent signals were then assessed using observed land use, production and trade trends from 2000 to 2022, with particular focus on the US and Brazil. Results show that UK-bound forestry-derived biomass was mainly associated with land footprints in the US, Canada, Latvia and Estonia, while UK-bound 1st generation biofuel land demand became increasingly concentrated in the US and Brazil by 2022. Sensitivity analysis showed that lower productivity assumptions increased estimated land requirements, but did not alter the main supplier-country patterns. Overall, UK bioenergy imports represented a small share of total land use in major supplier countries. The study found no persistent national-scale ILUC signal detected in the US or Brazil. The findings suggest that ex-post land use monitoring can complement model-based ILUC assessment and improve the evidence base for bioenergy sustainability policy. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Deep-QLP and Spline based Quadrature Rules for Fredholm Integral Equations of the First Kind
Source title: Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
Abstract: In this paper, we propose a numerical method to construct an approximate solution to Fredholm integral equations of the first kind. These equations are common in image processing, spectroscopy, and other engineering sciences but are often ill-posed. Moreover, the right hand side of such equations could be error-contaminated. To effectively tackle the mentioned challenges, we propose suitable quadrature rules to discretize the continuous problem. The resulting discrete system is solved in a regularized least-squares framework by adopting the Deep-QLP factorization: a novel algorithm that automatically computes an approximate truncated singular value decomposition based on a user-defined tolerance. Additionally, two regularization approaches are introduced. In the first one, given a perturbed right-hand side, a Hankel matrix is constructed and then, the so-called de-Hankelization is performed by adopting the same Deep-QLP algorithm. In the second approach, we rely on locally refined discretization spaces to increase the accuracy of the computed approximate solution, by keeping low the number of the used degrees of freedom. Title: DCET: Multi-scale decomposition and channel clustering enhanced multivariate time series forecasting
Abstract: Existing multivariate time series forecasting methods address multi-scale structures and channel heterogeneity by either enhancing model expressiveness with deeper and wider network architectures or by preprocessing sequences to attenuate certain frequency components. However, these approaches often lead to increased training costs, instability from over-reliance on model capacity, difficulty in handling multiple scales, and failure to consider differing structural relationships between channels. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel framework called DCET (Decomposition and channel Clustering Enhanced multivariate Time series Forecasting), which integrates a cascading two-stage decomposition process, channel clustering, and a ChebyKAN residual head within a single unified model. The main contribution of DCET lies in its ability to directly address multi-scale and channel heterogeneity in a more efficient manner by simplifying the model structure while preserving its expressiveness. Specifically, DCET introduces an unsupervised learning-based module for parameter sharing among similar variates, and applies the two-stage decomposition to capture multi-scale features. Nonlinear models are used to represent complex fluctuations, while linear models capture long-term trends. Moreover, a multi-objective training approach minimizes both the overall prediction error and the errors of decomposed components. Title: Negotiation across the social sciences: An interdisciplinary review
Abstract: Psychological investigations have generated numerous insights into how two parties bargain. To build on this literature, we review recent research across multiple disciplines, focusing on aspects of negotiation that have received relatively little attention, namely individual differences, multiparty negotiations, and contextual factors. Insights into individual differences are observed in the developmental psychology, artificial intelligence, and social psychology literature. Investigations in these domains show that young children can think strategically about exchange, that individual differences shape the information negotiators obtain and how they utilize information, and that situational factors can constrain or facilitate the expression of individual differences. Insights into multiparty negotiations emerge from the social networks and political science literature. Investigations in these domains explore novel multiparty dynamics, highlighting the importance of structural position in bargaining, and demonstrating that relationship history can shape coalition formation. Insights into contextual factors emerge from the economic and public health literature. Investigations in these domains challenge assumptions about core negotiation concepts such as power and alternatives. Overall, an interdisciplinary perspective on negotiation complements and enriches psychological understanding, and provides implications for interventions, future theoretical development, and empirical research. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy: A bibliometric study and systematic literature review
Abstract: The forces of globalization and digital transformation have intensified attention toward the need to strengthen cultural identity through education, including the use of folklore as a meaningful learning resource. However, existing studies on folklore in learning remain fragmented. While much of the literature focuses on either cultural preservation or specific educational applications, the gap lies in a systematic exploration of folklore's pedagogical role across different contexts and educational levels. This study addresses this gap by examining the development of research on folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy through a bibliometric approach combined with a systematic literature review. For the bibliometric analysis, metadata records of articles published between 2015 and 2025 were processed from the Google Scholar database. Data for the systematic literature review were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and the article selection process followed PRISMA procedures. A total of 41 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Bibliometric mapping was conducted using VOSviewer, while article identification and screening were supported by Publish or Perish. The bibliometric findings indicate a significant increase in publications over the past decade, accompanied by a thematic shift from cultural heritage preservation toward the integration of cultural values within educational contexts. The SLR findings show that the research is predominantly qualitative in nature, with folktales and legends as the most frequently used forms of folklore, and books and e-modules as the main learning media employed to strengthen cultural literacy. The findings suggest that folklore-based learning fosters students’ cultural awareness, internalizes values, strengthens identity formation, and deepens the understanding of local culture. This study contributes by providing a more integrated understanding of folklore as a pedagogical tool for cultural literacy, emphasizing its role in curriculum design. Title: Nonlinear river distance effects on housing prices: Integrating XGBoost and GeoShapley for spatially explicit valuation
Abstract: Urban river landscapes not only provide recreational and aesthetic benefits but also generate tangible market value. Quantifying the externalities of such amenities on housing prices is critical for evidence-based policy making and spatial planning. Focusing on Tianjin's six central districts, this study integrates conventional spatial models with interpretable machine learning, to identify the nonlinear influence of river water systems on housing prices in Tianjin and the threshold effect. Using 2020 data from the early pandemic period captures pre-regulation market conditions while avoiding structural distortions from post-pandemic policy interventions during 2021–2022. We have compared OLS, GWR and XGBoost; the latter increased R2 by 10.4 % (CV-R2 = 0.712). The winning XGBoost model is subsequently combined with GeoShapley to visualize local marginal effects. Results reveal a three-regime, non-linear distance–price gradient for proximity to the Haihe River and its tributaries, emergent transition zones approximately within 1.0–1.5 km, with suggestive inflection points around 1.0 km and 1.3 km: within 1 km, a 1 % reduction in distance raises prices by 0.155 %; with a 0.074 % increase per 1 % additional distance in the 1–1.3 km sub-zone. These findings provide quantitative benchmarks for tiered river buffer management in Tianjin's Territorial Spatial Master Plan (2021–2035): intensive amenity investment within 1 km, standard regulations for transitional zones (1–1.5 km), and accessibility-focused planning beyond 1.5 km. Spatial heterogeneity across river segments further indicates that uniform zoning is suboptimal, with eastern and northern corridors warranting targeted investment and western and southern segments requiring functional repositioning. Title: Efficiency and vulnerability in natural monopoly ferry infrastructure under peak load
Abstract: The ferry services on many islands operate under market conditions that make it possible for one company, in practice, to provide the service at the lowest cost. This situation is due to the very high fixed costs required for ferry operations and the need to offer a continuous service. However, in the event of increased demand, vulnerable systems may suffer as congestion grows and the utilisation limit of ferry services is reached. The paper introduces the Natural Monopoly Ferry Framework (NMFF). The framework is developed through a conceptual synthesis of natural monopoly theory, ferry economics and infrastructure vulnerability research. It is suggested that even if a ferry service operates effectively, it may still be put under stress due to a sudden increase in demand. In particular, the paper argues that even the economic efficiency of a ferry service is not always enough to make the service operate well. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Beyond data disclosure: A health system transparency framework informed by evidence and Iranian insights
Abstract: Objectives: Although transparency is widely recognized as a cornerstone of good health governance, existing studies have often addressed individual dimensions of transparency, with limited integration of these dimensions into a comprehensive conceptual framework for health systems. This study aimed to develop a conceptual framework for health system transparency by integrating evidence from Iran. Methods: This qualitative study was conducted in six sequential phases between 2021 and 2024. Three systematic scoping reviews synthesized existing transparency frameworks, implementation principles, and the applications, benefits, risks, barriers, and opportunities of transparency in health systems. Findings were complemented by in-depth interviews with 35 Iranian experts, refined through three expert panels involving 16 participants, and finalized using a three-round modified Delphi study with 23 participants in the final round. Results: The resulting framework conceptualizes transparency as a multi-level governance system comprising strategic contexts and infrastructures, stakeholder interactions, implementation drivers and constraints, transparency application domains, and tactical and technical implementation principles. Rather than viewing transparency as information disclosure alone, the framework emphasizes dynamic interactions between governance conditions, data users, feedback mechanisms, and potential contributions to organizational learning and system improvement. Conclusion: The proposed framework provides an integrated conceptual foundation for designing, implementing, and evaluating transparency reforms in health systems. Although informed by evidence from Iran, its governance-oriented architecture may be transferable to other health systems, provided that context-dependent components are adapted to local institutional, political, legal, and socio-cultural conditions. Public interest summary: Health system transparency is more than making information publicly available. This study developed a framework showing how transparency can become part of everyday health system governance. It identifies the political, administrative, economic, and social conditions needed to support transparency, the role of citizens, researchers, media, and other data users in creating demand for information, and the factors that can either support or hinder implementation. The framework also identifies key areas where transparency is needed, including governance, finances, medicines, workforce, research, and healthcare services, and provides practical and technical principles for implementation. Although developed using evidence from Iran, the framework addresses transparency challenges that may also arise in other health systems and may help policymakers design more coordinated and sustainable transparency reforms. Title: Under pressure: High-Stakes exams and media-reported student suicides in India
Abstract: We estimate the temporal association between high-stakes exam timing and media-reported student suicides in India using geocoded news data. Student suicides are 17.5 percent higher during months in which NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examinations are held, with no comparable pattern around lower-stakes board exams or among adults. The association is concentrated when national entrance exams coincide with board exams, suggesting the salience of cumulative exam burden. These patterns are stronger among girls, in states with higher exam participation, and in urbanised districts. Event-study estimates show suicides increasing immediately before and during exams, while movements around result announcements are weaker and less precisely estimated. We find no evidence that broad shifts in media attention during cyclone or election months account for the pattern, although exam-specific reporting bias cannot be ruled out. In the absence of mental health data, we generate an alternative database to address a policy question and spur future research. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: A fairness-aware TabTransformer framework for credit scoring with high-cardinality regional bias
Abstract: This study examines whether fairness constraints must come at the expense of performance in credit risk models. We introduce a deep learning framework rooted in the TabTransformer architecture, integrating a Normalized Covariance Penalty into the loss function to mitigate regional bias over a high-cardinality sensitive attribute, the 27 Brazilian states. A real-world mortgage dataset of 1,529,211 contracts, under a strict unawareness-at-inference protocol and calibrated using Platt scaling, is benchmarked against industry standards and against fairness-aware alternatives from the pre-, in-, and post-processing families. The fairness-constrained model achieved an AUC of 0.751, above its unconstrained counterpart (0.745; DeLong p < .001) and Random Forest (0.735), while reducing the maximum True Positive Rate (TPR) gap across states to 0.445, against 0.499 for XGBoost, and reaching the lowest Demographic Parity difference among all evaluated models. XGBoost retains a statistically significant advantage in raw discrimination (ΔAUC (Formula presented)); among models that keep inference blind to the regional attribute, however, the proposed framework offers the most favorable fairness–performance profile and dominates the equity-constrained region of the empirical Pareto frontier. A decomposition across the 27 states shows that the penalty compresses the regional TPR distribution in both directions, raising the mean TPR of the three worst-served states, and a leakage audit confirms a measurable reduction in the regional information carried by the scores. Sensitivity analyses over the penalty weight and training seeds, module ablations, and replications on public credit datasets support the robustness of these findings. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Why this AI app? The impact of generative artificial intelligence on educators’ choices in educational apps
Abstract: In elementary education, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being incorporated into educational applications, despite still-emerging evidence of its effects on children's learning and development. Educators, who are already overwhelmed with choice in the commercial app space, may increasincly have to decide whether to incorporate GenAI-enabled apps for their classrooms. Thus, the present study investigates how mentioning GenAI in app store descriptions impacts K-6 educators' selection of educational apps. Over two studies, K-6 educators (each n = 101) from Canada, the US, and the UK viewed and evaluated eight researcher-created educational math apps with and without GenAI. Study 1 tested whether mentioning GenAI in app descriptions affected educators' app evaluations but found no effect. In Study 2, results from a repeated measures MANOVA revealed that educators rated apps without AI higher than those mentioning GenAI, but there were no significant effects of GenAI on likelihood to download or willingness to pay for apps. A hierarchical cluster analysis identified three distinct groups of educators: 1) selectors (n = 28), who exhibited a preference for downloading, rating, and paying for apps including GenAI; 2) agnostics (n = 59), who exhibit minimal preferences; and 3) avoiders (n = 14), who prefer apps without AI. Most educators were agnostic to the use of GenAI in educational apps, highlighting the need to support educators' informed decisions about when to adopt GenAI tools and encourage critical evaluation of GenAI's role in education. More research is needed to understand how educators' GenAI preferences relate to their attitudes, knowledge, and use of GenAI. © 2026

Title: XAI in the human-agent-environment loop: how do task, explanation strategy, and AI literacy shape user engagement?
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: This study explored how tasks, explanation strategies, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy levels collectively influenced human interaction with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in a single-target prediction task. Using a within-subjects experiment with 70 participants, the study examined combinations of four AI-assisted prediction tasks—varying in prediction target (human-related vs. human-unrelated) and stakes (high vs. low)—and six explanation strategies (model-based, comparison-based, input influence-based, sensitivity-based, demographic-based, and case-based), across participants with varying AI literacy (AIL). Results showed that explanation strategies had the most significant impact on human-XAI interaction in most aspects, especially on prediction change with XAI assistance. Additionally, explanation strategies significantly affected all perception and experience indicators, except for curiosity. Compared to the scope of explanations, the content provided by strategies had a greater influence on user predictions. Strategies with trends and ratios, such as case-based (CA) and demographic-based (DE), were more effective. Conversely, strategies lacking trends and ratios, such as model-based (MO) and comparison-based (CO), were generally the least effective. For users, AI literacy influenced all performance metrics, especially re-prediction time. Higher AI literacy was significantly associated with longer re-prediction time. Tasks had moderate impacts on the XAI interaction process, especially experience measures. In the human-related tasks (recidivism and shipwreck survival prediction), participants reported lower subjective experience ratings among the tasks examined, particularly regarding perceived justice. In the high-stakes, human-unrelated task (wine quality prediction), participants gave the most favorable experiential ratings among the tasks in the study. Furthermore, second-order effects related to explanation strategies had significant impacts on various metrics. On the one hand, the interaction between explanation strategies and task characteristics influenced prediction changes. Global explanations, such as the input-influence-based (IN) and MO strategies, performed better on human-related tasks than on human-unrelated tasks. In contrast, local explanations, such as the sensitivity-based (SE) and CO strategies, showed the opposite pattern. On the other hand, the impact of explanation strategies on user perception and experience was moderated by AI literacy. Users with lower literacy tended to prefer local explanations, while users with higher literacy preferred global explanations. The content of the XAI explanation significantly affected the quality, while the scope had subtle interactive effects with different tasks and users. These effects with XAI, majorly interpreted through the Elaboration Likelihood model (ELM), provide evidence supporting adaptive XAI within the human-agent-environment loop. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Evaluating LLM–NACE divergence in firm classification: A multi-metric analysis in the experience industry
Abstract: This study examines whether patterns of divergence between large language model (LLM) firm classifications and the Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community (NACE) are more consistent with between-model inconsistency, information-availability effects, or taxonomic ambiguity. Using a registry dataset of 43,931 Finnish firms, of which 29,565 received at least one Experience Industry classification, we compare GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and Llama 3 70B. LLMs were prompted using company name and identifier only, and the resulting keywords were mapped to sector profiles, enabling comparison between model outputs and formal taxonomic assignments without external descriptive text. We evaluate agreement with Krippendorff’s α, cosine similarity, and normalized HHI-based concentration measures, and examine variation by firm revenue, size, and sector-level keyword reliability. Using raw LLM-derived profiles, inter-LLM similarity is high (cosine 0.89–0.95), whereas LLM–NACE alignment is substantially lower (0.19–0.24). Confidence-level adjustment increases LLM–NACE similarity, as expected, because adjusted profiles partly incorporate NACE information. Agreement increases in revenue-weighted and larger-firm analyses, but declines in sectors with low keyword reliability and diffuse boundaries. Across all weighting schemes and size classes, inter-LLM similarity exceeds LLM–NACE similarity. The findings suggest that LLM–NACE divergence is more consistent with information-availability effects and taxonomic ambiguity than with large between-model inconsistency. The study contributes a multi-metric framework for evaluating classification under unstable category systems and shows how LLM-based profiling can complement formal industry coding in hybrid sectors. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Paving the Way toward Sustainability and Improving Performance in Renewable Power Projects Through Risk Management Practices
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Risk management (RM) is an integral and essential component of project management. Addressing two vital aspects is critical: improving project performance and enhancing sustainability. Past studies have illustrated several RM practices without revealing their actual impact on these aspects, especially in addressing the unique characteristics of renewable power project development. This study fills the gaps and aims to explore critical RM practices and examine their influence on project performance and sustainability in developing renewable power projects. The present study identified 25 risk management practices from the existing literature and publicly available documents of 32 leading enterprises in the renewable sector in India. Furthermore, data were collected through a questionnaire survey from 104 renewable sector experts. An underlying structure of these practices was established, and factors were extracted using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). A partial least squares structural equation model (PLS-SEM) was then developed to evaluate their influence on the project's performance and sustainability parameters. The analysis revealed that RM practices such as systematic risk assessment, recording, and training (F1), inclusive and long-term planning (F2), engaging dedicated risk officers (F3), and identifying, documenting, and updating RM policy (F4) significantly and positively influence the performance and sustainability of renewable power projects. Moreover, the study provides a comprehensive insight into the current RM practices in the renewable power sector. The study enhances the body of knowledge by identifying critical RM practices and quantifying their impact on improving the performance and sustainability of renewable power projects. Adopting these crucial practices would help practitioners enhance the success of the power project, paving the way for achieving the sustainable development goals (SDGs).  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Caffeine in sugar-sweetened beverages: A silent amplifier of preference and intake
Abstract: Sugar-sweetened beverages remain a major source of dietary sugar exposure, yet the behavioural contribution of caffeine within these products is often treated as secondary to sweetness, branding and convenience. This commentary argues that caffeine in cola-style sugar-sweetened beverages is better understood as a behavioural and nutritional amplifier than as a benign flavour adjunct. Although caffeine is a bitter tastant in water, psychophysical evidence indicates that caffeine at commercial concentrations is largely imperceptible within cola matrices because sweetness, acidity, carbonation and flavour complexity mask low-intensity bitterness. Its post-ingestive effects may nevertheless reinforce learned preference, support habitual intake and contribute to higher voluntary consumption. Product level evidence also suggests that caffeine-containing variants can carry slightly higher sugar concentrations than their caffeine-free counterparts. Integrating sensory science, flavour-nutrient learning, caffeine pharmacology and consumer behaviour provides a more complete account of how caffeine may silently increase sugar exposure. This framing has implications for formulation, labelling, dietary guidance and future research on beverage choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Sha X.; Xu Z.; Park K.-S.; Su M.
Title: Urban economic resilience and low-altitude logistics industrial agglomeration: Implications for reliable deployment
Abstract: Low-altitude logistics (LAL) is a complex urban cyber-physical freight system comprising uncrewed aerial vehicles, eVTOL aircraft, airspace management, and ground infrastructure. Reliable deployment requires technical validation, regulatory compliance, and commercially sustainable operations, while urban socioeconomic conditions may provide supporting resources. This paper develops an interpretable causal learning framework to evaluate how urban economic resilience influences LAL industrial agglomeration, measured by the log-transformed stock of registered LAL-related enterprises. Utilizing panel data from 296 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2010–2024, we quantify urban economic resilience via an improved entropy-weighted TOPSIS model and integrate panel fixed-effects, double machine learning, causal forests, and SHAP attribution to estimate average effects under identifying assumptions and examine spatial heterogeneity and nonlinear predictive contributions. The results indicate that urban economic resilience significantly fosters LAL enterprise concentration, yet reveals a distinct resilience saturation pattern: mid-resilience cities exhibit the largest estimated effects on LAL industrial agglomeration, whereas marginal returns diminish in highly resilient metropolitan centers. SHAP decomposition reveals that household wealth accumulation, income levels, and fixed-asset investment are primary contributors to industrial presence. These findings identify urban economic conditions associated with LAL industrial agglomeration and offer implications for the economic foundations supporting reliable deployment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Cross cultural patterns of linguistic aggression and aggressive combat content enjoyment: A computational study of PUBG reviews across six continents
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: This study explores global patterns of linguistic aggression and appreciation for aggressive combat content as expressed in reviews of PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds (PUBG), analyzing over 18.7 million Google Play Store English language reviews from over 80 countries. Grounded in the General Aggression Model (GAM), it integrates media psychology, cross cultural communication, and computational social science to assess emotional expression in user generated content. Two indices, Aggression Score and Appreciation of Aggressive Content (AAC), were constructed using NLP, sentiment analysis, and lexicon-based tagging to capture hostile sentiment (anger) and positive reinforcement (joy, ratings, likes) in aggression-related reviews. Results reveal a significant increase in the average intensity of both scores over time, with reviews grouped under South America exhibiting higher average aggression and AAC scores within the dataset, while reviews grouped under Australia show comparatively lower levels of these measures. Authors: Fei X.; Yu Y.; Li Y.
Title: Sharing blame with me: How AI anthropomorphism encourages individual unethical behavior
Abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: THE POWER OF FACIAL EXPRESSIONS IN SALES AVATARS: ELEVATING CONSUMER INTERACTION IN METAVERSE COMMERCE
Abstract: Metaverse commerce is reshaping e-commerce by offering immersive and interactive shopping experiences. Sales avatars, defined as digital representations of firm frontline employees in metaverse commerce, play critical roles in delivering real-time and interactive experiences. Drawing on the theory of affordances and the needs-affordances-features framework, this study investigates how the facial expressions of sales avatars (smiling vs. crying) influence consumer avatars’ interaction outcomes and the underlying mechanisms through subcultural appeal. Further, we test when the mechanism by which sales avatars’ facial expression leads to consumer interaction outcomes via subcultural appeal is amplified or weakened depending on sales avatar’s anthropomorphism. We conducted four experiments in which consumers were exposed to virtual commerce contexts that we built on the VRChat metaverse platform. The results reveal that unlike real-world interactions, crying sales avatars compared to smiling sales avatars elicit higher intentions to interact with the sales avatar, purchase a virtual item from the sales avatar, and spread positive WOM about the experience. This counterintuitive effect is driven by consumers’ heightened perceptions of subcultural appeal in the crying sales avatar context. However, when sales avatars exhibited high anthropomorphism (human-like vs. cartoon-like), the positive effect of the crying expression weakened. These findings provide actionable insights into how to strategically leverage sales avatars’ facial expressions in highly immersive metaverse commerce, where consumers’ desire for subcultural values is relatively high. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. Title: VPP-Based Park-Level Integrated Energy Scheduling System with Carbon Emission and Integrated Demand Response Mechanism Using Data-Driven Distributionally Robust Optimization
Abstract: This paper investigates the effective management of distributed Renewable Energy (RE) sources in multi-user Park-level Integrated Energy Systems (PIESs), aiming to coordinate power supply, cooling, and other forms of energy through a Virtual Power Plant (VPP) while enhancing environmental and economic benefits in regulation markets. Title: The Type III realisation conjecture of Kirkland and Šmigoc
Abstract: Kirkland and Šmigoc constructed a family of stochastic matrices realising the Type III boundary polynomials of the Karpelevič region and conjectured that, conversely, every stochastic realisation of such a polynomial must come from their construction. We prove this conjecture for the full nonzero parameter range 0<α≤1, for the reduced Ito polynomials fα(x)=xy(xq−(1−α))d−αd,n=qd+y, associated with Type III Farey-neighbour arcs of order n. For 0<α<1, the boundary theorem of Dmitriev and Dynkin restricts the possible nonzero entries of a realising matrix. After relabelling the vertices, its directed graph consists of the edges i→i+n1 and a selection of edges i→i+n(n+1−q), with indices taken modulo n. Coates' coefficient formula and a weighted form of Turán's theorem then show that the directed cycles of length q fall into d classes. Any two cycles in the same class share a vertex, while cycles in different classes have no vertices in common. Each class has the same sum of cycle weights, where the weight of a cycle is the product of its edge weights. The positions of these cycles along the n-cycle then yield the product condition required by Kirkland and Šmigoc. The case α=1 is treated separately, and an explanation is provided for the failure when α=0. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Choice set expansion and dual-domain loss aversion in food delivery platforms: Evidence from price-time trade-offs
Abstract: This study examines how delivery-tier expansion shapes online food delivery choices when price-time trade-offs are held constant. Drawing on context-dependent choice theory and prospect theory, we conducted a between-subjects discrete-choice experiment with 438 South Korean consumers assigned to either a two-tier menu (Free and Economy) or a three-tier menu (Free, Economy, and Single-order). Paid options offered the same price per minute saved, isolating choice-set structure from economic efficiency. Adding single-order delivery significantly reduced free delivery selection and captured 30.49% of choices. Title: Organisational capability for digital health transformation in long-term care: development of a conceptual framework
Abstract: Background: Digital health transformation in long-term care (LTC) involves more than the adoption of digital technologies. Organisations must coordinate leadership, workforce capability, infrastructure, governance and implementation processes to sustain digital systems within continuing care environments. Existing implementation and digital maturity approaches address important aspects of digital transformation but provide less explanation of how organisational capabilities interact as a system within LTC. Objective: This study develops an evidence-informed organisational capability framework for digital health transformation in LTC and proposes relationships among capabilities potentially relevant to sustained digital system use. Methods: An evidence-informed framework development approach was used. Published evidence from digital health, healthcare management, implementation and organisational research was examined to identify recurring organisational mechanisms associated with digital transformation. Related mechanisms were grouped into capability domains, and proposed relationships among the domains were conceptualised. The resulting domains were integrated into the Long-Term Care Digital Capability and Alignment (LTC-DCA) framework. Results: LTC-DCA comprises seven interdependent organisational capability domains: strategic digital leadership, organisational readiness, workforce development systems, technology and data infrastructure alignment, governance and ethical oversight, implementation and integration mechanisms, and performance and learning systems. The framework conceptualises these domains as a connected capability system in which changes in one domain may influence others. Performance and organisational learning are proposed as feedback mechanisms that may support continued adjustment and alignment. Conclusions: LTC-DCA shifts attention from technology adoption towards the organisational capabilities potentially involved in integrating, sustaining and adapting digital systems within long-term care. The framework is evidence-informed and conceptually specified rather than empirically validated. Future research could examine its domains, proposed relationships and indicators across different LTC settings and investigate whether they are associated with sustained digital system use and organisational performance. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

Authors: Yin T.
Title: The paradox of withdrawal: How managerial turnover intention and attitudes shape performance appraisal quality in high-contact service
Abstract: Purpose: Performance appraisal quality depends on the discretionary effort of the rater. This study examines rater-side psychological antecedents of appraisal rigor among hospitality managers, focusing on how managers’ positive attitudes toward the job and the organization drive appraisal quality and whether that relationship is disrupted by the managers’ own turnover intention. Design/methodology/approach: Data were collected from 318 U.S. hospitality managers through a multi-stage screening protocol on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Because job satisfaction and organizational commitment were empirically indistinguishable in the sample (r = .976), a higher-order Managerial Attitudes factor was specified to test the two attitudinal hypotheses jointly. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to estimate direct and moderating effects. Common method variance was addressed procedurally and through a marker-variable technique combined with an unmeasured latent method construct. Findings: Managerial Attitudes had a strong positive relationship with self-reported appraisal quality (β =.71 in the method-adjusted model). Contrary to the “withdrawal–negligence” prediction of Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, turnover intention showed a small but significant positive direct association with appraisal rigor, and its interaction with attitudes was not statistically significant. The pattern is consistent with a “Lame Duck Objectivity” account in which anticipated exit releases managers from certain political constraints on evaluative candor, but reverse causality, statistical power, and measurement limitations remain plausible alternatives that the design cannot rule out. Originality/value: The study reframes managerial withdrawal as a scope condition of COR rather than a uniform trigger of task disengagement, and it demonstrates the utility of a higher-order attitudinal factor for handling discriminant-validity breakdown in hospitality data. Title: Leaning into risk: How slanted typeface logos increase perceived risk of efficacious products
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Marketing practice commonly uses slanted typeface logos on product packaging to convey movement and vitality, yet existing research has paid limited attention to the potential conflict between this low-level visual feature and the core claims of specific products. Drawing on the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), this research examines when and why slanted typeface logos on packaging increase consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products, revealing the underlying mechanism and boundary condition. Across three controlled experiments and one incentive-compatible experiment, this research manipulates the form of typeface logos on packaging and evaluates its effects and subsequent behavioral responses. Study 1 shows that, compared with an upright typeface logo, a slanted typeface logo increases consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products. Study 2 supports the mediating role of design instability: a slanted typeface logo triggers a visually perceived sense of imbalance, which further induces consumers’ risk inferences about the product; meanwhile, arousal, perceived movement, and perceptual fluency do not emerge as significant mediating mechanisms. Study 3 identifies the moderating role of cognitive load, showing that high cognitive load amplifies the effect of a slanted typeface logo on perceived risk. Study 4 further provides behavioral evidence through an incentive-compatible experiment, showing that consumers are less likely to choose the product in the slanted typeface logo condition. Overall, this research reveals a boundary of the visual marketing principle that “slanting implies vitality” in the context of efficacious products. These findings enrich theoretical understanding of the boundary conditions under which peripheral visual cues operate within the ELM framework and offer practical implications for the context-specific management of brand visual identity systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Transforming hospitality and tourism services through artificial intelligence: The influence of experiential dimensions on user satisfaction, continuance intentions, and word-of-mouth

Title: How contribution streaks form and their role in long-term retention in OSS projects
Abstract: Contributor turnover is a major challenge in open-source software (OSS) projects, affecting project sustainability, quality, and many other dimensions of project performance. Although turnover has been widely studied in the OSS context, the importance of sustained contribution periods to long-term contributor survival remains poorly understood. In this context, contributor survival refers to the probability of sustained activity over time. We investigate the effect of contribution streaks, defined as consecutive months of contribution, on long-term survival, and analyze what kind of engagement, at different levels of ownership, predicts short-term contribution streaks. Using five years of data from 14 open-source projects, we applied landmark analysis to understand long-term survival based on peak streak lengths and logistic regression to identify the activities supporting short-term streaks. In both cases, we identified a three-month contribution streak to be an important threshold for sustained contributions. We found that development and communication related activities across ownership levels are important predictors of whether contributors continue their streaks, even though the relative importance shifts over time. In addition, we found that prior experience plays a stronger role early on, but its effect diminishes during later streak months. These findings suggest that contribution streaks are important predictors of long-term survival and provide practical insights for open-source practitioners on how to improve the retention of new and existing contributors through supporting short-term contribution streaks. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Hard-work orientation as an individual difference: Passion and subjective vitality as sequential mechanisms of student engagement
Abstract: Effort has a well-documented dark side: excessive work has been linked to burnout, and persistence after failure to hopelessness. Effort is also an individual difference, in that people vary in how strongly they believe effort is valuable and necessary for achievement. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study asks why an effort-oriented disposition might generate psychological resources rather than deplete them. Passion and subjective vitality were tested as a sequential motivational and energetic process linking hard-work orientation to student engagement, using three-wave time-lagged data from 524 students in northern India. Title: A Block-Wise Updating Strategy for Approximate Duplicate Detection
Abstract: Approximate duplicate detection in data streams aims to determine whether an item is present within a small subsequence of the data stream. It is a fundamental query problem needed in several network applications, such as web crawling and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tag management. Most of the existing algorithms are not space-efficient as they overlook the distributional information of query frequency and membership likelihood. In this paper, we propose CEll Bloom Filter (CEBF) algorithm, a space-efficient data structure designed by adopting a block-wise updating strategy, to solve this problem, and two typical distributions are considered: two typical distributions: (1) uniform query frequency of items, and (2) uniform membership likelihood of items. For an arbitrary sliding window size n and an arbitrary average false positive rate ε ∈ (0, 1), the proposed algorithm needs approximately O(nlog2(1/ε)) bits, which is significantly less than the number of bits used in existing methods. Space lower bound is also derived for these two typical distributions, which demonstrates that the proposed algorithm is near-optimal in terms of space consumption. Experiments are conducted on both synthetic and real datasets, and the experimental results clearly demonstrate that the proposed method is clearly and significantly more effective and promising compared to existing other methods. © The author(s) 2027.

Title: Mathematical and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) investigation of thermo-hydraulic behaviour and cooling performance of an air-cooled server rack under steady information technology (IT) loads
Abstract: This study presents mathematical and three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) assessments of an operational 42U air-cooled server rack under five steady information technology (IT) loads from 10 to 20 kW. The principal contribution is not a new CFD algorithm, but a load-dependent integration of rack-scale thermal, hydraulic, turbulence, convective heat-transfer and facility-energy indicators within a single validated framework. The realizable k–ε model reproduced the measured thermal and hydraulic responses with R2 = 0.985–0.993 and a maximum Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) below 3.61%. Increasing IT load raised the maximum rack temperature from 307.6 to 328.8 K and the pressure drop from 35.2 to 68.1 Pa, while rack-average cooling effectiveness decreased from approximately 0.91 to 0.74, corresponding to an 18.7% reduction. Although the inlet condition remained unchanged, the Reynolds number remained approximately 1.92 × 105, whereas the Grashof number increased from 1.64 × 1010 to 3.76 × 1010 and the Richardson number from 0.45 to 1.02, demonstrating a progressive shift from predominantly forced convection toward mixed-convection behaviour. The resulting buoyancy-assisted redistribution promoted upper-rack recirculation, hotspot expansion and increasingly localized turbulence and convective cooling. Numerical energy closure remained above 97% for all cases. In contrast to the deteriorating rack-level thermal performance, facility Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) improved from 1.61 to 1.42 as IT utilization increased. This divergence shows that minimum PUE does not necessarily correspond to the thermally preferable operating state. For the investigated configuration, 15–17.5 kW is therefore identified as a practical compromise operating range between facility energy utilization and rack-level thermal reliability, rather than a universal optimum. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Improved sinh–cosh optimizer for photovoltaic parameter identification

Title: Environmental qualities in green and natural spaces: Fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature as pathways to perceived visit-related health benefits
Abstract: Rising levels of stress and mental ill-health have intensified interest in nature-based public health approaches, including green social prescribing and nature as medicine. However, it remains unclear whether different environmental qualities are associated with different aspects of visit experience, and how these experiences relate to perceived visit-related health benefits. This study examined direct associations of biodiversity, safety, accessibility and cleanliness problems with perceived visit-related health benefits, and indirect associations involving fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature. Cross-sectional data from 19,814 adults in England who reported a recent visit to a green or natural space in the People and Nature Survey (PaNS) were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). In the direct-effects model, biodiversity, safety and accessibility were positively associated with perceived visit-related health benefits, whereas cleanliness problems showed a negative association. Most of these direct associations were substantially attenuated when the two visit experiences were included, and both experiences were positively associated with perceived benefits. The pathway model also revealed differentiated associations across experiences, with safety most closely associated with fresh air / peace and tranquillity, biodiversity with feeling closer to nature, and cleanliness problems showing a negative indirect association through fresh air / peace and tranquillity. By considering qualities of the setting alongside experiences during the visit, the findings highlight the value of a quality-experience-benefit perspective in which different environmental qualities may show different patterns of association with perceived visit-related health benefits through particular visit experiences. Authors: Shi W.; Jin Y.
Title: THE VALUE OF RECOMMENDATIONS FROM SOCIAL MEDIA ANALYSTS IN ONLINE INVESTMENT COMMUNITIES
Abstract: This study examines the informational value of stock recommendations issued by social media analysts through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using comprehensive data from Seeking Alpha, we demonstrate that these recommendations significantly predict abnormal stock returns over a two-month horizon, with no subsequent reversal, suggesting that they convey incremental information not captured by sell-side analysts or textual sentiment. Guided by SDT, we further show that predictive accuracy varies systematically with analysts’ motivational contexts. Recommendations are more informative when issued by analysts identified as traders, whose direct financial stakes deepen the internalization of extrinsic incentives, and by analysts with high comment-section engagement, where interactive feedback supports needs for competence and relatedness. Conversely, predictive ability declines with longer platform tenure, consistent with motivational saturation as psychological needs become satisfied, and with higher posting frequency, where cognitive overload undermines need satisfaction. Finally, we find that both editorial selection and user-driven engagement effectively identify recommendations with greater ex-post informativeness. In an era of information abundance in online investment communities, our SDT-grounded analysis offers investors guidance for signal extraction and provides platform designers with principled insights for fostering higher-quality content ecosystems. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. Title: Predictive maintenance for aero-engine fleets integrating uncertainty-aware remaining useful life estimation and maintenance decisions
Abstract: Prognostics and health management plays a critical role in improving flight safety and reducing lifecycle costs in aero-engine systems. However, existing predictive maintenance studies generally focus on individual engines or treat remaining useful life (RUL) estimation and maintenance scheduling as separate processes, limiting their applicability to fleet-level operations under uncertain degradation conditions. To address this limitation, this study develops an end-to-end predictive maintenance framework that couples uncertainty-aware RUL estimation with multi-objective maintenance optimization for aero-engine fleets. First, an integrated deep learning model based on Transformer and Monte Carlo dropout is constructed to estimate the RUL and quantify its predictive uncertainty. The resulting uncertainty information is subsequently propagated into a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model through risk-related constraints, thereby establishing a closed-loop connection between the prediction and scheduling layers. The model simultaneously minimizes the total maintenance completion time and operating cost under maintenance-resource and sequencing constraints. An iterative ϵ-constraint method is employed to obtain exact Pareto solutions for small-scale fleet instances. For large-scale instances, a tailored multi-objective artificial bee colony algorithm integrated with Q-learning, termed MOABC-QL, is developed by redesigning the search operators, constraint-handling mechanism, and learning-based strategy selection. Unlike iterative methods that repeatedly invoke commercial solvers, MOABC-QL directly approximates the Pareto front with reduced computational overhead. Title: Ready to blossom? African city skylines, an empirical puzzle, and a proposed solution
Abstract: This paper shows that global skyscraper construction both accelerated and globalized after the 2001 attacks on the Twin Towers in New York, into the twenty-first century. Despite being increasingly incorporated into the global economy as a ‘new frontier’ for global investors, Sub Saharan Africa (SSA) did not share in this construction boom. This paper demonstrates that the absence of skyscrapers in SSA is an empirical puzzle. The key drivers of skyscraper construction – economic growth, population increase and migration, globalization, and vanity-driven competition – should all be pushing SSA into building upwards. The key to resolving the empirical puzzle of why SSA doesn't build skyscrapers lies in land markets: better functioning land markets would directly increase the supply and indirectly increase the demand for skyscrapers. This paper suggests a mechanism to allow city governments to focus their capacity on protecting the property rights of developers building skyscrapers, allowing a skyscraper project to be granted the status of a standalone Special Economic Zone (SEZ). The resulting construction of skyscrapers may simply increase the supply of luxury residential accommodation and office space and displace any pre-existing informal construction to a less advantageous location on the city periphery. The demand for formal residential accommodation is also influenced by more than price – culture matters. Consequently, the paper concludes by noting that inclusive or affordable housing construction needs to be rooted in a more holistic development strategy. © 2026 .

Title: The prompt-response paradox: A cybernetic perspective of generative artificial intelligence usage and corner-cutting behavior

Abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. While existing GenAI literature has largely focused on the scale, frequency, and operational patterns of its application, it has largely overlooked the inherent imbalances within these P-R cycles. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. Title: Beyond the noise: Early identification of emerging technologies through weak signal prediction in higher-order networks
Abstract: The early identification of emerging technologies from weak signals is a critical strategic imperative. Existing network-based methods remain largely confined to lower-order representations and static, snapshot-based conceptualizations of weak signals, emphasizing retrospective detection over prospective prediction. The ICL-LLM achieves the best predictive performance among the tested models, with a Macro-F1 score of 61.25%, outperforming the MLP (49.76%), DHCN (56.84%), and ZS-LLM (46.35%). Title: Corporate strategy for the green transition: Are executive incentives effective?
Abstract: This paper examines whether green incentives embedded in executive compensation schemes are associated with a reorientation of firms' innovative activities toward environmentally sustainable technologies. Drawing on agency theory and the attention-based view of the firm, we conceptualize green incentives as governance and management-control devices that can mitigate managerial short-termism and channel executive attention toward long-horizon environmental objectives, thereby redirecting firms' technological search. Using a panel of publicly listed U.S. and European firms that participate in the Carbon Disclosure Project over the period 2010–2020, we analyse green innovation as a multi-stage process comprising the reorientation of technological search (the distance of firms' patent portfolios from green domains), knowledge recombination (the citation of green prior art in non-green patents), and realized green innovation output (green patent counts and shares). Title: Policy-driven electrification in rural areas: Integrating carbon pricing and activity-based costing in strategic decision models
Abstract: Rural electrification is essential for sustainable development; however, balancing upfront infrastructure investment, carbon reduction, and long-term economic performance remains a significant decision problem. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework that combines Activity-Based Costing (ABC), carbon taxation, and optimization modeling to compare Progressive Replacement, Hybrid Carbon Market Electrification, and One-Time Replacement. Sensitivity analysis further indicates that One-Time Replacement remains the lower-cost strategy across the reported carbon-tax and discount-rate scenarios. Title: Institutional co-development cues in retail food choice: Reducing perceived risk in alternative protein acceptance

Title: Conceptualising a scale to measure customers’ off-premise dining experience (OPDineX) with third-party food delivery services
Abstract: Third-party food delivery services (TPFDs) have reshaped how consumers experience restaurant meals. Addressing this gap, this study develops and validates the OPDineX scale as a unified, journey‑based measure capturing customers’ holistic experience with salient attributes across pre‑meal, in‑meal, and post‑meal phases. The study followed a four-stage scale development process, and qualitative item generation and refinement were combined with four quantitative studies conducted in Australia and Singapore. The resulting OPDineX scale comprises eight dimensions and demonstrates strong reliability, convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity, as well as measurement invariance across contexts. Title: Ethics practices in ai development: An empirical study across roles and regions

Title: Evaluation of cost reduction effects by sector-coupling synergies in timber processing and bioenergy for sustainable forestry in Japan
Abstract: The greenhouse gas sequestration capacity of forests is an important pillar in combating global warming; therefore establishing a forest resource circulation system is crucial. Forestry, which includes everything from cultivation to harvesting forests that store carbon dioxide as they grow, and the sawmill industry, which processes this timber, frequently face significant economic challenges. It evaluates the economic interdependence between timber processing and energy utilization when all wood is harvested from forests and both uses are combined. Additionally, using inexpensive electricity from biomass power generation for sawmilling lowers sawmill costs. Title: Vibe Coding: An experiment with test-driven development
Abstract: Context: Conversational Large Language Models (CLLMs) can automatically generate code by collaborating with users through natural language. However, poor collaboration can lead to poor quality output. Objective: This exploratory study aims to investigate how humans and CLLMs can collaborate as peers through vibe coding, an approach that integrates principles from prompt engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation to enhance collaboration. Method: We designed four interaction models representing different collaboration patterns in the software development process: the solo model (human-only development), the collaborative model (human–CLLM collaboration), the fully automated model (development autonomously performed by a CLLM), and the agentic model (development autonomously performed by the MetaGPT X platform). Based on these models, we implemented corresponding Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflows using structured prompts and Python scripts. We then conducted a controlled pre-experimental study with TDD professionals to compare the solo and collaborative workflows. In addition, we performed repeated exploratory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on the same development tasks to obtain complementary evidence. Results: Our findings suggest that the choice of interaction model should depend on the development objective. Agentic workflows are best suited for rapid development and functionally correct production code but may introduce additional implementation complexity. However, they may also introduce additional implementation decisions that are not explicitly required by the functional specifications, resulting in untested decision points. In contrast, collaborative workflows produce higher-quality, better-organized test suites. Conclusions: Our work explored how humans can collaborate with CLLMs in generating code in highly intensive and demanding development process. Our results also show that accurately reproducing development process workflows is yet an open problem, also in the new agentic technologies. © The Author(s) 2026.
