Title: Software-defined vehicle ecosystems in transformation
Abstract: Context: The automotive industry is transitioning from hardware-centric development toward software-defined vehicles (SDVs), where software drives functionality, value creation, and competitive differentiation. This shift challenges proprietary software development, firm-centric innovation, and traditional supply chain models, giving rise to ecosystem-based collaboration. However, SDV transformation is primarily framed as a technical change, leaving its broader ecosystem implications insufficiently understood. Objective: This study explores the transformation of SDV ecosystems, their stakeholders, collaborative structures, roles and authority, and highlights associated challenges and opportunities. Methods: This systematic literature review collected 351 studies from six databases and selected 25 for detailed analysis. Results: Four interrelated shifts (from hardware-centric to software platforms, from supply chains to collaborative ecosystems, from proprietary to open and standard solutions, and from firm-level control to distributed governance) characterise the transformation, with six levels of collaboration involving twelve stakeholder groups. These collaborations are influenced by five dimensions of authority. The literature also highlights six core software development challenges and various organisational, industry and market, and regulatory, legal, and ethical challenges. It identifies five software development opportunities and various organisational, industry and market, and public value and ethical opportunities. Conclusion: The first contribution integrates previously fragmented literature on the SDV ecosystem transformation, demonstrating how SDVs are transforming the automotive industry through the four interrelated shifts driven by software advancements. Second, it proposes an SDV ecosystems model that integrates SDV architecture, stakeholder groups, collaboration structures, and governance levels to facilitate sustainable SDV ecosystems. Additionally, agendas for research and practice are outlined. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Structural Determinants of Household Resilience in Earthquake-Affected Communities: A Case Study from Bawean Island
Abstract: This study examines the socioeconomic impacts of the March 2024 earthquake on household resilience in Bawean Island, East Java, Indonesia. Data for this study were collected through a survey with a snowball sampling technique, with a total of 221 valid respondents from affected regions. Using a household survey across 12 affected villages and partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), the study identifies critical factors contributing to household resilience, namely social, economic, human, and physical capital assets. The findings can be explained in two ways. First, the result confirms social, economic, human, and physical capital as critical resilience determinants. Second, higher household resilience could reduce the impact of natural disasters. This study can be an input for policymakers to strengthen household resilience in disaster-prone areas to support sustainable development goals (SDGs). © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Participatory short film production and student well-being: A narrative review from media literacy and sociocultural perspectives
Abstract: In an AI-driven media ecology, short-form video platforms have intensified interest in participatory filmmaking (PFM) as a learner-centered practice in higher education. However, the relationship between student-led short-film production and holistic well-being remains conceptually scattered and methodologically uneven. This narrative review examines how PFM may support student well-being through media literacy and sociocultural learning processes, with particular attention given to the transferability of these mechanisms to Chinese higher education. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2025 were searched in Scopus, Web of Science, and CNKI using combinations of “participatory video,” “filmmaking,” “higher education,” and “well-being.” A total of 238 records were screened. Studies were excluded if they focused on non-higher-education settings, addressed media consumption rather than student production, contained no interpretable well-being-related outcomes, or lacked peer-reviewed empirical content. Fifteen studies were retained for full analysis. Data were extracted on context, modality, participants, methods, well-being domains, and pedagogical mechanisms and then coded through a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke and sensitized by media literacy and sociocultural theory. Three recurring mechanisms emerged: reflective authorship, which supports meaning making, critical judgment, and psychological resilience; collaborative scaffolding, which strengthens belonging, shared regulation, and social confidence; and embodied practice, which connects tool-mediated action to attention, physical vitality, and situated learning. However, the evidence base remains small, course bound, and dominated by short-term qualitative designs, with limited work in non-Western settings. This review therefore proposes the participatory filmmaking well-being framework (PFWF) as an empirically anchored synthesis and outlines implications for curriculum design, student support, and future mechanism-testing research in Chinese universities. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: The fantasy of digital immateriality: AI, ecologically unequal exchange, and appropriation of lived human time
Abstract: The purported immateriality of AI technologies is as illusory as the general understanding of conventional technologies as simply the application of politically neutral knowledge to nature. The materiality of technologies and their foundation in global inequalities has been illuminated by studies of ecologically unequal exchange (EUE). The aim of this article is to extend the applicability of EUE theory to digital technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) by highlighting how even the data that they process have an inevitably biophysical history. AI technologies represent a novelty mainly in the sense that, in addition to exploiting extractive areas through EUE, they are based on the appropriation of data from the public. We argue for understanding the materiality of data as derived from lived human time. AI's dependence on data can thus be regarded as representing and embodying biophysical processes and asymmetric transfers implicating issues of justice. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. Title: The impact of reverse wording on cross-cultural comparisons of food-related attitudes
Abstract: Reverse-worded items (RWIs) are commonly used in multi-item scales to reduce acquiescence bias, yet their implications for cross-cultural food attitude measurement remain underexamined. This study compared positively worded items (PWIs) and RWIs across four established food-related attitude scales using data from 6300 adult consumers across ten countries. RWIs generally showed lower internal consistency and weaker inter-item correlations than PWIs. Items showing the largest cross-country variation in standardized loadings from multi-group confirmatory factor analysis were predominantly reverse-worded. RWIs also produced lower mean scores and generally greater response dispersion than PWIs. These wording-related differences varied by construct and country, followed no uniform pattern across measurement indicators, and may reflect the combined influence of item content, linguistic structure, and culturally patterned response tendencies. Across these indicators, PWI and RWI subsets did not consistently function as psychometrically equivalent components of the same scale. The findings suggest that the use of RWIs in cross-cultural food attitude measurement may introduce wording-related measurement instability, and that wording-direction effects require explicit consideration in the design and evaluation of international consumer research instruments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The grass is not always greener: The effects of local labor market information on search and employment
Abstract: We examine how information about local labor market conditions shapes search and employment outcomes for Indian job seekers. Treated respondents are more likely to be employed seven months later. This overall effect varies considerably by baseline employment status. Among the initially employed, treatments reduce search off the portal and increase employment, with suggestive evidence of higher persistence in baseline jobs. In contrast, among the initially unemployed, treatments increase search activity but do not raise employment. Abstract: The current study establishes how lean tenets contribute to the circular economy (CE) with exploration of lean tools with circular economy core principles and framework development. Also, the lean tenets and their allied tools enabled value optimization through effective mapping of non-value-added processes and minimizing wasteful aspects. These findings are intended to inform engineers, construction managers, and legal practitioners about actionable strategies for promoting sustainable, legally compliant project execution. Title: Hidden Markov Model variants for prognostics: A comprehensive review and model selection framework
Abstract: This paper reviews and systematizes the use of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and their semi-Markov extensions for prognostics within Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). It argues that prognostic models should be evaluated not only by prediction error but also by four key characteristics: uncertainty quantification, robustness, interpretability, and feasibility. The review organizes HMM-based methods into three groups: standard HMMs, Hidden Semi-Markov Models (HSMMs), and non-homogeneous HSMMs. Each group is assessed based on how it contributes to the four characteristics. Building on this analysis, the paper formalizes four representative models under a common notation for prognostics: HMM, HSMM, Adaptive HSMM (AHSMM), and Similarity Learning HSMM (SLHSMM). These models are benchmarked on the C-MAPSS turbofan dataset and on impacted open-hole composite specimens to evaluate both controlled and out-of-distribution scenarios. Results show that SLHSMM achieves the highest accuracy and provides sharper, well-calibrated uncertainty when test trajectories resemble training patterns. In contrast, AHSMM shows greater robustness to unexpected shifts and impact-induced behaviors. HMM and HSMM remain attractive choices when simplicity and computational efficiency are most important. The study concludes with practical guidance for selecting among HMM-based approaches based on the four key characteristics required for real-world PHM applications. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Influence of environmental stimuli on sustainable food choices: the moderating role of AI-source disclosure
Abstract: Reducing meat consumption is necessary for public health and environmental sustainability. However, while the benefits of positively-valenced nature have been explored, the comparative behavioral effects and mediational patterns of positively-valenced and negatively-valenced environmental stimuli remain unclear. Across three studies, we examined how positively- and negatively-valenced environmental stimuli influence food choices. Study 1 showed that both types of environmental stimuli reduced meat-heavy meal choices compared to the control. Study 2 tested serial mediation models within a dual-system framework, and the results showed that positively-valenced stimuli were associated with stronger nature connectedness and greater consideration of future consequences (CFC), whereas negatively-valenced stimuli were associated with higher guilt and greater CFC. Study 3 manipulated AI-source disclosure for the environmental stimuli. Although AI-source disclosure did not significantly interact with environmental stimuli condition in predicting meat-heavy choices, it significantly attenuated the link between negatively-valenced stimuli and guilt, but did not attenuate the association between positively-valenced stimuli and nature connectedness. Collectively, these findings suggest that the environmental stimuli valence may be associated with food choices through two partially overlapping yet distinguishable psychological pathways, offering insights for nudging sustainable eating. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Text-driven causal mapping of PET/rPET circularity in Australia: A dynamic factor–network analysis
Abstract: PET circularity is often evaluated by recovery volumes, although performance ultimately depends on whether recovered material can be converted into quality-assured outputs and absorbed by viable end markets. Yet the mechanisms connecting policy, markets, technology, and stakeholder behavior remain dispersed across heterogeneous evidence. We developed a source-attributed, time-stamped causal-network approach using 750 Australian government, industry and NGO, corporate, and media documents published during 2010–2025. Causal extraction, semantic normalization, sentiment assignment, and graph construction yielded 2794 factor nodes and 1588 unique causal edges. The network was strongly externalized: policy, market, and social factors were more numerous and highly connected than internal technical and operational factors. Persistent barriers combined cost and price volatility, inconsistent recyclate quality, infrastructure gaps, and weak policy implementation. Positive mechanisms clustered around standards and measurement, design for recyclability, operational capacity, and end-market development; their circular value depended on retained material quality and the end use reached. Source attribution revealed systematic framing differences, with media coverage concentrating negative implementation narratives. Temporal and regional analyses indicated a shift from limited attention to rapid expansion and subsequent consolidation, alongside national structural hubs and differentiated state pathways. A full-text academic shadow corpus preserved the broad problem domains but changed their hierarchy: academic evidence foregrounded material and processing mechanisms, whereas the primary corpus foregrounded institutional coordination and market implementation. The contribution is therefore not a universal ranking of Australian interventions, but an auditable framework for identifying how technical feasibility becomes, or fails to become, operational circularity under different institutional conditions. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Hedging against asset-heavy network expansion delays through rapid deployments of FACTS and BESS
Abstract: Transmission expansion delays represents a critical barrier to the timely and cost-effective development of modern power systems, particularly for integrating renewable energy. Although network congestions arising from postponed major infrastructure projects (e.g., new transmission lines) can severely impact system efficiency, these effects can be mitigated through the rapid deployment of flexible technologies such as FACTS devices and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). In this paper, we propose a two-stage stochastic optimization framework that complements first-stage, asset-intensive network expansion decisions with second-stage, scenario-dependent investments in flexible transmission assets, including FACTS and BESS. The formulation explicitly captures the probabilistic nature of project delays, accounting for zonal variations in the likelihood of such delays and their implications for system planning. Through a set of case studies, we demonstrate that the strategic use of FACTS and BESS can serve as an effective hedge against the adverse impacts of transmission expansion delays. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.
